detail.abstract: A cultura organizacional deixou de ser um discurso institucional para se tornar um campo de disputa real entre valores e práticas. A entrevista evidencia que o assédio e a discriminação não nascem nas empresas, mas são importados da sociedade — e é justamente por isso que as organizações têm o poder (e a responsabilidade) de interromper esse ciclo. Mais do que compliance, trata-se de coerência: empresas que não toleram comportamentos antiéticos precisam provar isso em decisões difíceis, inclusive quando envolvem clientes ou reputações externas. Em um mundo hiperconectado, onde atitudes individuais viralizam e impactam marcas, a ética deixa de ser opcional e passa a ser estratégica. No fim, não são os discursos que transformam culturas, mas as escolhas que as empresas têm coragem de sustentar.

detail.title: Human-AI Interaction in Creative Tasks: an Experimental Investigation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Department of Economics Research Paper Series No. 16/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Department of Economics, Ca' Foscari University of Venice Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We investigate how generative AI shapes creative performance and human-AI interaction in an open-ended writing task that employs a laboratory experiment in which participants are randomly assigned to either receive access to a large language model (ChatGPT-4.2) or not. Creative performance is measured by the average score assigned by independent evaluators recruited through the Prolific platform, and detailed logs of human-AI interaction are analyzed to measure AI use, prompting intensity, ideation requests, and the textual overlap between AI outputs and participants' final writings. Three main results emerge. First, AI access increases performance, but the gain is entirely driven by active use: participants with access who do not submit queries perform no better than those without AI. Second, the relationship between interaction intensity and performance is concave, peaking at roughly eight queries, consistent with iterative exploration rather than mechanical copying. Third, structural mediation analyses show that ideation requests affect performance primarily indirectly, by increasing downstream incorporation of AI-generated language; the direct effect of requesting an idea from the AI is negligible once execution-stage reliance is accounted for. We further document heterogeneity in AI reliance: cultural capital (proxied by books owned) predicts lower AI use, while prior AI exposure predicts higher use. By contrast, incentive schemes have limited effects on both outcomes and AI-related behaviors.

title: Who Decides When Algorithms Advise? The Empowerment Paradox in Consumer Choice

detail.title: Who Decides When Algorithms Advise? The Empowerment Paradox in Consumer Choice

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual paper and no human participants were involved.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Consumer decision-making research rests on a foundational assumption now under threat: that individuals meaningfully exercise agency over their choices. Algorithmic systems have moved beyond advising consumers to acting on their behalf. This article introduces an empowerment paradox, that the act of cognitive delegation that boosts perceived competence simultaneously erodes experienced agency and psychological ownership. Drawing on Power-Dependence Theory and Self-Determination Theory, we argue that structural reliance on algorithmic decision support satisfies the need for competence while frustrating the need for autonomy. This paradox is progressive, as each act of delegation normalises the next and weakens expectations of volitional control. We develop a conceptual framework specifying mechanisms, boundary conditions and design responses through which firms and policymakers can preserve consumer agency while retaining efficiency gains. The analysis has implications for consumer satisfaction, loyalty, trust and market functioning, and reframes algorithmically mediated choice as a tension between personal autonomy and operational efficiency.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the key factors influencing tourism consumer behaviour in Bangladesh, with a particular focus on the decision-making process of domestic tourists. A structured questionnaire survey was conducted among 83 respondents to identify the determinants of destination choice, travel patterns, and overall satisfaction. The study employs descriptive statistics and chi-square tests to analyse the collected primary data. Findings reveal that natural beauty, safety and security, price, and recommendations from friends and family are the most influential factors in travel decision-making. Sea Beach destinations, particularly Cox's Bazar, remain the most preferred among Bangladeshi tourists. The majority of respondents expressed a moderate to high level of satisfaction with their tourism experiences. The study provides practical implications for tourism marketers and policymakers in Bangladesh aiming to enhance the domestic tourism experience.

detail.abstract: Grounded in the practice of China's engineering construction sector, this study takes the mediating role of the tendering and bidding system as an innovative entry point. By conducting a systematic analysis that accounts for differences in stages of social development, the research uncovers and formalizes the macro-micro dual characteristic inherent in the scale of aggregate social fixed asset investment. The study originally proposes the 'Dual Demand + Dual Constraints Theory'. A theoretical function comprising only two parameters—"Human Resources-Investment Scale"—is constructed, alongside conversion formulas between macro and micro perspectives, thereby forming an analytically solvable theoretical model. The study overcomes the disciplinary barriers surrounding "Human Resources-Investment Scale", and the constructed theoretical model is concise and practical. At this stage, the research has only achieved the construction of the theoretical model; the two core parameters have not yet been assigned quantitative values. In the next phase, once the two parameters have been quantified, this theoretical model can be directly advanced into a quantitative model of "Human Resources-Investment Scale", providing practical decision-making references for the annual estimation, medium- to long-term planning, and forecasting of aggregate social fixed asset investment.

title: AI and Public Safety: Detecting Online Radicalization

detail.title: AI and Public Safety: Detecting Online Radicalization

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
Background: Online radicalization poses a serious challenge to public safety in the contemporary digital era. Social media platforms, applications allowing message encryption, and anonymous imageboards are serving as channels for extremist ideologies, allowing swift distribution of radicalizing content and the establishment of groups that normalize political violence. Conventional rule-based monitoring systems that are predicated on lists with predefined keywords and pattern-matching heuristics, have shown inadequate efficiency against the complex, changing linguistic techniques utilized by extremist players.

Objective: This research examines whether AI-based natural language processing (NLP) models considerably surpass conventional rule-based systems in the identification of online radicalization across different ideological groups and digital platforms, and whether AI-driven identification at an early stage leads to quantifiable drop in the growth of extremist engagement behaviors.

Methods: A quantitative methodology was adopted, which relied on a multi-platform comparative investigation of a carefully selected and organized dataset of 690 user posts obtained from platforms including Twitter/X, Telegram, Reddit, Discord, Facebook, and 4chan. Annotation of posts was done through a four-stage radicalization framework and organized across five ideological groups. A total of five AI/ML models were tested against two conventional rule-based baseline systems. These models were BERT, RoBERTa, LSTM, GPT (fine-tuned), and an Ensemble Hybrid. Efficiency of identification was evaluated through standard NLP indicators including precision, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and recall. In addition to this, evaluation also incorporated time-to-detection metrics. Results of growth in extremist behavior were monitored across groups that were categorized on the basis of stage of intervention and adopted identification methods.

Results: The Ensemble Hybrid model secured an F1-score of 0.9748, precision of 0.9508, and recall of 1.000. In comparison to this, the best rule-based system's F1-score was 0.6558. AI models exhibited an average identification rate of Day 4.8 following radicalization onset, compared to Day 10.1 for rule-based systems, indicating a statistically significant difference (p < 0.001). Groups that got Stage 1 AI identification had 78.0% less growth in engagement than those that got Stage 2 rule-based identification, which stood at only 20.3%. The success rate of deradicalization was 68.1% for AI early-identification groups and 32.1% for rule-based groups.

Conclusion: AI-based NLP models show statistically and pragmatically significant advantage as compared to rule-based monitoring in all performance areas that were examined. Early AI identification is strongly linked to a lower risk of radicalization. These results have significant impact on counter-terrorism policy, content moderation on platforms, and the ethical regulation of AI in the domain of public safety. Future research should focus on cross-lingual radicalization, adversarial evasion, and the equitable reduction of bias.

detail.abstract: This study examines tourist perceptions of destination hospitality in Kashmir through qualitative secondary data analysis of online reviews for four major destinations: Srinagar, Gulmarg, Pahalgam, and Sonmarg. Drawing on hospitality frameworks centred on hospitable behaviour, atmosphere and safety, and infrastructure and services, the study identifies recurring patterns in visitor experience and satisfaction. Findings indicate that while natural scenery and local warmth are consistently praised, infrastructure gaps and safety perceptions remain influential in shaping the overall destination image. The interplay between service quality, local hospitality, and perceived safety is discussed, and targeted recommendations are offered for tourism stakeholders in the region. Directions for future research in destination management are also proposed.

title: The Hidden Value Creation: On Cognitive Capacity as a Socioeconomic Resource

detail.title: The Hidden Value Creation: On Cognitive Capacity as a Socioeconomic Resource

detail.abstract:
Sarah is a nurse with moderate debt and a tight budget. David is a management consultant with a high salary and no debt. Society's verdict: David is thriving, Sarah is struggling. Both verdicts look in the wrong place.

This paper argues that external measures — income, debt, employment — capture only one dimension of human capacity. A second dimension exists, is systematically eroded, and has never been measured: whether a person actually has cognitive capacity available, or whether it is quietly consumed by structures not designed for them. The article advances four observations as hypotheses open to empirical testing.

We introduce two concepts. Cognitive realisation is the process of bringing forward capacity that exists but has been made unavailable by structural burden. Capability erosion is the mechanism that explains why it disappears — the gradual breakdown of cognitive capacity when people function over time in conditions that work against them.

The mechanism is well-documented. Sustained financial stress activates an alarm response that does not switch off, consuming the same capacity that drives judgement, creativity, and contribution. Sarah and David are not edge cases. This dynamic is universal.

The cost is large and unmeasured. Every person running on depleted capacity is a gap between what is and what could be — across families, workplaces, and nations. Societies have spent centuries measuring what is visible. They have never measured what drives it.

Drawing on behavioural economics (Mullainathan & Shafir, 2013; Mani et al., 2013), the capabilities approach (Sen, 1999; Nussbaum, 2000), self-determination theory (Ryan & Deci, 2000), stress physiology (McEwen & Stellar, 1993) and research on creative capacity (Florida, 2002, 2017), we argue that societies failing to realise the full cognitive potential of their population are not merely unjust — they are inefficient. This is a position paper and working hypothesis. Formal empirical validation is planned as the next phase.

title: Customer Satisfaction of Women Commuters: A Comparative Study of Rapido and Pink Rapido Services in Chennai
affiliations: Shanmugha Arts, Science, Technology & Research Academy (SASTRA) - SASTRA Deemed University and Shanmugha Arts, Science, Technology & Research Academy (SASTRA) - SASTRA Deemed University

detail.title: Customer Satisfaction of Women Commuters: A Comparative Study of Rapido and Pink Rapido Services in Chennai
detail.abstract: This study examines customer satisfaction among women commuters using Rapido and Pink Rapido services in Chennai, with specific reference to service quality dimensions derived from the SERVQUAL framework-Tangibility, Reliability, Responsiveness, Assurance, and Empathy. The study adopts a comparative and quantitative research design. Primary data were collected from 309 respondents, of which 150 responses were obtained through physical questionnaires and 159 through online Google Forms, ensuring coverage across different user groups. The analysis was carried out using SPSS. Focusing on the two core inferential analyses, correlation analysis indicated significant positive relationships among all service quality dimensions. Multiple regression analysis identified Reliability, Responsiveness, Assurance, and Empathy as significant predictors of customer satisfaction, while Tangibility was found to be statistically insignificant. Among the predictors, Assurance showed the highest influence, followed by Empathy, Responsiveness, and Reliability. The findings suggest that customer satisfaction in bike taxi services is primarily influenced by factors related to trust, safety, and service interaction rather than physical aspects.

title: Managing Creator Dependence on Follower-Targeted Recommendation: Evidence from a Field Experiment
affiliations: Peking University,  and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Managing Creator Dependence on Follower-Targeted Recommendation: Evidence from a Field Experiment
detail.abstract: Problem Definition: Follower-targeted recommendation is a default allocation strategy on most content-sharing platforms, yet its causal value to individual creators is not well understood. Delivering content to existing followers generates reliable engagement but, under finite recommendation capacity, reduces the exposure available for new-audience discovery that could sustain creator growth and long-run ecosystem vitality. This paper studies how platforms should manage this tradeoff when creator dependence is heterogeneous. Methodology/Results: Using a large-scale randomized experiment involving 584,741 creators on a major short-video platform, we estimate the causal effect of restricting follower-targeted recommendation. On average, blocking follower-feed reduces engagement but increases new follower acquisition, consistent with an aggregate exploitation--exploration tradeoff. However, these average effects mask substantial heterogeneity. Combining the experiment with double machine learning, we recover creator-level causal dependence and show that dependence-based targeting materially outperforms scale-based heuristics such as follower count. The results imply that observable creator size is an incomplete proxy for vulnerability to follower-feed removal. We further show that the apparent engagement--growth tradeoff is largely compositional rather than creator-specific: creators most harmed in engagement are typically also harmed in audience growth. As a result, explicit multi-objective targeting adds little aggregate value beyond dependence-based protection in our setting. Finally, because protecting a creator consumes recommendation capacity in proportion to follower scale, efficient reallocation requires combining causal dependence with capacity cost. We develop an exposure-efficiency rule based on capacity released per unit of engagement harm and show that it dominates policies based on either signal alone. Managerial Implications: Our findings reframe follower-feed governance from a uniform policy choice to an exposure-efficiency allocation problem and offer a practical rule for determining which creators to protect, which to transition, and at what cost.

detail.abstract: The transition of urban food delivery from a localized service to a globalized, platformmediated industry represents one of the most significant shifts in contemporary logistics. Platforms such as Uber Eats and Deliveroo have replaced traditional human-mediated dispatch systems with highly complex algorithmic architectures that synchronize millions of concurrent interactions across three independent sets of actors: consumers, merchants, and couriers.[1, 2, 3] This orchestration is predicated on the ability of digital systems to ingest vast streams of real-time geospatial and temporal data, converting physical movement into predictable, manageable units of labor and inventory.[4, 5] The resulting ecosystem is characterized by a constant tension between the pursuit of operational efficiency-often achieved through sub-second decision-making and predictive modeling-and the socioeconomic realities of the labor force that sustains it.[6, 7] Understanding this landscape requires a deep examination of the technical foundations of demand modeling, the logistics of dispatch and matching, the economic structures of rider earnings, and the evolving regulatory framework governing algorithmic management.[8, 9]

title: Unemployment Insurance Savings Accounts in a Labor Market with Informality
affiliations: , Insper Institute of Education and Research and Insper Institute of Education and Research

detail.title: Unemployment Insurance Savings Accounts in a Labor Market with Informality
detail.abstract: We develop a search and matching model with heterogeneous agents to study the effects of an unemployment insurance savings account (UISA) system on insurance provision and labor market outcomes in an economy with a high incidence of informal jobs. We discipline the model and incorporate several stylized facts about the informal sector through a calibration based on Brazilian microeconomic evidence. Quantitatively, we find that introducing a UISA design with the same benefit level but a longer duration than the baseline economy reduces consumption dispersion at the cost of lower job formalization. Despite the negative labor market effect, we show that the UISA design provides insurance to workers more efficiently vis-à-vis a traditional UI system because it internalizes the cost of remaining outside the formal sector. Finally, to improve the UISA design, we analyze the role of a more selective benefit provision mechanism in reducing these distortions.

title: Sun Hygiene: A Framework for Daily UV Protection as a Family Health Behaviour
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Sun Hygiene: A Framework for Daily UV Protection as a Family Health Behaviour
detail.abstract: Ultraviolet radiation is among the most pervasive and consistently underestimated environmental health risks facing families today. Rising skin cancer rates globally, combined with lifestyle patterns that increase cumulative UV exposure, make daily sun protection an increasingly urgent family health priority. Yet daily ultraviolet protection remains widely underpractised across families globally, despite growing awareness of UV-related skin damage. Existing frameworks address sun protection primarily as a clinical recommendation or a skincare behaviour, leaving the broader family population without a structured, named daily practice to adopt. This paper proposes sun hygiene as a distinct behavioural category, defined as the daily practice of protecting oneself and one's family from ultraviolet radiation through deliberate, consistent behaviour including sunscreen application, protective clothing, shade-seeking, and eyewear. Unlike other sun protective behaviours that carry natural physical triggers, sunscreen demands a deliberate daily decision made before any signal of damage appears. For lighter skin tones this signal is delayed. For darker skin tones it is muted, a phenomenon termed here the silent burn. Both conditions suppress daily adoption. This paper argues that advancing sun hygiene requires more than product innovation or awareness campaigns. It requires the right sunscreen designed for daily frictionless family use, paired with a behavioural framework as a single unit. Neither alone is sufficient. It further argues that the family is a particularly effective unit of adoption, as witnessed daily behaviour transfers across generations without deliberation, compounding in ways no other channel can replicate. Sun hygiene is presented here not as a reframing of existing concepts but as a first definition of a practice that has existed without a name, without a structure, and without the product infrastructure to support it.

title: Sequential Bias Contamination in Regulatory Investigations: An Overlooked Risk
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Sequential Bias Contamination in Regulatory Investigations: An Overlooked Risk
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the concept of Sequential Bias Contamination in regulatory investigations. Sequential Bias Contamination describes the process by which early assumptions, framing decisions, or incomplete information can become embedded in an investigative record and carried forward through later stages of regulatory review. As a matter moves from intake to investigation, legal review, decision-making, and possible adjudication, each stage may rely on the record created by the stage before it. If the record has been shaped by untested assumptions or premature framing, those assumptions may influence how later reviewers interpret evidence, assess credibility, and evaluate the seriousness of the matter.

The paper argues that this risk is not limited to individual cognitive bias. It can also arise from the structure of regulatory processes themselves, particularly where staged decision-making, file handoffs, summary records, and institutional risk aversion shape how information is collected, organized, and presented. While each individual decision may be defensible in isolation, the cumulative effect can distort the fairness and accuracy of the overall process.

The paper concludes that regulatory bodies should treat early framing, investigative scope, and record construction as key fairness issues. To reduce the risk of Sequential Bias Contamination, regulators should create opportunities to revisit assumptions, distinguish evidence from interpretation, maintain disciplined scope, and ensure later decision-makers are not unknowingly anchored to untested conclusions.

title: The Success of the Embedded State in England
affiliations: , Northwestern University, University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy and Harvard University

detail.title: The Success of the Embedded State in England
detail.abstract: Many states exhibit high degrees of capacity without the fiscal resources necessary to fund a modern bureaucracy. We argue that they achieve this by exploiting features of the social structure of the societies they govern to motivate individuals to engage in bureaucratic and governance tasks without pay. We develop and illustrate the concept of the "Embedded State" using a unique survey of British urban government from 1835. Since British local authorities had few resources, only two-thirds of positions were paid. We first show that unpaid positions were significantly more productive than paid ones. We then show that unpaid positions conveyed prestige and were 'stepping stone' positions, provided different on-the-job incentives, and were taken up by the socioeconomic elite. We also show that the successful Embedded State featured patronage and corruption and could not fully motivate unpaid bureaucrats to implement onerous tasks.

title: Think Twice Before You Sign! An Experiment on a Cautionary Function of Contractual Formalities
affiliations: Texas A&M University School of Law

detail.title: Think Twice Before You Sign! An Experiment on a Cautionary Function of Contractual Formalities

publicationDetails.detailsText: Texas A&M University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Texas A&M University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Legal scholarship has long maintained that contractual formalities, such as written signatures, serve a cautionary function by protecting individuals from entering into ill-considered agreements. With the rise of digital contracting, however, it remains unclear whether online forms of assent can fulfill this role. In an incentivized laboratory experiment, I compared four modes of contract conclusion: clicking "OK," typing one's name, entering a PIN code (analogous to a qualified e-signature), and handwritten signing. The study examined how these different forms of confirmation influence intertemporal choices between smaller-sooner and larger-later rewards. Specifically, I tested whether handwritten signatures promote greater patience, leading individuals to defer gratification in favor of larger future payoffs. The results show that participants were more impulsive when confirming by clicking "OK" or typing their name, compared to handwritten signing. By contrast, no significant differences emerged between handwritten signatures and entering a PIN code. These findings indicate that the most common digital confirmation methods do not replicate the cautionary effect of handwritten signatures, underscoring the need to develop alternative online mechanisms that could serve this function more effectively.

title: Technology Adoption and Optimal Policy
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics, Washington University in St. Louis and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond

detail.title: Technology Adoption and Optimal Policy
detail.abstract: We study optimal policy in a dynamic general equilibrium model where heterogeneous monopolistic competitive firms pay a fixed cost to adopt a frontier technology that grows exogenously. Using Mean Field Games tools, we show that the optimal policy consists of exactly two time-invariant subsidies: one correcting the static misallocation from market power, and one correcting the dynamic under-incentive to adopt. This holds outside of balanced growth paths, for any initial distribution of technology gaps. We analyze a simplified version of the model that aggregates to a Neoclassical Growth Model with an S-shaped production function whenever complementarities are strong, and fully characterize when the optimal policy uniquely implements the first best. When it does not, two novel results emerge: the efficient allocation prescribes escaping a poverty trap-providing an explicit optimality foundation for a Big Push-and, more surprisingly, escaping an abundance trap, where dismantling adopted technologies is optimal. In both cases, a temporary, costless supplementary policy restores unique implementation.

title: Audience Perception of National Broadcasting Commission's Regulatory Roles in Ogun State
affiliations: , Olabisi Onabanjo University (OOU) and Olabisi Onabanjo University (OOU)

detail.title: Audience Perception of National Broadcasting Commission's Regulatory Roles in Ogun State
detail.abstract:
This study x-rayed the extent to which The National Broadcasting Commission (NBC) has been carrying out her regulatory roles of the broadcast industry in Ogun State. This study adopted descriptive survey design with the use of questionnaire as research instrument for data collection. The study comprised residents of Ogun State across the three senatorial districts with a sample size of three hundred (300) respondents selected through a combination of stratified sampling and simple random sampling techniques. Data gathered from the field work were analyzed and presented using frequency distribution and simple percentage. Findings of the study showed, among many others, that Nigerian media content are believed to be within the control of NBC; Ogun state media houses operate within the modalities given by NBC and notably, radio stations in the state are in concordance with NBC policy that broadcast media programme content must be 100% locally sourced. The study, however concludes that, the deregulated Nigerian broadcasting environment has taken off brilliantly under the supervision of NBC. However, for effective delivery of professional services to the people and maintenance of sanity within the system, the agency's National Broadcasting Code must be allowed to operate in full force. The study, among others, recommended that more trainings and workshops should be facilitated for media practitioners so as to give room for more achievement in terms of professional practices; that double standard practices should be eschewed while politics should not allowed to determine the tone of practice.

 

 

 

Key words: National Broadcasting Commission (NBC) Audience, Radio, Television, Communication.

title: Financial Intermediation in SFEcon Model 3
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Financial Intermediation in SFEcon Model 3
detail.abstract:
SFEcon Model 0 demonstrated that ordinary marginalist causality suffices to control the efficient, stable adjustments of a generic input-output formulation to external stimuli. SFEcon Model 3 is a cumulative response to identified limitations of Model 0 as an instrument of policy. These issues inhere with the marginalist premise underlying our formal model of economic calculation, i.e.: marginalism cannot explicate economic agents having no calculable marginal cost of production.

Such is the case for those sectors whose products have no physical embodiment, e.g.: financial intermediaries, governments, and public sector dependents. But sectors having no readily tangible outputs do nonetheless consume assets, which does impact prices, and which thereby necessitates their differentiated presence in useful systems of economic calculation. 

As these sectors are becoming increasingly important, their demands on the economic system require distinct representations, even while their motives remain beyond marginalism’s capabilities to articulate.

This paper proposes expansions upon the familiar input-output framework so as to express a fully realized, detailed financial superstructure that efficiently guides SFEcon’s matrix presentations into general optimality. Model 3 reformulates the input-output notion as a rectangle rather a square. It integrates financial, government, and household sectors among its ordinary profit-motivated sectors; but it entails no representation for any product corresponding to those sectors for which the conception of profit remains elusive.

title: PUHCA 2.0
affiliations: Yale University - Law School

detail.title: PUHCA 2.0
detail.abstract: Many electric utilities today are vertically integrated and own both rate regulated (transmission and distribution) and competitive (generation) affiliates. This structure gives them incentives to make investments that favor their affiliated generators and shift risk onto captive ratepayers. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and state public utility commissions have adopted a variety of rules to address these concerns, including limits on affiliate transactions and functional unbundling requirements. Unfortunately, these requirements have failed to prevent utilities from using their control over grid infrastructure to benefit affiliates that participate in competitive markets. This Article therefore calls for a structural solution: a modern Public Utility Holding Company Act (PUHCA). It describes why Congress enacted PUHCA in 1935 to prevent cross-affiliate abuses, explains why those safeguards eroded over time, and argues that its repeal has left electricity markets vulnerable to the very harms it was designed to prevent. It then proposes four principles that should guide a modern PUHCA: separate monopoly networks from competitive generation, require independent system operators to run and plan the grid, limit multi-state holding company structures that shift costs across jurisdictions, and mandate transparent data so regulators can evaluate need and invite competitive alternatives. * © 2026 Joshua C. title: PUBLIC FUNCTION, PRIVATE IMMUNITY: THE CONSTITUTIONAL INFIRMITY OF SECTION 14(2) OF THE NATIONAL SPORTS GOVERNANCE ACT, 2025
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: PUBLIC FUNCTION, PRIVATE IMMUNITY: THE CONSTITUTIONAL INFIRMITY OF SECTION 14(2) OF THE NATIONAL SPORTS GOVERNANCE ACT, 2025

keywords: National Sports Governance Act 2025Right to Information

detail.abstract: The National Sports Governance Act, 2025 enacts a comprehensive regulatory framework for National Sports Bodies in India, declaring their governance, elections, ethics, athlete welfare, and dispute resolution to be matters of national public interest. Yet Section 14(2) of the Act confines RTI applicability to bodies receiving government funds, and even then, only with respect to the utilisation of those funds, insulating the most commercially dominant and publicly powerful sports bodies from the transparency obligations the Act otherwise professes. This article argues that S. 14(2) is constitutionally untenable on multiple converging grounds. Applying the three-fold proportionality test from K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, the provision fails at the second prong, there is no legitimate State aim the restriction serves, and fails independently at the third on the ground that the funding criterion is counterproductive to any conceivable legitimate objective. The provision further fails the intelligible differentia requirement under Article 14, whose differentia operates in inverse relationship to the very object it purports to serve. It defeats the legitimate expectations of athletes, citizens, and taxpayers arising from the Act's own recognition framework. And it is repugnant to the foundational premise of the statute that contains it. The article also examines the BCCI dimension: contemporaneous legislative record reveals that the amendment was introduced specifically to foreclose BCCI's RTI exposure, representing an attempt at legislative resolution of a constitutional question the courts were still deliberating. The article concludes that S. 14(2) is not merely inconsistent legislative policy — it is constitutionally ripe for challenge.

title: Eco-Friendly Extraction of Bioactive Compounds from Agricultural Biomass via Microbial Enzymatic Hydrolysis for Food Preservation Applications

detail.title: Eco-Friendly Extraction of Bioactive Compounds from Agricultural Biomass via Microbial Enzymatic Hydrolysis for Food Preservation Applications
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of the global agro-food sector has led to the generation of massive quantities of agricultural waste, often referred to as lignocellulosic biomass. Simultaneously, there is growing consumer concern regarding the adverse health effects of synthetic food preservatives. This research explores a sustainable "Green Chemistry" approach to address both challenges. The study investigates the efficacy of using specific microbial enzymes (Cellulases, Pectinases, and Xylanases) to hydrolyze the cell walls of agricultural residues (such as fruit peels and crop straw). The objective is to release bound phenolic compounds and antioxidants to be utilized as natural, safe antimicrobial agents in food systems. This bio-valorization strategy aims to reduce environmental pollution while providing high-value additives for the food industry.

title: Real options gaps in resilient supply chain design
affiliations: Novo Nordisk

detail.title: Real options gaps in resilient supply chain design
detail.abstract: Real options and resilient supply chain network design both study how firms should act under uncertainty, yet they have largely evolved along separate lines. The real options stream values managerial flexibility under volatile prices, exchange rates, demand, and sourcing conditions, usually through dynamic valuation models that treat switching, deferral, expansion, contraction, or abandonment as contingent rights. The resilient supply chain design stream, by contrast, studies how to configure networks that can absorb disruptions and recover at acceptable cost, usually through reliable facility location, stochastic programming, robust optimization, and fortification models. What remains thin is the literature that joins these two traditions into a unified theory and model class for resilient network design with endogenous flexibility value. The field therefore shows a striking asymmetry. Real options models are strong on timing, path dependence, and the value of waiting, but they usually simplify physical disruption processes, recovery, multi-echelon structure, and resilience measurement. Resilient network design models are strong on disruption scenarios, backup assignment, redundancy, and cost-based recourse, but they usually freeze strategic design at the initial stage and do not value staged adaptation as an option portfolio. This article maps those literatures, shows where they overlap, and identifies the gaps that a more integrated research agenda must address. The main conclusion is that the next frontier is not simply adding disruption terms to an option model or adding recourse to a stochastic network design model. The deeper gap lies in linking resilience as a dynamic recovery property with flexibility as a timed contingent claim. That requires models with richer uncertainty processes, multi-stage design revision, endogenous recovery, operational and financial hedging, and empirical calibration grounded in real network reconfiguration behavior. A field-level synthesis suggests that progress will come from hybrid models that combine the temporal discipline of real options with the structural realism of resilient network design.

title: Improving the Completeness and Comparability of Segment Disclosures: A Large Language Model Approach
affiliations: , Stanford University and University of Rochester

detail.title: Improving the Completeness and Comparability of Segment Disclosures: A Large Language Model Approach
detail.abstract: Segment-level disclosures are a central component of financial reporting, providing insight into firms' internal organization and the allocation of economic activities across operating units. However, segment information is often presented in both qualitative and quantitative forms, dispersed across tables and narrative sections of Form 10-K filings. Empirical research relying on structured databases faces both completeness and comparability challenges, as some firm-year observations may be missing, nested segment disclosures are not captured, and support for longitudinal and cross-firm comparability is limited. This study develops a large language model-based framework to extract segment disclosures directly from Form 10-K filings and to preserve both reportable and nested segment information. We further design a retrieval augmented system that incorporates information across multiple filings to support comparability. We use two representative settings to demonstrate its application: longitudinal analysis within a firm to interpret segment changes over time, and cross firm alignment of geographic segments across firms with different reporting structures. The results indicate that the artifact accurately extracts segment-level information and effectively addresses questions that require cross-period knowledge, demonstrating the potential of LLM-based approaches to enhance the measurement and interpretation of segment disclosures.

title: A comment on "Malleability of Preferences for Honesty" *
affiliations: University of Toronto - Department of Economics, McGill University, University of Haifa and Saint Mary's University

detail.title: A comment on "Malleability of Preferences for Honesty" *
detail.abstract: Abeler et al. (2025) report that enrolling children in a year-long mentoring program made them more honest, as measured by an experimental task in which they imagine a number and are rewarded if their self-reported number matches the outcome of a die-roll. The authors suggest that reported treatment effects are due to moderating a deficiency in the home environment in terms of warm parenting style and mother's trust. We examine these claims using the same data reported by the authors, with the caveat that we reconcile data definitions across tables. We reject the statistical significance of the point estimates reported by the authors for key outcomes. We examined the first three tables reported in the original paper. Table 1 uses a different subset of the data from Table 2 and Table 3. The treatment classification in the original paper is done with "intent to treat" (ITT). Our robustness checks report estimates for classification by "actually treated" (ATE). The original Table 1, using ITT and limited to untreated + unqualified children (N=348), shows warm parenting style and mother's trust increase honesty. The original Table 2, using ITT, adding treated and excluding unqualified subjects (N=394) shows a treatment effect, and the original Table 3, with the same sample as Table 2, shows significant interaction of treatment and warm parenting style. We attempt to reconcile the tables using a more uniform set of definitions. When we take the same sample of Tables 2 and 3 and apply it to Table 1, we lose the significance on warm parenting style-one of the main results on Table 1. When we apply the ATE definition of treatment instead of ITT, we lose the marginal significance reported in the original study for mother's trust in Table 1. Lastly, when we apply ATE to table 2, we completely lose the treatment effect. That is, when we compare the control and treatment, based on ATE, the treatment effect is insignificant.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops an integrated framework for assessing the financial security of banking institutions by combining capital adequacy, liquidity, asset quality, market risk, operational resilience, and managerial capacity into a unified analytical model. The study introduces a managerial component captured through a human capital stability coefficient (K_hr), reflecting governance quality and personnel stability.
The methodology applies normalization and weighted aggregation techniques to construct a composite Financial Security Index (FSI), enabling cross-institutional comparability and early-warning diagnostics. Unlike conventional approaches focused primarily on financial ratios, the proposed model incorporates institutional and governance dimensions, enhancing analytical depth and interpretability.
The framework aligns with international regulatory standards and supervisory practices and is adaptable to advanced financial systems, including the United States. The proposed approach contributes to improving financial stability assessment and strengthening risk governance in complex banking environments.

title: OPINION: Time to act to prevent foreign interference in Canadian elections
affiliations: Carleton University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: OPINION: Time to act to prevent foreign interference in Canadian elections
detail.abstract:
Abstract:
This article argues that the Hogue Commission has moved Canada’s foreign interference debate from speculation to an evidentiary record, showing that the principal threat lies not only in ballot manipulation but in the erosion of confidence, participation, and the information environment that makes democratic choice meaningful. It assesses Canada’s emerging response, including Bill C-70, the proposed foreign influence registry, election-security mechanisms, information monitoring networks, and the need for stronger protections against transnational repression. The article contends that Canada now requires both immediate implementation and deeper institutional redesign: a functioning registry and commissioner, clearer public communication protocols, improved riding-level intelligence briefings, stronger safeguards for nominations and leadership races, lawful open-source monitoring, and a meaningful complaints process. Its central claim is that Canada already has much of the blueprint; the urgent task is to operationalize it before foreign actors exploit remaining ambiguity.

title: ShinyEnet: An In-House Simulation Software for Data-Driven Waste-to-Energy Gasification and Pyrolysis

detail.title: ShinyEnet: An In-House Simulation Software for Data-Driven Waste-to-Energy Gasification and Pyrolysis
detail.abstract: ShinyEnet is an open-source software tool for modelling waste-to-energy processes, including gasification and pyrolysis. Developed at IT4Innovations, the National Supercomputing Centre of the Czech Republic at VSB-Technical University of Ostrava, it utilizes operational data from experimental facility at the Centre for Energy and Environmental Technologies-Explorer (CEETe), also part of the same university. The software models a modular, mobile, and scalable system that converts waste into gaseous or liquid fuels. ShinyEnet supports dynamic simulation, including component-failure cases, optimization, and scenario analysis. The platform thus facilitates development and assessment of compact and mobile waste-to-energy units and provides tools for addressing municipal waste-management challenges. ShinyEnet is based on real operational datasets, with continuously updated data currently available for the pyrolysis process via real-time monitoring system. The interactive web application is implemented using open-source Python libraries and employs validated historical data and machine-learning models to simulate and optimize system performance.

title: "Fading Frontiers: Unpacking Post-Materialist Societies and the Gender Gap in STEM Graduates Across OECD Nations."
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: "Fading Frontiers: Unpacking Post-Materialist Societies and the Gender Gap in STEM Graduates Across OECD Nations."

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict
declarations.ethicsApproval: No human subjects
declarations.funderStatement: No funder

detail.abstract: Although women now surpass men in overall higher education attainment across OECD countries, they remain persistently underrepresented among STEM graduates. This contradiction is most pronounced in advanced, gender-progressive societies. This study investigates how postmaterialist cultural values contribute to this paradox and shape cross-national differences in STEM gender gaps. We leverage longitudinal data from 26 OECD countries (1998-2015) and employ generalized linear and negative binomial regression models to analyze women's graduation rates in tertiary education (ISCED 5-8). The results reveal that more gender-equal, postmaterialist societies exhibit significantly lower female STEM graduation rates, even after controlling for economic development, labor market conditions, and educational enrollment; by contrast, traditional structural factors alone cannot fully account for women's STEM underrepresentation. Our longitudinal, cross-national approach provides novel evidence that cultural values and preferences play a critical role in sustaining STEM gender gaps. These findings extend theories of postmaterialism and modernization by demonstrating their unintended consequences for gender inequality. The study offers new insights for scholars and policymakers, suggesting that efforts to close the STEM gender gap must address cultural norms and value-driven career preferences alongside structural barriers.

title: Central Asian Startup Race: Who Is Leading and Why, 2020–2025

detail.title: Central Asian Startup Race: Who Is Leading and Why, 2020–2025
detail.abstract: In the period from 2020 to 2025, only changes occurred in the startup landscape of Central Asia. Venture capital increased from approximately $81 million to $670 million, rising by 727% within five years. In Uzbekistan, there was a 688% increase in investment. The number of deals in Kazakhstan doubled, along with an improvement in the seed-to-Series-A transition ratio from 12% to 31%. Yet, the impressive figures reveal significant variations. While Kazakhstan's startup ecosystem matured, Uzbekistan exhibited asymmetric maturity, characterized by disproportionate growth in inputs rather than outputs. This study contrasts the startup ecosystems of all five Central Asian countries across various dimensions throughout different years, presenting not only the changes witnessed from 2020 to 2025 but also their root causes. It identifies the decrease in specific issues, the persistence of others, and the key institutions behind the variation. The evolution of Kazakhstan's startup ecosystem is explored in-depth as a model for developing the necessary infrastructure to prevent common pitfalls: the Kaspi unicorn effect, the legal legitimacy of the AIFC, the formation of angel networks, investors' openness to pivot, and mentorship opportunities. The analysis incorporates five original comparative data tables and eight figures. This paper concludes with clear recommendations for bridging the performance gap by 2025 based on evidence.

title: The "Last-Patent Problem" in Patent Portfolio Licensing

detail.title: The "Last-Patent Problem" in Patent Portfolio Licensing
detail.abstract: Companies often license patents in portfolios because doing so can reduce transaction costs and infringement uncertainty. However, some companies include static royalty rates in their patent portfolio licenses, requiring licensees to pay the same royalty rate until the last patent in the portfolio expires or is invalidated. Such a practice turns the last remaining patent in the portfolio into a lever and imposes a "public-domain tax" that inflates prices, depresses output, and stifles innovation. This Article introduces and analyzes the problem created by such a practice as the "last-patent problem." Part I explains why companies transact in patent portfolios and how patent portfolio licenses with static, non-diminishing royalty rates, though often efficient ex ante, become distortionary as the patents in the portfolio expire or are invalidated. Part II formalizes the last-patent problem with several simple economic models showing that a static portfolio royalty rate magnifies pricecost wedges over time relative to a proportional step-down rate tied to the share of remaining value-bearing patents. Part III situates the analysis in the history of the U.S. patent system. Part IV shows that the patent-misuse doctrine, narrowed by statute and case law, does not reach the last-patent problem, and that because relief under antitrust's rule of reason is costly, under-deterrence follows. Part V proposes structural and behavioral remedies that administrative agencies, legislatures, and courts can adopt or mandate to alleviate the last-patent problem. The goal of the remedies offered in this Article is to preserve the efficiencies of patent portfolio licensing while restoring fidelity to the mandate of the Constitution's Intellectual Property Clause to "promote the Progress of Science and useful Arts."

title: CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF DANGEROUS GOODS DOCUMENTATION AND ITS IMPACT ON AIR CARGO SAFETY: An Empirical Study of Documentation Practices and Error Patterns

detail.title: CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF DANGEROUS GOODS DOCUMENTATION AND ITS IMPACT ON AIR CARGO SAFETY: An Empirical Study of Documentation Practices and Error Patterns
detail.abstract: This study investigates the role of dangerous goods (DG) documentation in air cargo safety. Dangerous goods-including flammable liquids, gases, toxic substances, radioactive materials, and lithium batteries-must be documented in accordance with ICAO Technical Instructions (Doc 9284) and IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR). In spite of these well-established rules, documentation errors continue to be a recurring problem in day-today cargo operations. Data were gathered through a structured questionnaire administered to 50 respondents-cargo staff and MBA aviation students in Chennai-along with interviews with seven cargo documentation practitioners. The results indicate that only 24% of respondents have full knowledge of IATA DGR; 62% come across documentation errors on a regular basis; just 44% consistently follow the mandatory DG checklist; and 56% point to time pressure as a direct reason for mistakes. Based on these findings, the study calls for wider adoption of digital documentation tools, more frequent and structured training, and tighter internal audit routines.

title: An International Cooperative Agreement that Solves our Climate Problem 1

detail.abstract: This article proposes WTO-compatible climate clubs for carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide that are based on the science of how to design effective cooperative agreements on common resources. The clubs require reciprocal commitments at the national level toward net-zero emissions, close monitoring of progress toward net-zero emissions, and the clubs impose measures designed to effectively encourage wide climate-club participation. These measures are: substantial penalties on non-participants and delinquent members, and a carrot for low developing countries with low emissions. The clubs are compatible with existing WTO laws, and, compared with some other climate clubs, they avoid economic distortions and have political advantages. This is a short policy-oriented article based on the related SSRN paper, Tarr (2025), and journal publication, Tarr (2026).

title: International Trade Finance and Learning Dynamics
affiliations: Central Bank of Chile, World Bank, University of British Columbia (UBC) and CMU Tepper School of Business

detail.title: International Trade Finance and Learning Dynamics
detail.abstract: We study how relationship-specific learning affects the joint dynamics of exports and trade finance. Using micro-level Chilean data, we document that new exporters initially rely on cashin-advance payments and gradually transition to providing trade credit as relationships mature, with faster transitions in riskier destinations and for less experienced firms. Motivated by this, we develop a general equilibrium trade model that integrates learning about foreign demand and counterparty risk together with firms' endogenous export and trade finance choices. We use the model to investigate the role of learning and risks in shaping export adjustments and quantify the impact of shocks to the cost of trade finance on aggregate exports. We find that the response to these shocks depends on the riskiness of the destination and is amplified by the disruption of long-term trading relationships.

title: Signal Processing Architectures for Systematic Asset Allocation: A Cross-Disciplinary Framework

keywords: Signal Processing Econophysics Systematic Asset Allocation Transfer Entropy Nonreciprocal Dynamics Regime Switching Portfolio Damping State-Space Forecasting Financial Time Series Hidden Markov Models Quantitative Finance Information Theory Cross-Asset Risk Transmission Dynamic Hedging Non-Stationary Markets

detail.abstract: This paper develops a cross-disciplinary framework for systematic asset allocation by combining ideas from signal processing, information theory, condensed matter physics, and quantitative finance. The central claim is that financial time series are better understood as noisy physical signals than as purely statistical objects. Once this shift in framing is made, several practical implications follow. First, trend extraction should be treated as a filtering problem rather than a moving-average problem. Second, cross-market leadership should be measured through directional information flow rather than simple correlation. Third, portfolio stabilization should be understood as a damping problem in a dynamic system exposed to recurrent shocks. The paper therefore proposes a three-layer architecture: Butterworth-based zero-phase filtering for low-lag signal extraction, transfer-entropy-based lead-lag analysis for nonreciprocal market discovery, and regime-sensitive damping rules for dynamic hedging and liability-aware asset allocation. The contribution is not merely metaphorical. Each physics concept is translated into a usable financial procedure with equations, implementation logic, and an empirical validation template. In contrast to backward-looking models that often fail under structural breaks, the proposed framework is designed for non-stationary environments in which volatility clusters, correlations shift, and transmission channels change over time. The result is a more robust and theoretically coherent basis for long-horizon investing, especially in pension, credit, and multiasset risk management settings. 1

title: The Strange Case of Possibilities Is Recursion
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Strange Case of Possibilities Is Recursion
detail.abstract: Possibilities occupy a stratum of reality that science has systematically neglected. They are the only genuinely recursive structure in the universe — the only entities that are self-referentially self-grounding, requiring no external cause, no medium, no substrate to persist. This paper argues that this uniqueness has a consequence: because possibilities cannot be annihilated (any attempt to eliminate them presupposes the possibility of elimination), they must be the cause of all reality. Everything else — logic, stable relationships, matter, physical law — is freedom that has progressively crystallised through a four-stage densification process formalised as the FLRP stack: Freedom generates Logic through differentiation; Logic generates Relationships through collision; Relationships generate the Physical through long-duration stability. Matter is long-term freedom. Physics is metaphysical. The paper then asks what follows from this practically: if everything navigates, everything is algorithmic, and any system can be understood and redesigned by mapping its Distortion geometry. We develop the master equation Freedom = (Perception / Distortion)^Alpha-infinity in full, present a taxonomy of Perception across six levels, develop thirty counterfactual comparisons establishing the ontological uniqueness of possibilities, state twenty falsifiable predictions, and provide a complete positive-definition glossary. The Lambert Wall — Alpha-infinity = e^(1/e) ≈ 1.4447 — is the maximum scale of topological friction beyond which real navigation ceases and physical form is born.

title: The effect of informal competition on the performance of formal firms: A systematic review of the literature

detail.title: The effect of informal competition on the performance of formal firms: A systematic review of the literature
detail.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to examine the empirical literature on the effects of informal competition on firm performance and provide direction for future research. Design/methodology/approach We search the Scopus and Web of Science databases and adopt a specific protocol to perform a systematic review of the literature. We screen 536 documents and apply three inclusion criteria for filtering. Findings We identify the impact of informal competition on nine types of formal firms' performance. We assess the findings according to the explanatory and response variables and the data samples of the articles reviewed and find that five areas are under-researched because they analyze country or region-specific data, or are in lack of consensus regarding the findings. Originality To the best of our knowledge, this is the first review of the empirical literature on the effect of informal competition on the performance of formal firms.

detail.abstract: This paper studies firm conduct in a regulated, growing prenatal supplement market where prices are uniform across the country but competition is distorted by trade sanctions and import restrictions. We used 16 quarters (2019-2022) of county-level sales data on prenatal supplements in Iran and matched them to product characteristics and county-level demographics. Demand is estimated using a random-coefficients logit model, highlighting the importance of women's age and college degree. Estimated own-price elasticities decline in magnitude over time, consistent with increasing attachment to prenatal supplements. On the supply side, marginal costs and markups are recovered under several alternative conduct assumptions: Bertrand, full collusion, and a set of group-specific collusive regimes. Average markups under all scenarios systematically exceed the 20 percent regulatory cap. Rivers-Vuong model selection tests and continuous conduct parameters indicate that imported brands behave as a collusive bloc, while domestic producers exhibit more competitive behavior, with the degree of coordination rising over time. The results show how national policies, including uniform price ceilings, foreign-exchange rationing, and import bans, can interact to shape market power and welfare in regulated health-related product markets.

detail.abstract: Based on the criticism that estimates of the fiscal and economic effects of Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) derived from firm-level data are not sufficiently accurate, this paper surveys the literature on BEPS (2003-2024) that analyzes country-level data. The findings indicate possible gaps in current tax policies to address BEPS and emphasize the need for improved international coordination and tailored policies to effectively tackle profit shifting, ensuring fair tax competition and robust public revenues. Directions for future research concern the effects of effective tax rates on real vs. "phantom" foreign direct investment (FDI) and the distinctions between immediate vs. ultimate FDI.

title: Illusion of Knowledge and Its Inversion: A Theoretical Framework for Pedagogy in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
affiliations: Independent Educational Researcher

detail.title: Illusion of Knowledge and Its Inversion: A Theoretical Framework for Pedagogy in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

declarations.ethicsApproval: This article is a theoretical study and does not involve any research with human participants or animals performed by the author. Therefore, institutional ethics approval and informed consent were not required for this work
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: The accelerated development of artificial intelligence systems has produced a fundamental transformation in the epistemic conditions of learning. Knowledge no longer primarily emerges as the product of an ongoing cognitive process, but increasingly appears as an available, immediate, and external output relative to the subject. This transformation gives rise to a phenomenon conceptualized in this paper as the "Illusion of Knowledge": a subjective sense of understanding that emerges from availability and processing fluency, yet is not grounded in deep cognitive processing or in the ability to operate on knowledge. The paper proposes a three-part theoretical framework. In the first part, the Illusion of Knowledge is analyzed as an epistemic failure resulting from the algorithmic shortcut, in which coherent outputs replace the cognitive process required for understanding and generate a systematic gap between perceived knowledge and actual knowledge. In the second part, a theoretical inversion is proposed, situating the phenomenon along a scarcity-abundance axis, while distinguishing between the "Illusion of Incompetence", characteristic of conditions of scarcity that restrict entry into learning but enforce process, and the "Illusion of Knowledge", characteristic of conditions of abundance that enable action through an initial sense of capability but do not require processing. This distinction allows the Illusion of Knowledge to be understood not only as a failure, but also as a potential psychological condition for action. Based on this, the third part proposes a pedagogical framework of conversion, in which the algorithmic output serves as a point of departure rather than a point of completion. Learning is redefined as the ability to operate on knowledge rather than merely to produce it. Within this framework, a staged model for converting perceived understanding into cognitive action is presented, alongside a shift in the role of the teacher from evaluator of output to activator of process, and a reorientation of assessment from the evaluation of products to the evaluation of operation, focusing on actions such as analysis, transformation, and transfer. The paper concludes that the central challenge in the age of artificial intelligence is not the accessibility of knowledge, but the reconfiguration of the conditions under which understanding is formed. Although the proposed framework is theoretical, it indicates the need for the development of empirical research and dedicated assessment tools capable of identifying and evaluating cognitive operational processes and distinguishing between passive Illusion of Knowledge and its activation as a mechanism for learning.

title: Evidence from the shadows: Unreported income, undeclared work and tax morale in Greece

detail.abstract: This chapter reviews the literature on the determinants of the activity in the Greek shadow economy and presents estimates of unreported income, undeclared work and tax morale in Greece with data from the Greek Shadow Economy Observatory. It conducts a bibliometric and systematic review of the literature on several aspects of the Greek shadow economy and presents estimates generated from a large dataset of approximately 15000 responses.

title: Calibration & Validation of Probabilistic Valuation Ranges
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Calibration & Validation of Probabilistic Valuation Ranges
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a practical method to calibrate and validate probabilistic valuation ranges generated by Monte Carlo discounted cash flow (DCF) models. It adapts standard ideas from probabilistic forecasting—coverage and sharpness—to the realities of illiquid real estate markets, where transaction evidence is sparse, heterogeneous, and observed with time lags. The paper defines workable back-test units (asset–valuation-date observations linked to the next relevant price-discovery event), recommends stratification by evidence quality and lag, and introduces a compact calibration scorecard for quarterly governance packs (coverage, miss severity, interval width, and stability). The aim is to make probabilistic valuation a governable and auditable output: ranges are produced, tested against subsequent price discovery, and refined through a documented feedback loop.

detail.abstract: This paper constitutes the third stage in a systematic theoretical inquiry that seeks to redefine the conditions of understanding, learning, and intelligence in the age of algorithmic mediation. Following the first paper, which identified a fundamental epistemic rupture in the traditional relation between knowledge and understanding, and the second paper, which defined the conditions and mechanism that enable epistemic conversion, the present paper focuses on the reorganization of learning processes themselves.

title: A Low-Latency FFT Pricing Architecture with Analytical Greeks in C++
affiliations: , , Polytechnic University of Milan - Politecnico di milano, Polytechnic University of Milan - Politecnico di milano, Polytechnic University of Milan - Politecnico di milano, Polytechnic University of Milan - Department of Mathematics and Polytechnic University of Milan - Department of Mathematics

detail.title: A Low-Latency FFT Pricing Architecture with Analytical Greeks in C++

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study relies entirely on mathematical models, numerical simulations, and publicly available financial market data. It does not involve human participants or animal subjects.

detail.abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of a low-latency, hybrid option pricing engine leveraging the Carr-Madan Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) framework. While traditional pricing engines based on Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) or Monte Carlo simulations suffer from performance bottlenecks and rigid architectures, our FFT approach completely decouples the numerical integration engine from the underlying stochastic dynamics. To overcome the computational latency of pure Python implementations during intensive calibration procedures, we developed a hardware-sympathetic architecture: the core execution loops, complex arithmetic, and FFT algorithms are implemented natively in C++ and interfaced seamlessly via Pybind11. By requiring only the analytical characteristic function of the log-price, the architecture supports advanced market models-ranging from Black-Scholes and Heston stochastic volatility to Levy-driven processes like Merton Jump-Diffusion (MJD) and Variance Gamma (VG). Crucially, model calibration is formulated directly in implied volatility (IV) space rather than price space, ensuring robust gradient dynamics across all moneyness regimes. Furthermore, we extend the framework to the analytical frequency-domain derivation of the Greeks (Delta, Gamma, Vega). This allows for the simultaneous, high-precision computation of entire sensitivity surfaces across thousands of strikes in O(N log N) time, bypassing the computational overhead and numerical noise of traditional finite-difference bumping techniques.

title: Environmental Policy Stringency and Corporate Financial Risk: Are Politically Connected Firms Better Off?
affiliations: Manchester Metropolitan University, Kean University, Muhlenberg College, University of Salford - Salford Business School and Ball State University - Miller College of Business

detail.title: Environmental Policy Stringency and Corporate Financial Risk: Are Politically Connected Firms Better Off?
detail.abstract: This paper examines how stringent environmental policies influence corporate financial risk and the role political connections play in this dynamic. Based on a sample of U.S. energy firms from 1996 to 2018 and employing panel regression models, our empirical analysis reveals that firms experience heightened financial risk in response to stricter environmental regulations, an effect that holds across different policy measures, estimation techniques, and models with additional controls, including risks related to energy security, climate, geopolitics, and economic policies. Notably, both market-based and non-market-based regulations contribute to this impact. The findings further suggest that this effect is not confined to firms of a particular size or financial standing, nor does it depend on the degree of policy stringency—indicating its broad applicability. However, firms with political ties exhibit resilience against these regulatory pressures, i.e., those with more substantial political spending can effectively buffer against the risk amplification caused by stringent environmental policies. This moderating effect remains robust even after accounting for selection bias through matched sample analysis. Additionally, capital expenditure emerges as a potential transmission channel for such effects. Our findings offer important implications for businesses, investors, and policymakers navigating the financial challenges posed by stricter environmental regulations.

title: Credit Without Proximity: Informational Frictions and Unequal Gains from Technology
affiliations: , The Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond and Marshall School of Business - University of Southern California

detail.title: Credit Without Proximity: Informational Frictions and Unequal Gains from Technology
detail.abstract: We study how the organization of information production-and its response to economic and technological forces-affects informational efficiency, credit allocation, and borrower risk. Using U.S. administrative data linking mortgage applications to loan officers and subsequent loan performance, we show that underwriting facilitated by officers located close to the borrower increases approval rates without worsening ex-post performance or processing speed, but is not always deployed where it is most valuable, because lenders allocate loan-officer labor elastically with respect to local wages. These gains are especially large for observably riskier borrowers. We develop and estimate a model that combines a core information-production problem over latent borrower risk, an endogenous choice over local versus remote underwriting, and equilibrium in mortgage and labor markets. We find substantial baseline credit rationing-up to 15 percent in high-risk segments-with local officers eliminating roughly half of it while also reducing excessively risky approvals. A technology shock that raises the processing productivity of remote officers induces lenders to substitute away from local screening, lowering informational efficiency, increasing excessively risky approvals and expected defaults, and tightening rationing for marginal borrowers despite only modest reductions in interest rates.

title: Global conflicts and Their impact on India’s Economy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Global conflicts and Their impact on India’s Economy
