title: Evaluating AI Trading Strategies Using a Paper Trading Framework
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Evaluating AI Trading Strategies Using a Paper Trading Framework
detail.abstract: Conventional evaluation of AI driven stocks trading models are often relies on classification measures such as directional accuracy and F1-score.But these metrics fail to capture the actual growth of real world trading performance because they don't take into consideration portfolio dynamics, risk exposure and capital growth.To address this limitation we purposes a framework for evaluating a AI models that is base on simulations and take place in a real world paper trading environment. This approach enables to testing under those conditions which are very similar to how the market works in real world taking into considerations like market volatility and compounding effects. We implement this framework in AlphaScope which is a full stack trading platform built using the tech stack Django, REST Framework and react. We do a comparison of three AI paradigms: Reinforcement Learning using Proximal Policy Optimization, Supervised Machine Learning using LightGBM,and a Large Language Model LLaMA 3 via Groq. These model are tested on 20 stocks from the S&P 500 over a five-year period (2020-2024).The results shows that the RL agent has the highest average portfolio value ($110.30),which shows that it do a best job to maximize the results. While,the LLM based strategy has the maximum drawdown(-12.86%)and the highest Simulation Performance Score(SPS= 0.5802)which indicates strong risk adjustment performance from both PPO (0.5711) and LightGBM (0.5265). The Large Language model approach has directional accuracy of 49.39%but it does better in SPS and drawdown measures. This shows a gap between how accurate predictions are and how they work well in real world. We present a Simulation Performance Score(SPS),a combined statistic design to assess trading strategies in simulated environment by simultaneously evaluating return, risks and stability. These results show how important it is to use execution-aware, simulation-in-the-loop evaluation as a more accurate and realistic approach to test AI-driven trading systems.

title: Algorithmic Delegation and Aggregate Volatility: Coordination Thresholds, Firm Heterogeneity, and Cross-Border Spillovers
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Algorithmic Delegation and Aggregate Volatility: Coordination Thresholds, Firm Heterogeneity, and Cross-Border Spillovers
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how algorithmic delegation affects macroeconomic volatility through coordination thresholds, firm-level heterogeneity, and cross-border spillovers. We extend a beauty-contest framework by allowing firms to differ in their reliance on algorithmic signals. The model predicts a quadratic volatility function were greater heterogeneity in AI use buffers aggregate fluctuations. Using a novel panel of 60 economies (2000-2024), we construct a multidimensional algorithmic intensity index based on AI patents, robot density, and digital infrastructure. Fixed-effects, panel threshold, and system GMM estimates reveal a robust non-monotonic relationship. At low adoption levels, algorithmic use reduces volatility by improving information processing. Beyond an endogenous threshold (0.423; 95% CI: 0.391-0.452), further diffusion raises volatility through correlated decision rules. A one-standard-deviation increase in trading partners' AI intensity amplifies the domestic volatility effect by approximately 30%. Economies with greater within-country heterogeneity in firm-level AI exposure exhibit significantly weaker amplification, validating the heterogeneous-λ micro-foundation. Human capital moderates the relationship by raising the coordination threshold and reducing synchronization. These findings highlight a fundamental trade-off between informational efficiency and systemic risk: the macroeconomic consequences of AI depend critically on the diversity of decision architectures and the network structure through which shocks propagate.

title: Aid for Reconfiguration: How the EU won multilateral protection of Geographical Indications
affiliations: Utrecht University - School of Economics, KU Leuven - Faculty of Business and Economics (FBE)

detail.title: Aid for Reconfiguration: How the EU won multilateral protection of Geographical Indications

declarations.funderStatement: This study was supported by funding from the strategic theme Pathways to Sustainability at Utrecht University for the project “Follow the Food”.

detail.abstract: This article leverages data on the regional allocation of development aid to test a novel theory: the European Union and several of its member states strategically use and orchestrate aid to support the establishment of Geographical Indications (GIs), such as Kampot pepper in Cambodia. As a result, the recipient countries' material interests change and they become more supportive of GI protection in the global trade regime. In 2020, this resulted in a multilateral GI register under the Geneva Act, in spite of US opposition. I label this mechanism "aid for reconfiguration", and argue it is not reducible to aid for policy or aid for trade. Regressions of Geneva Act accessions on GI aid corroborate the hypothesized mechanism. The article complements the GODAD geo-coded aid data by coding the location of aid-sponsored GIs, which are found to be more likely to be located in country leaders' birth regions, and to lead to pro-GI multilateral policy changes. The findings suggest that sector-relevant aid to leaders' birth regions is more effective at generating multilateral policies favored by the donors.

title: Why Underwriting Standards Matter More Than Interest Rates
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Why Underwriting Standards Matter More Than Interest Rates
detail.abstract:
This paper reexamines the conventional emphasis on interest rates as the primary lever of credit expansion, arguing that while rates influence the volume of borrowing, they do not determine the quality of financial systems. Interest rates act as a broad pricing mechanism, but they do not distinguish between borrower risk. Underwriting serves as the critical filter governing the allocation of credit.

 

Drawing on historical evidence from the Savings and Loan Crisis and the 2008 Financial Crisis, the analysis shows that financial instability is more closely associated with deteriorations in underwriting discipline than with movements in interest rates alone. Weak underwriting facilitates the expansion of credit to marginal borrowers, leading to the accumulation of systemic risk, asset mispricing, and capital misallocation—vulnerabilities that often remain obscured during periods of growth but are exposed during downturns.

 

The paper further examines how securitization and the originate-to-distribute model have weakened the alignment between risk-taking and risk-bearing, contributing to the erosion of underwriting discipline. It also considers the role of artificial intelligence in modern underwriting, arguing that while technological tools can improve efficiency, they cannot substitute for sound judgment and may amplify existing weaknesses.

 

The paper concludes that financial stability depends less on the cost of credit than on the discipline governing its extension. Interest rates shape credit cycles; underwriting standards determine their outcomes.

title: TF-IDF Based Fake News Classification: A Lightweight Machine Learning Study with Linear SVM Dominance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: TF-IDF Based Fake News Classification: A Lightweight Machine Learning Study with Linear SVM Dominance
detail.abstract: Due to the daily circulation of fake news on online media now become a significant challenge for society, shaping public views and spreading fake information. Detecting fake news automatically by using machine learning has become a significant area of research. This study shows an automated fake news identification system leveraging NLP combined with a machine learning approach. A publicly sourced Kaggle dataset comprising both authentic and fabricated news articles was utilized for training and evaluation purposes. The textual data is first pre-processed to remove inconsistencies in the data and further prepare it for analysis. To convert raw text into a format suitable for classification, TF-IDF vectorization was applied, which assigns numerical importance scores to terms proportional to their document level frequency. In order to determine what is not real news from real news, different classification models have been considered four classifiers: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Naive Bayes, and Linear SVM. Experimental results revealed that from all four evaluated classifiers, like Linear SVM, achieves higher accuracy with 99.51%. Consequently, traditional ML techniques combined with TF-IDF proved to be highly useful in identifying fake news, showing the desired result of a machine learning approach for misleading detection

title: Taux de taxation optimale et croissance économique : une application empirique au cas du Liban
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Taux de taxation optimale et croissance économique : une application empirique au cas du Liban
detail.abstract: Many studies highlight the significant impact of fiscal policy on the economic growth rate, in countries with a precarious financial and economic situation, similar to the Lebanese case. An empirical study, covering the period 1971–2017, is conducted in this paper, to determine the optimal tax burden that maximizes the economic growth rate in Lebanon. A non-linear relationship between the tax burden and economic growth is exa-mined, using the Scully static model Scully (1996, 2003). Looking at the country ’ s periods of political conflict and economic instability, the econometric model estimates lead to an optimal tax burden of 20.62%.

title: Mothers, Schools, and the Making of American Human Capital Mobility
affiliations: Stanford University, Yale University and Universitat Pompeu Fabra (UPF) - Centre de Recerca en Economia Internacional (CREI)

detail.title: Mothers, Schools, and the Making of American Human Capital Mobility
detail.abstract:
How did the US become a land of opportunity? Previous historical research on intergenerational mobility has focused on father-son income correlations, masking the role of mothers. We introduce a new mobility measure that incorporates both parents' human capital, develop a latent variable method leveraging literacy as a proxy, and construct a representative linked panel that includes women. We find that intergenerational mobility—in both human capital and income—rose sharply from the 19th to the 20th century. Initially, maternal human capital was most predictive of children's outcomes. However, as schooling expanded, this reliance declined and intergenerational mobility rose. America's investment in mass education has therefore been central to its rise as a mobile society.

title: AI Managed Household Portfolios: A Preliminary Report
affiliations: Rice University, Michigan State University - Department of Finance and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: AI Managed Household Portfolios: A Preliminary Report
detail.abstract:
How does AI manage household stock portfolios? We collect a prospective, daily time-series of stock recommendations using several LLM's and study AI's investment style. AI recommends undiversified portfolios that positively load on momentum, large companies, and low book-to-market firms. AI primarily recommends stocks based on how much media attention firms receive. Using multiple versions of queries and requests, we find that buy-and-hold and actively managed AI portfolios do not appear to earn statistically-significant abnormal returns based on the methodology of Daniel et al (1997).

title: Automation, Learning, and Career Dynamics
affiliations: Columbia University, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, University of Texas at Austin and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Automation, Learning, and Career Dynamics
detail.abstract:
We study how an automating technology affects career dynamics, human capital, and welfare in an economy where workers acquire skill through the tasks they perform. In a continuous-time general equilibrium model, learning-by-doing is determined jointly with the share of tasks automated, the frontier of tasks managers maintain, and the worker-to-manager career transition. Economies with high learning capacity admit pairs of stationary equilibria strictly ranked by the aggregate learning rate. Cheaper technology has opposite effects across the two: in the high-learning equilibrium, it raises welfare through the learning channel itself; in the low-learning equilibrium, it tips the economy into a human-capital trap. The planner's first-best combines a tax on automation profits with a subsidy on frontier-maintenance expenditures at a common rate.

title: Replacement and Reputation
affiliations: Yale University, Yale University and Northwestern University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Replacement and Reputation
detail.abstract:
Does electoral replacement ensure that officeholders eventually act in voters’ interests? We study a reputational model of accountability. Voters observe incumbents’ performance and decide whether to replace them. Politicians may be “good” types who always exert effort or opportunists who may shirk. We find that good long-run outcomes are always attainable, though the mechanism and its robustness depend on economic conditions. In environments conducive to incentive provision, some equilibria feature sustained effort, yet others exhibit some long-run shirking. In the complementary case, opportunists are never fully disciplined, but selection dominates: every equilibrium eventually settles on a good politician, yielding permanent effort.

title: Trade and the End of Antiquity
affiliations: Geneva Graduate Institute and SciencesPo - Sciences Po - Department of Economics

detail.title: Trade and the End of Antiquity
detail.abstract:
What was the role of trade, and how did economic activity evolve at the End of Antiquity, when political power shifts away from the Mediterranean towards northern Europe and the Middle East? To answer those questions, we assemble a database of hundreds of thousands of ancient coins from the fourth to the tenth century, estimate a dynamic model of trade and money where coins gradually diffuse along trade routes, and recover granular regional trade and real consumption time series. Our estimates suggest that: Mediterranean trade was disrupted by the newly formed border between Islam and Christianity; economic activity shifts away from the Mediterranean starting in the fifth century; real consumption peaks in the Middle East in the eighth century; and by the end of the ninth century, Atlantic regions from Islamic Spain to Frankish northwestern Europe have become the wealthiest regions of the ancient western world.

title: Mosaics of Predictability
affiliations: , City University of Hong Kong (CityU), City University of Hong Kong (CityU) and City University of Hong Kong (CityU)

detail.title: Mosaics of Predictability
detail.abstract:
We argue that return predictability is a latent, asset-specific, and state-dependent characteristic. We develop an interpretable Panel Tree that endogenously partitions the U.S. equity panel into out-of-sample and persistent “mosaic” patterns, and estimate cluster-specific forecasting models. Predictability concentrates in stocks with large earnings surprises, high earnings–price ratios, and low trading volume. It is countercyclical, stronger when market dividend yields are high and liquidity is low. Accounting for predictability heterogeneity, which conventional models ignore, improves forecasts and yields portfolios with out-of-sample Sharpe ratios around 2. Across 50 years of data, the mosaic map shows where signals arise and where noise dominates.

title: Data Neutrality, Data Supply, and Market Competition
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics and Chung-Ang University

detail.title: Data Neutrality, Data Supply, and Market Competition
detail.abstract:
We analyze the effects of data neutrality regulations on downstream market competition, the incentive of the platform to produce data, and consumer welfare. In our framework, data neutrality requires that firms seeking access to the platform’s data be treated equally, irrespective of whether they are affiliated with the platform. We consider two forms of regulation. Under weak data neutrality, the platform must provide the same amount of data to affiliated and unaffiliated sellers; under strong data neutrality, it must also charge the same price. We show that weak data neutrality can be largely ineffective, as the platform may restore exclusion through discriminatory pricing. Strong data neutrality is more consequential, but it does not necessarily raise welfare. Although it broadens access and intensifies downstream competition, it also reduces the incentive of the platform to refine and produce data. Consequently, data neutrality can reduce the equilibrium amount of data available in the market, and this data-reduction effect can dominate its benefits, which enhance competition. These findings suggest that regulating access to platform data requires balancing fair competition against the incentive to generate valuable data inputs.

title: The Competitive Effects of Qualcomm's No-License, No-Chips Policy in FTC v. Qualcomm: An Equilibrium Analysis*

detail.title: The Competitive Effects of Qualcomm's No-License, No-Chips Policy in FTC v. Qualcomm: An Equilibrium Analysis*
detail.abstract: In FTC v. Qualcomm, the Ninth Circuit accepted Qualcomm's argument that its no-license, no-chips ("NLNC") royalty surcharge was "chip-neutral" because it applied uniformly to handsets containing rival and Qualcomm modem chips. This paper develops a formal model of competition in the modem chip market and shows that the chip-neutrality argument fails. While the royalty surcharge has the same effects on rival's pricing incentives as the tax does, Qualcomm has a weaker incentive to raise its prices under the surcharge than under the tax of the same magnitude. Under the conditions that would make a non-discriminatory tax chipneutral, an otherwise identical private royalty surcharge raises rival prices by strictly more than Qualcomm's-biasing handset makers toward Qualcomm. I also analyze the role of discriminatory royalty surcharges. * I served as an expert witness adverse to Qualcomm in the Korea Fair Trade Commission's investigations of Qualcomm's licensing business model and in a class securities action against Qualcomm in the United States.

title: Adolescent Behavior, Learning, and Knowledge Diffusion: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
affiliations: European University Institute, University of Chicago, European University Institute and World Bank

detail.title: Adolescent Behavior, Learning, and Knowledge Diffusion: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
detail.abstract:
Improving classroom behavior is a persistent challenge in low-resource education systems, where disruptive environments often derail instruction and limit learning. Yet little rigorous evidence exists on whether behavior management can serve as a lever for academic improvement. We evaluate a program that shifts responsibility for establishing behavioral norms and reducing classroom disruptions from teachers to students. Covering over 7,500 adolescents across 127 middle schools in Bangladesh, the program significantly improves the classroom social climate, fostering stronger cooperation, better behavioral norms, and more supportive peer networks. High-performing students benefit most, showing significant gains in math and verbal tests after the program. A follow-up 1.5 years later reveals that while social climate improvements fade, academic gains persist and extend to a broader set of students, though they remain concentrated among higher-ability peers. A key mechanism is enhanced academic support networks among high-ability students, facilitating peer learning and knowledge diffusion within this group.

title: Shaping Society's Character: The Role of Schools in Developing Social and Emotional Skills
affiliations: European University Institute

detail.title: Shaping Society's Character: The Role of Schools in Developing Social and Emotional Skills
detail.abstract:
This chapter examines how schools cultivate socio-emotional skills that influence both individual success and broader social cohesion. Moving beyond the traditional focus on cognitive ability, I argue that education plays a crucial role in fostering traits that promote cooperation, trust, and long-term societal well-being. Drawing on insights from neuroscience, psychology, and economics, I explore how schools shape not only academic and labor market outcomes but also intergenerational beliefs, attitudes, and the formation of social capital. Using evidence from experimental studies, I highlight how school-based interventions can instill perseverance, enhance social learning, and create environments that curb anti-social tendencies, promote prosocial behavior—ultimately influencing the cultural fabric of society. This perspective reframes education as a mechanism for building more equitable and cohesive communities.

title: Why Bans Fail: Tipping Points and Australia's Social Media Ban
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics, University of Pennsylvania, Bocconi University, University of Chicago, University of Chicago, University of Cologne and Harvard Law School

detail.title: Why Bans Fail: Tipping Points and Australia's Social Media Ban
detail.abstract:
In December 2025, Australia became the first country to ban youth under 16 years old from holding accounts on major social media platforms, a policy now under consideration in more than a dozen countries and in numerous states. Because social media use is inherently social, the effectiveness of a ban that is easy to circumvent may depend on whether compliance reaches a tipping point: a share of compliant peers high enough to make it optimal for individuals to comply themselves. We surveyed 835 Australian teenagers four months after the ban took effect and find that only about one in four 14–15-year-olds comply. The social environment around use has barely moved: most banned teens believe that their peers are still using banned platforms and cite social reasons for continuing use. Sustaining high compliance requires two ingredients: the share of compliers must be high enough and those who comply must find it preferable to continue complying. The current ban achieves neither. Teenagers report that they require roughly two-thirds of peers to stop using social media to stop themselves, far above the share currently complying. They also perceive compliers as less popular than non-compliers, so the more influential teens disproportionately stay on the platforms. Together, these patterns suggest that compliance is more likely to diminish than to rise. Sustaining higher compliance will likely require pairing the ban with instruments that act on social norms and individual incentives directly.

title: How Poverty Fell
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics, University of California, San Diego (UCSD) and University of California, San Diego (UCSD)

detail.title: How Poverty Fell
detail.abstract:
The share of the global population living in extreme poverty fell dramatically from an estimated 36% in 1990 to 9% in 2015. We describe how this decline happened: the extent to which changes within as opposed to between cohorts contributed to poverty declines, and the key changes in the lives of households as they transitioned out of (and into) poverty. We do so using cross-sectional and panel sources that are representative or near-representative of five countries that collectively accounted for 75% of global poverty decline between 1990 and 2015. The data show that overlapping birth cohorts experienced the decline of poverty together over time, such that poverty decline can be viewed as a primarily within-cohort phenomenon. Within cohorts, the data reveal substantial churn, casting the challenge of escaping poverty as a “slippery slope” more than a long-term trap. The data also illustrate a diversity of pathways out of poverty: sectoral transitions, migration, and changing occupational choices and female labor force participation can all account for some part of poverty reduction, but in all but a handful of cases, a majority of households exiting poverty did so without experiencing these changes.

title: Consciousness-Soma Mismatch Hypothesis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Consciousness-Soma Mismatch Hypothesis

keywords: From Externalized Compensation to Substrate Reconstruction: Civilizational Transitions Driven by Consciousness-Soma Tension Consciousness-Soma Mismatch

detail.abstract: Existing scholarship on industrial revolutions predominantly relies on economic structures and institutional change as core explanatory variables, exhibiting a marked post-hoc causal attribution character. This hypothesis proposes an alternative a priori explanatory pathway centered on the structural mismatch between the human consciousness system and its biological soma as the core analytical variable, with the aim of providing a unified account of the driving logic behind the first four industrial revolutions and advancing predictive inferences regarding the direction of the fifth. Integrating the theoretical constructs of the autobiographical self, mental time travel, and symbolic consciousness, this hypothesis defines the core content of consciousness-soma mismatch, proposes the mechanism by which mismatch generates conscious tension that in turn drives externalized compensation, and predicts that the Fifth Industrial Revolution will mark a fundamental shift from externalized compensation to substrate reconstruction. The hypothesis operates within explicit explanatory boundaries, and its propositions remain subject to empirical verification.

title: Adaptation as sequence, not outcome: process-tracing repeated cyclone impacts in Madagascar
affiliations: , , affiliation not provided to SSRN, , affiliation not provided to SSRN, and

detail.title: Adaptation as sequence, not outcome: process-tracing repeated cyclone impacts in Madagascar

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The views expressed herein do not necessarily represent those of IDRC, its Board of Governors, or the UK Government’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study received ethical approval from the University of Reading Ethics Committee (SREC).
declarations.funderStatement: This work was carried out with financial support from the UK Government’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office and the International Development Research Centre, Ottawa, Canada as part of the Climate Adaptation and Resilience Program (CLARE) under Grant No. 110001 001.

detail.abstract: Cyclones in Madagascar are increasingly experienced not as isolated disasters but as recurrent disturbances that interrupt agrarian systems before recovery can stabilise. This paper empirically examines how agricultural adaptation unfolds under repeated cyclone exposure, focusing on processes rather than outcomes. Drawing on qualitative, multi-site fieldwork in four regions of Madagascar, the analysis reconstructs ordered sequences of impact, recovery, and recurrence to trace how constraints compound over time. The findings identify eleven recurrent mechanisms shaping adaptation trajectories. Early storms destabilise agrarian timing and generate stacked biophysical stresses that erode baseline conditions. Recovery becomes a bottleneck as seed loss, labour exhaustion, and asset depletion prevent consolidation before subsequent cyclones arrive, with impacts extending beyond farms through mobility breakdown and value-chain disruption. As shocks recur, recovery functions as a sorting process structured by gendered labour, land position, and access to tools, while households repeatedly recalibrate strategies oriented toward survival and reversibility. Tracing sequences rather than single events helps explain why adaptation remains active yet constrained, and why vulnerability accumulates despite sustained effort. Findings highlight the need to assess adaptation in relation to recovery completion and disturbance sequencing, rather than adoption metrics or post-event snapshots.

title: Regulating Non-Muslim Communities in the Seventeenth-Century Ottoman Empire: Catholics and Capitulations by Radu Dipratu

detail.title: Regulating Non-Muslim Communities in the Seventeenth-Century Ottoman Empire: Catholics and Capitulations by Radu Dipratu
detail.abstract: Capitulations have long been a subject in Ottoman economic and political historiography. But it is still appropriate to say that there is more to be studied. After Viorel Panaite's remarkable studies, for which he shared the results for several decades, were circulated in the English literature, the publication of new research by both him and his students led to the emergence of systematic knowledge and new approaches, especially in the context of ahitname texts. It is an exciting development to see that Radu Dipratu, who has published an important series of articles about the non-Muslims in the Ottoman lands in the seventeenth century, presents the subjects that form the focus of his studies to the reader in book form. Working at the Institute for South-East European Studies of the Romanian Academy in Bucharest, the author specializes in diplomatic relations between the Ottoman Empire and Protestant and Orthodox European countries, especially Catholic Europe.

detail.abstract:
Bài viết lập luận rằng Luật Đô thị đặc biệt cho Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh (TPHCM) cần được thiết kế như một “khung pháp định” mới cho siêu đô thị, thay vì chỉ là sự mở rộng rời rạc của các cơ chế đặc thù hiện hành. Trên cơ sở tổng quan lý luận về metropolitan government (chính quyền siêu đô thị) và metropolitan governance (quản trị siêu đô thị), các tiếp cận new regionalism (chủ nghĩa vùng mới), civic capital (vốn công dân), cũng như các nguyên tắc OECD về quản trị vùng đô thị, bài viết xây dựng một khung phân tích ba trục: cấu trúc thể chế, mức độ phân quyền – tự chủ và năng lực mạng lưới xã hội ở cấp vùng.

Kinh nghiệm quốc tế cho thấy các siêu đô thị muốn bứt phá phải gắn cải cách thể chế với khung Các Mục tiêu Phát triển bền vững, chiến lược whole-of-government (tiếp cận toàn chính quyền) và whole-of-society (tiếp cận toàn xã hội).

Từ đó, bài viết đề xuất sáu nhóm định hướng lớn cho Luật Đô thị đặc biệt TPHCM: (i) các nguyên tắc lập pháp nền tảng dựa trên SDGs và tiếp cận phân quyền “liệt kê quyền của Trung ương”; (ii) thiết kế lại cấu trúc chính quyền đô thị – vùng và thẩm quyền của TPHCM; (iii) các công cụ tài chính đô thị và đầu tư đặc biệt; (iv) khung pháp lý cho các khu vực chức năng đặc biệt và cụm ngành chiến lược; (v) cơ chế whole-of-government/whole-of-society và nuôi dưỡng civic capital vùng; (vi) bộ tiêu chí – chỉ số đánh giá việc thực thi Luật theo hướng cải thiện quản trị và tiến gần SDGs. Bài viết nhấn mạnh vai trò của Luật Đô thị đặc biệt như một “đột phá thể chế” – “phòng thí nghiệm” có kiểm soát cho cả hệ thống pháp luật Việt Nam.

title: Multidimensional Livelihood Security of Fish Farmers in the Valley Districts of Manipur: Evidence from the Post-COVID-19 Era

detail.title: Multidimensional Livelihood Security of Fish Farmers in the Valley Districts of Manipur: Evidence from the Post-COVID-19 Era
detail.abstract: The present study examines the livelihood security of fish farming households using a composite Livelihood Security Index (LSI) derived from six key dimensions: food, economic, education, health, social, and infrastructural security. Based on primary data collected from 96 households, the overall LSI value (0.53) indicates a moderate level of livelihood security, with notable variation across components. Education security (0.69) emerged as the strongest dimension, followed by infrastructure (0.59) and food security (0.58), while economic security (0.29) remained critically low, highlighting financial vulnerability. Classification of households revealed that a majority were concentrated in upper-medium and high livelihood security categories, although a significant proportion continued to fall under lower categories, indicating persistent disparities. Farm size-wise analysis demonstrated a positive association between landholding size and livelihood security, with marginal farmers exhibiting lower index values compared to medium and large farmers. Spatial analysis further revealed inter-village variation, with Oinam recording the highest average livelihood security (0.64), followed by Wangoi (0.58) and Mayang Imphal (0.56), while Waheng Khuman reported the lowest (0.36), indicating localized disparities. These differences are attributed to variations in infrastructure, market access, and institutional support. The findings underscore the need for targeted interventions to strengthen economic security, improve infrastructure, and reduce spatial inequalities to ensure sustainable livelihood outcomes among fish farming households.

detail.abstract: This paper examines Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall in dynamic portfolio optimization for shipping equities. Using a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman framework, the study constructs time-varying portfolio policies that maximize expected terminal log utility while restricting allocations to satisfy pre-specified downside risk limits. Unlike approaches that assess tail risk only after portfolio weights are obtained, the proposed method embeds VaR and ES directly into the admissible control set. The empirical application focuses on shipping sector equities, a volatility and cyclical market exposed to freight-rate uncertainty. The paper evaluates how tail-risk-constrained optimization affects model-implied tail risk, terminal wealth, realized drawdown, and riskadjusted performance.

title: Immigrant Entrepreneurship in Europe: Insights from a Bibliometric Analysis
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of New York Tirana and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Immigrant Entrepreneurship in Europe: Insights from a Bibliometric Analysis
detail.abstract: Immigrant entrepreneurs and their activities have received constantly increasing attention from academics and policymakers. While immigrant entrepreneurship is not new as an activity, with the globalization and development of technology, this field is at a different level, becoming one of the most popular avenues in entrepreneurship literature and playing a significant role in the economy, especially in a context like Europe. However, among emerging research attention, this field is becoming more diverse, complex, and confusing. Thus, literature reviews in this field are becoming critical to the overview of the field.Our study aims to provide an overview of academic research on Immigrant Entrepreneurship in Europe. An extensive bibliometric analysis was conducted to complete this, including bibliometric performance and graphic mapping of academic contribution in this field. A comprehensive performance analysis was carried out to pinpoint key authors, institutions, journals, and countries that are leading in shaping the landscape of research and development in this field. Furthermore, we use VOS viewer and R Biblioshiny software to graphically map the field. We do this by applying author co-citation and co-word analysis. Our research contributes to immigrant entrepreneurship literature by providing a better understanding of the phenomena in Europe and, based on the outcomes, directions for future research in the field.

title: Emissions, Liquidity, and Institutional Ownership
affiliations: University of Augsburg - Faculty of Business and Economics, ZHAW School of Management and Law, University of St. Gallen - School of Finance, Ludwig-Maximilians-University Munich, Faculty of Business Administration (Munich School of Management) and

detail.title: Emissions, Liquidity, and Institutional Ownership
detail.abstract: We examine how the introduction of standardized carbon emissions information affects equity-market liquidity and ownership. Using Trucost coverage data from 2010-2023 and a staggered difference-indifferences design, we find that first-time emissions information narrows bid-ask spreads by 2%, reduces Amihud illiquidity by 4%, and increases dollar trading volume and turnover by 4%. Institutional ownership increases by approximately 0.3 percentage points, representing roughly $30 billion in capital reallocated to newly covered firms. This ownership shift partially explains the liquidity improvement: a one-percentage-point increase in institutional ownership is associated with an additional 0.2% reduction in spreads. Liquidity gains are strongest for high-emission firms and late disclosers. Our results indicate that non-financial information, when standardized and comparable, is financially consequential: it attracts institutional capital, reduces adverse-selection costs, and enhances market efficiency.

title: Phase Time in Liquidity Systems: A Structural Framework within WLRT
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Phase Time in Liquidity Systems: A Structural Framework within WLRT

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest related to this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or animals and does not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces Phase Time as a structural framework for describing the evolution of liquidity systems within the Wave Liquidity Redistribution Theory (WLRT).

Unlike classical time representations, which rely on continuous duration, Phase Time is defined through the ordering of discrete structural transformations between admissible system states. Within this framework, market evolution is modeled as a sequence of transitions on a constrained finite state space, where each state corresponds to an Entry-4 configuration and each transition is induced by an Exit-5 event.

We formalize the system as a directed graph with strictly defined admissibility rules, ensuring that all possible trajectories are structurally consistent. This representation allows phase evolution to be interpreted as a path on a canonical transition graph, establishing a direct correspondence between structural dynamics and graph traversal.

The framework introduces several key properties, including determinism under admissible transitions, independence from astronomical time, and the ability to reconstruct missing events from observed state sequences. Additionally, the transition system naturally defines a constrained formal language over structural states, enabling the use of tools from automata theory and graph theory.

The proposed approach provides a rigorous alternative to continuous-time models, offering a discrete, structure-driven perspective on market dynamics. This perspective is particularly suited for analyzing environments where evolution is governed by admissible transformations rather than smooth temporal flows.

Within this framework, phase time is naturally interpreted as a path on the canonical transition graph.

title: Measuring Coping Responses to Pandemic Shocks: A Coping Strategy Index Analysis of Fish Farmers in Manipur
affiliations: College Of Agriculture, Indira Gandhi Krishi Vishwavidyalaya, Central Agricultural University and

detail.title: Measuring Coping Responses to Pandemic Shocks: A Coping Strategy Index Analysis of Fish Farmers in Manipur
detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic caused significant disruptions to fisheries and aquaculture systems, adversely affecting the livelihoods of fish farmers. This study examines the coping strategies adopted by fish farming households in the valley districts of Manipur using a perception-based Coping Strategy Index (CSI). A cross-sectional survey of 96 households was conducted, and coping strategies were analyzed in terms of severity, frequency, and their combined contribution to overall coping intensity. The mean CSI was 38.64 (SD = 9.66), with values ranging from 20.77 to 60.99, indicating moderate but heterogeneous coping behaviour. Results revealed that while migration (3.60) and asset sales (3.52) were perceived as highly severe strategies, the most frequently adopted strategies were child labour (2.46), spending of savings (2.27), and reduced input use (2.23). Contribution analysis showed that child labour (8.66) disproportionately influenced the CSI, followed by spending of savings (3.62) and reduced input use (3.34). A clear inverse relationship between farm size and coping intensity was observed, with marginal farmers recording higher CSI (42.29) compared to large farmers (34.54). Further, 44.80% of households were categorized under stressed and distress coping levels, indicating substantial livelihood vulnerability. The findings highlight the reliance on immediate but potentially detrimental coping mechanisms and underscore the need for targeted policy interventions to enhance resilience and reduce vulnerability among fish farmers.

detail.abstract: This paper presents Genesis III, a mathematical framework that derives a single self-stabilisation threshold * ≈ Γ 0.97 for institutional architectures from one action functional S[G_III] whose Noether currents are four invariants-governance integrity (), stewardship (), dignity (D×), and extraction (E). Twelve formal layers (OP1-OP12) Γ Λ ₚ close into a unified construction; the threshold is reached by four projections of S[G_III] onto established mathematical structures (cubic-kernel fixed point; Wilson-Fisher infrared fixed point; Bohr-Sommerfeld quantisation; Coleman-Weinberg radiative breaking) returning the same value to within stated precision bands. Four pre-registered falsifiers (F1-F4) are stated. The framework is cross-walked against the G7-led International Financial Framework (IFF) proposal to demonstrate operational embedding as an admission criterion. A refereestyle audit anticipates eight points of contestation, six of which are addressed by editorial discipline (v2.3.1 lock) and two of which (F2 universality-class instrumentation; band-dependence of the cascade-length calibration Lc) are flagged as pending empirical work.

detail.abstract: When outcomes are irreversible, systems that optimize for confidence without verifying the conditions that make that confidence meaningful will produce decisions that cannot be justified once executed. Lethal targeting systems built on probabilistic models are being deployed with governance frameworks designed for recoverable outcomes (Perrow 1984; Vaughan 1996). The resulting failure mode is not model error. It is a mismatch between the architecture of accountability and the irreversibility of the action.

title: The Closing Frontier: The Structural Closure of Agrarian Fallbacks in the Age of AI

detail.title: The Closing Frontier: The Structural Closure of Agrarian Fallbacks in the Age of AI
detail.abstract: During the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the industrial revolution, colonialism and economic recessions, agriculture has served as a shock absorber for the displaced workers, craftsmen and artisans. Displaced workers and craftsmen went back to their roots, ancestral or communal land, thus providing a subsistence safety net that prevented social collapse. This paper argues that this safety valve is now structurally getting closed and the AI revolution is occurring at precisely the historical moment when neither route of agricultural absorption remains viable. In developed economies capital-intensive and labourless AgTech has eliminated agricultural wage labour as a realistic fallback for displaced workers. In developing economies land fragmentation has rendered smallholdings incapable of absorbing additional labour without worsening disguised unemployment. The COVID-19 reverse migration crisis of 2020 constitutes an inadvertent natural experiment that confirms this thesis in real time. Approximately 30-50 million Indian workers were displaced from urban employment and returned to rural roots. The agriculture sector could not absorb them productively without disguised unemployment. AI driven displacement will be permanent and larger in scale. The consequence is the emergence of what this paper terms the 'Digital Lumpenproletariat' a class of atomised, high-literate, urban surplus labourers with no productive rural retreat and no welfare state cushion. These surplus labourers' political volatility represents the defining social risk of the AI age in the Global South. Policy responses, including platform cooperatives, skilling for rural production systems, capital-based social contracts and redefining those social contracts.

title: Protocol Taxation Under Plausible Elasticities: A Simulation Framework for a Flat, Transaction-Embedded Levy

detail.title: Protocol Taxation Under Plausible Elasticities: A Simulation Framework for a Flat, Transaction-Embedded Levy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This research received no external funding and was conducted independently, without institutional affiliation or sponsorship.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a simulation study using published aggregate tax and payment-system data; no human subjects, patient data, or participant research is involved.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding. Self-funded independent research.

detail.abstract: A flat tax embedded at the protocol layer of digital payment rails-levied on every transaction, with no exemptions, no filing, and no discretionary enforcement-has been proposed as a substitute for general taxation. Whether it can raise revenue comparable to current collection under plausible elasticities, and at what administrative cost, remains empirically unanswered. This paper builds a transparent, reproducible simulation framework and applies it to four illustrative country calibrations (United States, Brazil, Chile, Canada). We calibrate elasticities from the value-added-tax empirical literature without inventing new estimates, propagate uncertainty through 30,000-iteration Monte Carlo, and evaluate the proposal against preregistered threshold readings. The framework's primary defensible result is the transition operating point, which holds in every country profile under the static-substance reading of current bank-mediated payment infrastructure. Rate calibrations vary in a structured pattern driven by informaleconomy share (shifts rates up) and wholesale-settlement-to-GDP ratio (shifts rates down). A forward-looking secondary scenario-a mature steady-state at lower rates, conditional on self-custody adoption contracting bank intermediation over a decadeis reported as the framework's most-speculative input, with explicit sensitivity to alternative adoption paths in §4.2.1. NPV transition costs are dominated by NPV admin savings in all four countries; combined-system progressivity holds across the realistic UBI range. Operating points depend on country-specific payment-rail infrastructure and informal-economy share.

title: How sustainability report preparers and assurance providers frame sustainability assurance quality -- an interview study
affiliations: Curtin University, Curtin University, Curtin University and Yunnan University

detail.title: How sustainability report preparers and assurance providers frame sustainability assurance quality -- an interview study

publicationDetails.detailsText: China Accounting & Finance Review, volume 28, issue 2, 2026

detail.abstract:
Purpose-We explore the quality of sustainability assurance from the perspective of sustainability reporting preparers and assurance providers. 

Design/methodology/approach-The research design and data collection are guided by framing theory, which involves three framing tasks (i.e. sense-making, naming and storytelling) during the diagnostic framing process. A semi-structured interview method was employed with a sample of 40 sustainability reporting preparers and assurance providers. The data collected from the interviews is analysed following the three stages of the grounded theory method. 

Findings-The assurance providers demonstrated their commitment to the quality of sustainability assurance in the sense-making task. In contrast, the reporting preparers paid little attention to it. Results from the naming task indicate that assurance providers highlight the level of assurance quality in accordance with predetermined targets and prescribed procedures, while reporting preparers prioritise meeting the stakeholders' requirements. The storylines from both groups emphasise the quality of disclosure information. From their perspective, assurance providers emphasise that effective communication with client companies is associated with higherquality and more sustainable reporting. Preparers of assurance statements are concerned about the representation of assurance statements. 

Research limitations/implications-Our study is limited by the inherent limitations of qualitative research. A relatively small sample and other stakeholders were not included, which limited the generalisation of the findings of our study. 

Practical implications-Our study has practical significance and implications for reporting companies, assurance providers and regulators by offering a comprehensive view of assurance providers and reporting preparers on sustainability assurance quality. 

Originality/value-We integrate the applications of framing theory by Maroun (2019) and Durocher and Georgiou (2022) to develop a new framework that guides research design and data collection in qualitative research. Our study sheds light on the stagnant sustainability assurance market and contributes new insights to the existing literature on sustainability assurance. It contributes to our understanding of the quality of sustainability assurance from the perspective of assurance providers and sustainability reporting preparers. The theoretical framework we developed is useful for studying the perception of a concept or practice and the process of forming such perception in any discipline.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a customer-constrained optimization framework for personalized mortgage rate pricing in retail banking. The objective is to recommend the lowest feasible mortgage rate for each application while preserving near-optimal expected profit. The framework integrates borrower-level features, market-relative acceptance modeling, and default risk estimation within a unified expected profit formulation. Using a Freddie Mac-derived loan-level dataset spanning origination years 1999-2013, we demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves strong predictive performance (AUC ≈ 0.79) and consistent optimization behavior across a heterogeneous borrower population. Empirical results show that the customer-constrained strategy reduces average mortgage rates by approximately 12.2 basis points, while incurring only a 3.92% reduction in expected profit. These findings suggest that modest, data-driven adjustments to pricing can significantly improve customer outcomes while maintaining profitability. The framework provides a practical and interpretable approach for implementing customer-centric pricing strategies in competitive lending environments.
