title: Political connection and corporate digital transformation: evidence from China
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Nanjing University of Finance and Economics, Yangzhou University and Nanjing University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Political connection and corporate digital transformation: evidence from China

publicationDetails.detailsText: China Accounting & Finance Review, volume 28, issue 2, 2026

detail.abstract:
Purpose-The purpose of this paper is to examine how political connections impact corporate digital transformation in the era of digital economy. 

Design/methodology/approach-We conduct regression analyses using a sample of A-share listed companies from 2008 to 2021 to examine whether and how political connections impact the digital transformation of firms. The results show that political connections significantly impede the digital transformation of firms. 

Findings-The mediating effects analysis shows that the inhibiting effect is primarily exerted through two channels: weakening board supervision and suppressing innovation quality and the concealment of favoritism by local officials may account for the non-significance of the government subsidy mechanism. The moderating analysis shows that equity concentration and salary incentives mitigate the negative effects of political connections. The average age of executives strengthens the negative effects of political connections, while the heterogeneity of executive age weakens the negative effects of political connections. And customer concentration weakens the negative effects of political connections. 

Originality/value-This paper decomposes the mechanisms of political connections affecting DT of firms into the positive and negative sides and forms an analytical framework, which is used in the moderation and heterogeneity analysis. This provides some inspiration for the research of analyzing political and economic consequences of political connections, and has useful references for the government and firms on how to correctly treat the relationship between them.

title: A Standardized Multi-Cloud Governance Model for Policy Consistency and Drift Detection

detail.title: A Standardized Multi-Cloud Governance Model for Policy Consistency and Drift Detection
detail.abstract: The increasing adoption of multi-cloud architectures has introduced new challenges in governance, policy consistency, and configuration drift detection across heterogeneous cloud environments. Organizations commonly rely on providerspecific governance tools such as AWS Config, Azure Policy, and GCP Config Validator; however, these tools often operate independently, creating inconsistencies in enforcement, reporting, and compliance monitoring. This paper proposes a standardized multi-cloud governance model that introduces a centralized policy abstraction layer, a cross-cloud policy mapping mechanism, and a continuous drift detection pipeline. The framework is evaluated through a FinTech-oriented use case, demonstrating improvements in policy compliance consistency, drift visibility, operational efficiency, and reliability outcomes. The proposed approach provides a reusable model for organizations seeking unified governance, proactive drift detection, and improved compliance readiness across AWS, Azure, and GCP environments. Impact Statement-This work presents a practical and scalable framework for standardizing multi-cloud governance and detecting policy drift across distributed cloud environments. By integrating policy abstraction, cross-cloud mapping, observability, and remediation workflows, the proposed model supports improved reliability, compliance consistency, and operational efficiency.

title: Dynamic capabilities and the knowledge problem of ex ante platform regulation
affiliations: Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University) and Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University)

detail.title: Dynamic capabilities and the knowledge problem of ex ante platform regulation
detail.abstract: Ex ante digital platform competition regimes -- including the EU Digital Markets Act and its counterparts across the United Kingdom, Japan, India, Australia, and Brazil -- designate specific firms as platforms and attach conduct obligations to them as a class. Existing critiques argue that these regimes harm innovation or freeze moving market boundaries. We locate the error one level deeper. Platforms are not stable objects temporarily subject to competitive pressure-they are ongoing processes of capital recomposition whose apparent durability is produced by the capability activity that sustains them. We give dynamic capabilities theory the Austrian microfoundations it has been implicitly reaching for -- that sensing is Kirznerian alertness, seizing is Knight-Mises judgment under genuine uncertainty, and reconfiguring is Lachmannian recomposition of heterogeneous capital. Each generates a structurally distinct impossibility for the ex ante regulator -- alertness cannot be enumerated because the opportunities it identifies do not yet exist as observable demand, judgment cannot be priced because it operates under genuine uncertainty rather than calculable risk, and recomposition cannot be predicted because the act of regulating changes the structural parameters the regulator relied on to forecast its own effects. The regulatory error is not simply that the rules are too static, or that regulators forecast poorly, but that the ex ante designation form mistakes legal continuity and observed market position for stability of the economic object being governed.

title: Marginal Utility as the Sum of Distinct Components

detail.title: Marginal Utility as the Sum of Distinct Components
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a decomposition of marginal utility in which the marginal utility of wealth is represented as the sum of distinct component-specific contributions. Rather than treating diminishing marginal utility as a property of a single homogeneous function, the framework interprets the slope of utility as arising from multiple underlying mechanisms with different marginal properties. Specifically, marginal utility is decomposed into Relief, Comfort, Status, and Achievement components, corresponding to experiential and relational sources of utility. Each component exhibits distinct curvature, with experiential contributions declining more rapidly as material constraints are alleviated, while relational contributions persist over a broader range of wealth. The observed concavity of utility can therefore be understood as the aggregate outcome of heterogeneous marginal processes rather than as a primitive property of preferences. The decomposition yields a simple graphical representation and provides a mechanism-based interpretation of the income-well-being relationship that is consistent with existing evidence on absolute and relative income effects. More broadly, the paper contributes to a compositional framework in which utility is understood as arising from multiple underlying components whose contributions vary across contexts and across the wealth distribution.

title: Tribal Court Judgments
affiliations: University of Alabama - School of Law

detail.title: Tribal Court Judgments
detail.abstract:
Does a state court have to enforce a judgment issued by a tribal court? In 1991 the Arizona Supreme Court surveyed the current treatment of tribal court judgments and concluded that a majority of courts “extend[ ] the application of the full faith and credit clause” to decisions rendered by tribal courts. Just fifteen years later the Southern District of Florida castigated the Miccosukee Tribe for making the same representation; reasoning that “the clear majority of states addressing the issue have concluded that Indian tribes” are outside of the Full Faith and Credit Statute.

This Article corrects the judicial record. First, it actually surveys the split among state laws and concludes that most states that have considered the issue treat tribal court judgments as enforceable beyond the traditional comity extended to judgments from foreign courts, although not all of these states describe this recognition as full faith and credit. Second, it makes a normative argument, suggesting that the Supreme Court’s recent decision in a relatively obscure bankruptcy case, Lac du Flambeau v. Coughlin, actually resolves the conflict and mandates that state courts extend full faith and credit to tribal court judgments. Finally, the Article considers the limited enumerated powers of Congress and the federal courts, to suggest that while states must give full faith and credit to tribal court judgments, tribes are free to decide for themselves whether to reciprocally recognize state court judgments.

The implications are profound. The judicial record is replete with hundreds of cases, across dozens of states, searching for guidance on the scope of the Full Faith and Credit Statute when applied to Indian tribes. There is a circuit split. There are federal courts refusing to comply with nineteenth century Supreme Court precedent that has never been overturned. The congressional response has been piecemeal, requiring full faith and credit in specific circumstances, without ever articulating a standard for the recognition of other tribal court judgments. This Article unifies history and practice, statute and precedent, to articulate a single consolidated theory of the recognition of tribal court judgments.

title: Probabilistic Validation of Yield Curve Stress Scenarios: PCA-Based Projection, Heavy-Tailed Calibration, and Backtesting

detail.title: Probabilistic Validation of Yield Curve Stress Scenarios: PCA-Based Projection, Heavy-Tailed Calibration, and Backtesting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. The views expressed in this paper are solely those of the author and do not represent any employer or institution. The analysis uses publicly available U.S. Treasury yield data and does not use proprietary or confidential information.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a probabilistic framework for validating yield curve stress scenarios using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Conventional interest rate stress testing often relies on deterministic scenarios, such as fixed parallel shifts of the yield curve, without assigning explicit probabilities. The proposed framework projects deterministic shocks into a low-dimensional PCA factor space estimated from historical U.S. Treasury rate changes and maps the resulting factor distance to model-implied tail probabilities. The framework is extended from a Gaussian benchmark to a covariance-standardized Student-t specification to account for heavy-tailed factor dynamics. Empirically, the first three principal components explain 97.49% of total yield-curve variation. A 200 basis point parallel shock corresponds to a 12-month Gaussian tail probability of 0.84%, while the Student-t specification implies a higher tail probability of 3.72%. Backtesting shows that Gaussian thresholds materially understate factor-space tail risk, while the Student-t specification provides more realistic calibration. The results provide a reproducible link between deterministic stress scenarios and empirical yield curve dynamics.

title: When Corruption Indicators Get Louder: Producer Uncertainty and the Evidence Content of Annual Governance Change
affiliations: Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Public Policy

detail.title: When Corruption Indicators Get Louder: Producer Uncertainty and the Evidence Content of Annual Governance Change
detail.abstract: Perception-based governance indicators are central to empirical development research, but their published standard errors are rarely used to evaluate within-country movements. This paper proposes a simple diagnostic for annual index change: each country-year movement is decomposed into raw score change, producer-reported uncertainty, and a standardized signal-to-noise statistic. The method is applied to two leading corruption measures, the World Bank's Worldwide Governance Indicators Control of Corruption measure and Transparency International's Corruption Perceptions Index. Using the 2020 suspension of the World Bank's Doing Business report as a calendar reference point, the paper documents a sharp producer asymmetry. After 2020, both indicators shift toward more negative mean annual changes and both report lower pooled standard errors. Yet they diverge in the evidence content of annual movements: WGI-Control of Corruption records a decline in absolute standardized movement, while CPI records an increase. The contrast is not driven by scale, country coverage, Russia--Ukraine war cases, or the exact cutoff year. Additional checks show that the WGI-side pattern extends across most WGI pillars, while the CPI precision tightening is not concentrated in countries with initially low source counts. The results do not identify a causal effect of the Doing Business controversy. Instead, they show that two corruption indicators often treated as substitutes translate annual governance movements into different amounts of statistical evidence once producer-reported uncertainty is incorporated. This matters for applied research using corruption indicators to measure institutional change.

title: Measure Frictional Sorting *
affiliations: Queen's University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Measure Frictional Sorting *
detail.abstract: This paper constructs an index to measure sorting in a two-sided market with matching friction. The index uses the cumulative distribution function (cdf) of the matching partners for each individual and incorporates matching failures as a mass point at the lowest type of the partners. The area between this cdf and the cdf in the efficient allocation without friction represents the reduction in sorting. The sorting index is equal to one minus the aggregate reduction in sorting normalized by the amount under uniform matching. In contrast to most measures of sorting in the literature, the sorting index captures the effect of matching failures and compares the matching partner's type with the ideal type instead of the individual's own type. Relative to this sorting index, the correlation coefficient of matched types tends to overestimate sorting when sorting is positive. The over-estimation increases sharply when matching failures increase or when the market becomes more imbalanced.

title: The Infrastructure Finance Gap: Development-Induced Displacement and the Limits of Project-Based Safeguards

detail.title: The Infrastructure Finance Gap: Development-Induced Displacement and the Limits of Project-Based Safeguards
detail.abstract:
Development-induced displacement remains an under-governed domain within global displacement policy. Although generated through planned, state-led infrastructure investment, affected populations are typically managed through project-based safeguard frameworks that expire at project closure, leaving limited institutional responsibility for long-term outcomes. This paper argues that the resulting “orphan condition” reflects structural features of displacement governance rather than implementation failure. Drawing on cases from the Mekong region, it shows that safeguards are bounded by project timelines, jurisdictions, and defined populations, while displacement unfolds longitudinally, cumulatively, and across administrative boundaries.

The paper identifies a central gap: the absence of institutional linkage between project-level obligations and the national systems—social protection, civil registration, and fiscal transfers—required to sustain outcomes over time. It argues that reform lies not in strengthening safeguards alone, but in anchoring project finance within broader system capacity. Infrastructure finance, embedded in ongoing IFI–sovereign engagement, provides the most politically viable entry point for this shift. Using existing instruments, including country programming and results-based financing, displacement governance can be reframed as a problem of institutional design and fiscal integration. The paper concludes that effective displacement governance depends on building systems capable of absorbing displaced populations regardless of the source of displacement.

title: Disposal of household medication at Danish community pharmacies – a descriptive study
affiliations: University of Southern Denmark, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Copenhagen

detail.title: Disposal of household medication at Danish community pharmacies – a descriptive study
detail.abstract: A large share of health care spending is used on medications, but many medications end up not being used, which threatens patient safety, the environment, and the health economics. Medication waste can originate from many sources such as production, packaging, logistics, and use of medication in both hospitals and households. This study concerns discarded medications from households, and the objective was to describe the amount and type of medication waste delivered by citizens at community pharmacies.,At 33 Danish community pharmacies, all discarded medications received from citizens at the counter were documented for one or two weeks each, in total 39 periods of 1 week. Guidelines for handling medication waste were used to secure the work environment at the pharmacies.,In total, 4,384 registrations of discarded medications were completed, ranging from six to 546 medications per pharmacy (average 112). Of these medications, 21% were unopened packages and 57% had not expired. Most medications were tablets (55%). Of the discarded medications 3,655 (83%) were identified with item number, and these consisted of 1,614 different item numbers. The primary group of discarded medications were painkillers (9%). The price for the discarded medications totaled € 78,000; however, this figure is attached with uncertainties.,The amount and type of discarded medication delivered at community pharmacies was very fluctuating. However, if the same amount was delivered at all Danish pharmacies year-around, it would correspond to 5 discarded medications every minute, causing unnecessary costs to individuals and society. This highlights the need to reduce medication waste.

title: Portfolio Construction
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Portfolio Construction
detail.abstract: I review the Bellman-Merton formalism for portfolio construction.

title: Bridging Global Learning Curves and Local Capital Costs: A Localised Renewable Energy Cost Framework for South Africa
affiliations: Stellenbosch University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Bridging Global Learning Curves and Local Capital Costs: A Localised Renewable Energy Cost Framework for South Africa
detail.abstract: Global levelised cost of energy models underestimate deployment costs in emerging economies because they assume financing conditions typical of developed economies. This paper develops a localised cost framework that derives the weighted average cost of capital from the 3-month Johannesburg Interbank Average Rate plus a technology risk spread to project costs for solar PV, onshore wind, and concentrating solar power in South Africa through 2035. The model is validated against tariffs from the Renewable Energy Independent Power Producer Procurement Programme across seven bid windows (2011–2024). For onshore wind, the moderate scenario reproduces actual tariffs with an average deviation of 2%. For solar PV, tariffs exceed modelled values by 71% in Bid Window 1 but narrow to 29% by Bid Window 4, reflecting the decline of early-market risk premiums; tariffs from Bid Windows 6 and 7 provide an out-of-sample test, falling approximately 45% below the projection and indicating that cumulative deployment has eliminated the emerging-market capital cost premium. A 1% increase in the cost of capital raised the modelled cost by 6.5%, and the 2022–2023 monetary policy tightening raised costs by 8% despite concurrent reductions in technology costs, confirming the mechanism underpinning the climate investment trap hypothesis. The South African evidence, however, demonstrates that well-designed procurement frameworks can prevent the trap from closing: bid windows remained oversubscribed, indicating that sovereign-backed power purchase agreements provided sufficient de-risking to maintain investor confidence. The cost of capital, not technology cost, is now the binding constraint. Projections to 2035 indicate that the draft Integrated Resource Plan 2023 substantially overstates future renewable energy costs, with implications for energy policy and climate finance in emerging markets.

title: The Impact of ESG Performance on Corporate Value: Aggregate ESG Scores and Evidence from China
affiliations: Wuhan University and Wuhan University

detail.title: The Impact of ESG Performance on Corporate Value: Aggregate ESG Scores and Evidence from China
detail.abstract: Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors are increasingly recognized as critical determinants of corporate valuation. Nevertheless, the existing literature offers no consensus on the relationship between ESG performance and corporate value, largely due to substantial discrepancies across ESG ratings from different agencies. This paper attempts to address this issue by constructing aggregate ESG scores and using them to re-examine the ESG-value relationship. Drawing on four prominent ESG ratings in China, we employ three aggregation methods—equal-weighted averaging, entropy weighting, and principal component analysis—to construct composite measures. Using a panel dataset of 3,350 Chinese A-share listed companies from 2019 to 2024, we find that ESG performance has a significant negative impact on corporate value. The aggregate ESG scores enhance the understanding of ESG rating divergence and underscore the necessity of incorporating multiple ratings when assessing corporate ESG performance. And our empirical result is primarily attributable to the immature ESG valuation system in China's capital market, where traditional financial metrics remain dominant. The negative effect is particularly pronounced during periods of macroeconomic weakness and stock market downturns, when ESG-related costs may be perceived as a burden. Our conclusions provide new insights for alleviating ESG rating divergence, advancing ESG investment practices, and exploring the establishment of ESG valuation framework in emerging markets.

title: Can shadow prices from energy system optimization models serve as reliable electricity price indicators?
affiliations: , Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) and Vienna University of Technology

detail.title: Can shadow prices from energy system optimization models serve as reliable electricity price indicators?
detail.abstract: Shadow prices from energy system optimization models (ESOMs) are widely used as long-term electricity price proxies in research and policy analysis. While their structural limitations are broadly acknowledged, no systematic empirical evidence exists on their reliability as market price proxies. We address this gap with a novel three-stage statistical framework (Kruskal-Wallis tests, t-tests, Pearson correlations) applied to ENTSO-E day-ahead prices and shadow prices from GENeSYS-MOD - one illustrative example among many cost-minimising ESOMs - across 22 European countries and four temporal resolutions. We find that shadow prices are compressed relative to observed market prices across all temporal resolutions. Volatility compression is most pronounced at the day-of-week level (10x on average) and at the hour-of-day level (7x on average). Month-of-year and season resolutions show smaller but still substantial compression (3-4x on average). Despite this, month-of-year and season price patterns are structurally aligned with ENTSO-E observations. Hour-of-day alignment improves with model year but the observed market pattern is structurally shifting, making it the resolution hardest to use reliably. Day-of-week alignment is poor but the observed market pattern is near time-invariant, making the model failure identifiable and correctable. Independent literature projections from other LP-based models fall in the same compressed range, indicating that compression is a model-class property rather than a single-model artefact; direct empirical validation across other ESOM families remains an open task. Addressing these structural limitations is a promising avenue for future model development. In the interim, we propose resolution-conditional guidelines to support more principled shadow price applications.

title: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human-AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work (Working Paper)
affiliations: and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human-AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work (Working Paper)
detail.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming how firms create, process, and apply knowledge, yet little is known about the heterogeneity of its productivity effects across users. We report results from a randomized controlled experiment in which participants-analogs of early-career knowledge workers-were assigned to self-study a technical domain using either traditional resources or large-languagemodel (LLM) assistance. On average, GenAI access significantly increased task performance, but the distribution of gains was highly uneven. Improvements were not predicted by GPA or prior knowledge, but by AI Interaction Competence (AIC)-the ability to elicit, filter, and verify model outputs. High-AIC participants realized outsized gains; low-AIC participants saw limited or even negative marginal returns. A scaffolding intervention (conceptual maps) reduced outcome variance, indicating that standardized workflows can mitigate inequality in AI-mediated performance. We interpret these findings through the lens of human-AI complementarities: GenAI raises mean productivity while introducing a new axis of capability inequality. Managerially, firms should pair GenAI access with short AIC micro-training and simple standard operating procedures to capture value consistently and avoid uneven adoption outcomes.

title: Scarcity in an Age of AI Abundance
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Scarcity in an Age of AI Abundance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study does not involve human participants, patients, or case studies requiring ethics approval. All data used are publicly available.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently, without external funding or institutional support.

detail.abstract: A growing narrative in technology commentary and macroeconomics holds that advanced AI and robotics will deliver material abundance, near-zero marginal costs, and an end to economically meaningful scarcity. This paper challenges that view by introducing two original concepts. AI technological abundance (ATA) denotes a regime of strong cost compression and capability expansion in AI-intensive production, in which the marginal cost of many AI-mediated services falls sharply once systems are trained, deployed, and scaled. AI economic abundance (AEA) denotes a strictly stronger outcome: broad affordability of an essential living-standards bundle, requiring that household resources from labor income, asset claims, and transfers keep pace with bundle prices. The central claim of this paper is that ATA does not in general deliver AEA. Even dramatic cost compression does not eliminate scarcity; it reorganizes it, shifting binding constraints and migrating rents toward the layers that remain scarce. To make this argument precise, we develop a five-layer framework in which scarcity and rent formation arise in (1) physical resources and space, (2) infrastructure such as energy, compute, and semiconductor fabrication, (3) capabilities and organizational know-how, (4) institutions that govern access and deployment, and (5) jurisdictions that supply enforcement capacity and security. Layers 4 and 5 are analytically distinct: institutions are the rule systems governing access; jurisdictions are the territorial entities that give those rules coercive force and geopolitical weight. Ownership and control cut across all layers; actor-level rents follow from the interaction of a layer rent vector and a cross-layer exposure matrix, and AEA fails whenever rent intensity rises in layers with high bundle weights while household claims on those layers remain narrow. The framework is illustrated through the semiconductor supply chain in Asia, where infrastructural, institutional, and jurisdictional scarcities interact across borders, and maps plausible winners and losers across industries and households, with implications for inequality, investment, and the political economy of transfers.

title: Dynamic Reliability Assessment of Tree-structured Smart Power Grid Systems considering V2G Mode
affiliations: North University of China, North University of China and Beijing University of Technology

detail.title: Dynamic Reliability Assessment of Tree-structured Smart Power Grid Systems considering V2G Mode
detail.abstract: In response to the reliability challenges of tree-structured smart power grids under Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) mode, this paper proposes an innovative hierarchical modeling framework and presents the corresponding evaluation method. The study aims to address the challenges posed by the multi-state characteristics, random degradation of component performance and the vast state space of such systems. To achieve this, a system model evaluation framework is developed that integrates the Continuous-Time Markov Process (CTMP) and the Universal Generating Function (UGF). Firstly, the CTMP is used to accurately describe the random degradation process of key components, such as Electric Vehicle (EV) batteries, energy storage units, and cables, and to compute their instantaneous state probabilities. Secondly, based on the UGF method, the discharge level, charging level of EVs and transmission capacity of cables are aggregated layer by layer from the bottom up. This process fully considers the power sharing mechanisms and transmission capacity constraints between different layers. Lastly, the time and space complexity of the UGF algorithm are analyzed, and the instantaneous reliability of the entire tree-structured smart power grid systems is derived. Through specific numerical example analysis, the validity and accuracy of this method are verified. A comparative test is also conducted using the Monte Carlo (MC) simulation algorithm. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis of key parameters affecting system reliability is performed to explore the impact mechanisms of different parameters on system reliability, leading to the proposal of corresponding optimization strategies.

title: Dynamic Correlation Regimes and Predictive Decay
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Dynamic Correlation Regimes and Predictive Decay
detail.abstract: Diversification is often treated as a stable feature of portfolio construction, yet market stress repeatedly shows that relationships among assets can change quickly and sometimes all at once. This paper develops a framework for identifying dynamic correlation regimes across major asset classes and measuring the predictive decay of correlation-based warning signals before volatility events. Building on prior work examining correlation shifts around major VIX spikes, this study moves beyond static preevent and event-period correlation matrices by modeling correlations as time-varying, regime-dependent signals. The central question is not only whether asset correlations rise during periods of stress, but also how early those changes become visible, how long their predictive value persists, and when diversification begins to fail before the market fully reprices risk. The proposed framework tracks rolling and model-based correlations across equities, fixed income, commodities, and defensive assets, then classifies periods into correlation regimes using measures of average pairwise correlation, cross-asset correlation dispersion, and stress-alignment behavior. Predictive decay is measured by evaluating how the relationship between correlation signals and future volatility weakens or strengthens across different forward-looking horizons. Rather than presenting diversification as a fixed portfolio benefit, this paper treats diversification as a condition that can deteriorate over time. The goal is to make hidden portfolio risk more visible, especially for everyday investors who may believe they are protected simply because they hold multiple asset classes.

title: AUTORÍA FANTASMA: EL IMPACTO DE LA IA GENERATIVA EN LA REDACCIÓN CIENTÍFICA BOLIVIANA
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: AUTORÍA FANTASMA: EL IMPACTO DE LA IA GENERATIVA EN LA REDACCIÓN CIENTÍFICA BOLIVIANA
detail.abstract: La redacción académica en Bolivia está frente a una crisis de integridad e identidad debido a la adopción sistemática de la Inteligencia Artificial (IA) generativa; conceptos como autoría y producción intelectual se mezclan con sesgos algoritmos que desafían y en situaciones evaden los procesos editoriales tradicionales. Metodología: Esta investigación realizó un análisis estilometrico y computacional a los corpus de las revistas Orbis Tertius (UPAL), Punto Cero (UCB) y Búsqueda (UMSS) en el rango de años de 2017 a 2026; se utilizaron métricas de Riqueza Léxica (TTR), Longitud de Sintaxis (STD), algoritmos de tendencia y verificación manual bibliográfica. Resultados: Los resultados de la investigación revelan fenómenos como inflación estructural en secciones de Resultados y Discusión y canibalismo a otras secciones como Contenido o Marco Teórico, evidenciando una clara tendencia de redacción donde los autores favorecen el uso de IA en ciertas secciones. Discusión: Se identificó una homogeneización de la redacción, apoyada por una convergencia de TTR, presencia de alucinaciones bibliográficas, tendencia a uso de ciertas palabras y fuentes inexistentes. Conclusiones: El estudio concluye que la academia boliviana transita peligrosamente hacia una entropía lingüística donde la identidad de cada autor se verá reemplazada por una redacción algorítmica estandarizada. Palabras clave: inteligencia artificial generativa; estilometría; integridad académica; homogeneización léxica; sesgo lingüístico digital; entropía lingüística; revistas científicas de bolivia; TTR.

title:
שקיפות בעידן הבינה המלאכותית: המשפט הישראלי
Transparency in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: The Israeli Legal Perspective
affiliations: University of Haifa, and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
שקיפות בעידן הבינה המלאכותית: המשפט הישראלי
Transparency in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: The Israeli Legal Perspective
detail.abstract:
In recent years, there has been significant growth in the use of artificial intelligence (AI). Despite its efficiency, AI usage presents challenges, particularly in places where decisions have significant implications for human rights. This article focuses on algorithmic transparency in the AI era in the context of the right to freedom of information of government authorities.

Within this framework, the article examines the principles of transparency concerning the right to information in the AI era. It examines how Israeli courts address this issue regarding traditional algorithms, and how it affects the AI era. The article advocates recognizing algorithmic transparency as part of the right to freedom of information, considering both the language and the purpose of the law, and considering global trends advocating transparency in artificial intelligence. Algorithmic transparency as part of the right to freedom of information is crucial to enable continued effective oversight of government authorities’ actions.

title: The Compositional Utility of Goods

detail.title: The Compositional Utility of Goods
detail.abstract: This note proposes a compositional perspective on the utility of goods. Rather than treating the utility derived from a good as arising from a single homogeneous source, the framework represents utility as the sum of distinct component-specific contributions corresponding to different underlying mechanisms through which value is generated. In particular, utility is decomposed into Relief, Comfort, Status, and Achievement components, reflecting functional necessity, experiential quality, social signaling, and personal meaning, respectively. A key implication of this framework is that identical goods may generate utility in fundamentally different ways across individuals. Two consumers purchasing the same product at the same price may derive utility from entirely different components, implying that observed consumption patterns may mask substantial heterogeneity in the underlying sources of value. The decomposition therefore provides a structural interpretation of variation in consumer behavior that complements standard utility-based approaches. More broadly, the note contributes to a compositional framework in which utility is understood as arising from multiple distinct processes whose relative importance varies across individuals and contexts. By making these mechanisms explicit, the framework offers a simple but flexible approach for analyzing how goods generate value.

title: The Environmental Implications of AI Uncertainty Shocks: Evidence from a Novel Text-Based Index for the United States
affiliations: Cyprus International University and Central Bank of Nigeria

detail.title: The Environmental Implications of AI Uncertainty Shocks: Evidence from a Novel Text-Based Index for the United States
detail.abstract: Data centres powering artificial intelligence are among the fastest-growing sources of US electricity demand, yet the role of uncertainty about AI's trajectory in shaping the power sector's emissions footprint is unexplored. Using a novel text-based AI Uncertainty (AIU) index and monthly data from 2016 to 2025, we show that AIU shocks are associated with persistent declines in US electric-sector CO₂ emissions of roughly five per cent at horizons up to eighteen months. The result is robust across lag specifications, survives exclusion of the COVID-19 period, and holds under instrumental-variables estimation using foreign AI regulatory events as an external instrument. The pattern is consistent with a real-options mechanism in which AI uncertainty postpones irreversible grid and data-centre investment, suggesting that policy initiatives that reduce AI-related uncertainty may accelerate rather than mitigate near-term electricity-demand growth.

title: Reincarnation in Hindu Dharma: Death as Transformation of Energy and Continuity of Spiritual Missions (1600-2000)

detail.title: Reincarnation in Hindu Dharma: Death as Transformation of Energy and Continuity of Spiritual Missions (1600-2000)
detail.abstract: This paper explores the hypothesis that death is not the end but a transformation of energy, and reincarnation is the mechanism by which spiritual missions continue across centuries. Focusing exclusively on Hindu dharma, the study compares saints and spiritual leaders from 1600 to the present, analyzing similarities in thought, qualities, and missions. Using philosophical foundations from the Upanishads and Bhagavad Gita, historical case studies of saints, and scientific analogies from energy conservation, the paper demonstrates that reincarnation provides the most coherent explanation for the continuity of spiritual work across generations. Tables and charts illustrate recurring themes and unfinished missions carried forward, proving that reincarnation is not merely a belief but a logical framework for understanding spiritual continuity.

title: MECHANISM ECOLOGY: Loop Closure, Surplus Routing, and the Life of Mechanisms Induced Symbiosis as a Formal Specimen
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: MECHANISM ECOLOGY: Loop Closure, Surplus Routing, and the Life of Mechanisms Induced Symbiosis as a Formal Specimen
detail.abstract: This paper introduces mechanism ecology: the study of whether a system's profit opportunities remain coupled to the substrate that makes the system valuable. Within this broader field, induced symbiosis names a specific closed-loop phenomenon: self-interested agents become endogenous repair organs because substrate maintenance is the durable margin. The central distinction is between open-loop systems, in which surplus exits the substrate that generated it, and closed-loop systems, in which the cost of deviation is routed back into restoration of the substrate. I identify four conditions under which such closure produces induced symbiosis: a substrate equilibrium, participant discretion, genuine systemic cost, and loop closure. When these conditions hold, a scaling cost imposed on deviation from equilibrium creates an endogenous intermediary class whose profit motive is structurally aligned with system health.

title: Persistence Hallucinated? Research Integrity Issues in Voigtländer and Voth (2012)
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: Persistence Hallucinated? Research Integrity Issues in Voigtländer and Voth (2012)
detail.abstract: Voigtländer and Voth's (2012) study of the medieval origins of antisemitic violence in Nazi Germany has various research integrity issues. Their research design is supposed to rely on "unambiguous information" that often does not exist in their sources. Furthermore, when such information does exist, it frequently contradicts the dataset that is supposed to have been coded from those sources. There are also unexplained discrepancies in their dataset relating to the official statistics of the deportations of Germany's Jews during the Holocaust. As a result, Voigtländer and Voth's (2012) study cannot be replicated.

title: The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches
affiliations: Stanford University, Duke University, Stanford University, University of Pennsylvania, Stanford University and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches
detail.abstract:
Schools across the U.S. have sharply restricted student use of phones during the school day. We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining large-scale surveys, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that pouch adoption substantially reduces phone use as measured by GPS pings and teacher reports. In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase and student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption. However, effects on well-being become positive in later years and disciplinary effects fade. For academic achievement, average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects. We find little evidence of effects on school attendance, self-reported classroom attention, or perceived online bullying.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Wind Turbine Proximity and Health: Longitudinal Evidence from U.S. Households
affiliations: University of Augsburg, Columbia University and University of Pittsburgh

detail.title: Wind Turbine Proximity and Health: Longitudinal Evidence from U.S. Households
detail.abstract:
Rapid growth of wind energy plays a key role in global efforts to reduce carbon emissions, yet public concerns persist about its potential health effects, particularly through noise exposure. While some studies and media reports suggest that wind turbines may contribute to sleep disturbances, anxiety, and even suicide, existing evidence remains limited and inconclusive. This study combines geolocated data on turbines from the U.S. Wind Turbine Database with longitudinal survey data on over 120,000 households (2011–2023) and consumer purchasing records to assess whether proximity to wind turbines affects mental and physical health. We examine a wide range of outcomes, including depression, anxiety, sleep disorders, headaches, and use of sleep aids and painkillers. Comparing households before and after nearby turbine installations, we find no detectable adverse health effects from turbine exposure at typical exposure distances. While we cannot rule out small effects, our confidence intervals exclude moderate-to-large impacts, suggesting that fears about substantial health impacts are not borne out in population-level data. Other disamenities such as noise, shadow flicker, and visual intrusion may still affect quality of life even absent measurable health impacts.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Technology Adoption and Optimal Policy
affiliations: University of Chicago - Department of Economics, Washington University in St. Louis and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond

detail.title: Technology Adoption and Optimal Policy
detail.abstract:
We study optimal policy in a dynamic general equilibrium model where heterogeneous monopolistic competitive firms pay a fixed cost to adopt a frontier technology that grows exogenously. Using Mean Field Games tools, we show that the optimal policy consists of exactly two time-invariant subsidies: one correcting the static misallocation from market power, and one correcting the dynamic under-incentive to adopt. This holds outside of balanced growth paths, for any initial distribution of technology gaps. We analyze a simplified version of the model that aggregates to a Neoclassical Growth Model with an S-shaped production function whenever complementarities are strong, and fully characterize when the optimal policy uniquely implements the first best. When it does not, two novel results emerge: the efficient allocation prescribes escaping a poverty trap—providing an explicit optimality foundation for a Big Push—and, more surprisingly, escaping an abundance trap, where dismantling adopted technologies is optimal. In both cases, a temporary, costless supplementary policy restores unique implementation.

title: BARRIERS TO ADOPTION OF INTERNAL DEVELOPER PORTALS IN LARGE-SCALE ORGANIZATIONS

detail.title: BARRIERS TO ADOPTION OF INTERNAL DEVELOPER PORTALS IN LARGE-SCALE ORGANIZATIONS

keywords: of Computer Science and Software Engineering Barriers to Adoption of Internal Developer Portals

detail.abstract: Internal Developer Portals (IDPs) have emerged as a critical component in modern software engineering, enabling organizations to streamline development workflows, enhance developer experience, and enforce standardized practices across teams. Despite their growing popularity, large-scale organizations often encounter significant challenges in adopting and implementing these platforms effectively. This study examines the barriers to adoption of internal developer portals in large-scale organizations, focusing on organizational, technical, and cultural constraints. Key issues include resistance to change among development teams, lack of clear governance structures, integration complexities with legacy systems, and insufficient stakeholder alignment. Additionally, scalability concerns, inadequate documentation, and limited executive support further hinder successful implementation. The paper highlights how these barriers can reduce the perceived value of IDPs and delay digital transformation initiatives. By analyzing these challenges, the study provides insights into strategies for overcoming adoption obstacles, including fostering a culture of collaboration, investing in training, and ensuring strong leadership commitment. Ultimately, addressing these barriers is essential for organizations seeking to leverage IDPs to improve productivity, consistency, and innovation in large-scale software development environments.

title: Taxes and Financial Distress: Evidence from Establishment-Level Data
affiliations: and Fordham University

detail.title: Taxes and Financial Distress: Evidence from Establishment-Level Data
detail.abstract:
We use establishment-level data to examine the relation between corporate taxes and financial distress. Using a border discontinuity design, we document that higher corporate income tax rates significantly increase financial distress, particularly for geographically concentrated firms, with sizable spillovers across establishments. We further investigate how taxes affect establishment-level financial distress by exploiting the interest limitation rule introduced by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that affected firms experience a decline in financial distress. This occurs because the reduced tax advantage of debt induces firms to deleverage, reducing financial distress through capital structure adjustments.

title: The Value of Reliable Statistics
affiliations: , Cornell University, American Enterprise Institute (AEI) and American Enterprise Institute

detail.title: The Value of Reliable Statistics
detail.abstract:
On August 1, 2025, President Trump fired the head of the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and claimed that the agency’s data were “rigged.” In the aftermath, measures of economic policy uncertainty rose sharply, consistent with the idea that reduced trust in official data increases uncertainty for investors, businesses, and households. We use an event-study design to estimate the effect of the firing on policy uncertainty, and then map that increase in uncertainty into implied macroeconomic outcomes. This yields a back-of-the-envelope estimate of the marginal value of public trust in official statistics. Our baseline estimate implies that preserving trust in the integrity and quality of official statistics generates economic benefits of about $25 for every $1 spent on the agency’s budget.

title: Till the IRS Do Us Part: (Optimal) Taxation of Households
affiliations: , University of Pennsylvania and University of Southampton

detail.title: Till the IRS Do Us Part: (Optimal) Taxation of Households
detail.abstract:
This paper argues that a progressive tax system combined with individual taxation of married couples can generate more revenue than the current household-based U.S. system, especially when the extra revenues do not induce negative labor supply effects through increased government transfers. A progressive system that taxes individuals rather than couples jointly leads to larger labor force participation and higher average human capital, creates more “fiscal space”, Laffer curves shift up and social welfare potentially rises. In our model with one- and two-earner households, human capital and an extensive margin labor supply decision, the peak of the Laffer curve is 18 percentage points higher with an individual-based, progressive tax system than with the current U.S. tax system. The maximum revenue is attained with 100% more progressivity than the current system, and at an average tax rate of 42%. Progressive taxation, when imposed on individuals rather than households, lowers the average tax rate for individuals with modest potential income that are close to the participation margin. At the same time, it creates a positive income effect on the labor supply of these individuals by reducing the net income of their higher earning spouses and limiting their net earnings potential in the case of a high temporary labor productivity. Steady state social welfare is larger with individual taxation. The optimal progressivity is higher than the current U.S. status quo, and results in welfare gains of 0.8% in consumption-equivalent variation. Cohorts born during the transition also experience significant welfare gains from this reform.

title: Power to the Personnel? The Impacts of Managerial Discretion vs. Worker Democracy in Employee Recognition
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and Dartmouth College

detail.title: Power to the Personnel? The Impacts of Managerial Discretion vs. Worker Democracy in Employee Recognition
detail.abstract:
Worker agency—workers' influence over organizational decisions—is a commonly-cited determinant of employee engagement, productivity, and organizational culture. We conducted a firm-level RCT in India, randomizing whether employee recognition and associated bonuses were allocated: based on a worker vote (agency treatment), at the discretion of the manager (managerial discretion treatment), or at random and unrelated to performance (control). We find that workplace democracy increases worker attendance, but managerial discretion improves productivity. There are also implications for firm culture and knowledge spillovers, with the manager arm reducing work-related discussions between workers. Winners in the manager arm are positively selected on attendance and productivity, while those in the democracy arm are positively selected on attendance, social interactions, and likelihood of sharing the reward with co-workers in exchange for votes. These results highlight how what is valued in the workplace impacts worker behavior and firm culture, as well as the potential for informal contracts among workers to interact with workplace incentives.

title: Who Marries Whom? The Role of Segregation by Race and Class

detail.title: Who Marries Whom? The Role of Segregation by Race and Class
detail.abstract:
Americans rarely marry outside their race or class group, a pattern with well-documented implications for inequality and intergenerational mobility. Limited exposure—or interactions with members of other groups—may partly explain these low intergroup marriage rates. We instrument for exposure using variation in childhood neighborhoods based on whether other race and class groups had more opposite-sex children of similar age. Exposure increases interclass (high- and low-parent-income) marriage but has no detectable effect on interracial (White and Black) marriage. A spatial marriage market model predicts that residential segregation—one of many forms of exposure—accounts for more than one third of marital sorting by class but less than 5% by race.

title: The Microstructure of AI Diffusion: Evidence from Firms, Business Functions, and Worker Tasks
affiliations: U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Census Bureau, Center for Economic Studies - US Census Bureau, U.S. Census Bureau - Center for Economic Studies,  and

detail.title: The Microstructure of AI Diffusion: Evidence from Firms, Business Functions, and Worker Tasks
detail.abstract:
Using novel, nationally representative data from the 2026 AI supplement to the U.S. Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS), we characterize AI diffusion across three layers: firm-wide adoption, business-function deployment, and worker-task use. During Nov 2025–Jan 2026, 18% of firms used AI in at least one function (32%, employment-weighted), with adoption expected to reach 22% within six months. Use is concentrated in large firms and knowledge-intensive sectors, reaching 50%–60% (60%–70%, employment-weighted) among very large firms in Information, Professional Services, and Finance. Among adopters, scope remains limited: 57% use AI in three or fewer functions, most often Sales and Marketing (52%), Strategy (45%), and IT (41%). Worker-level use appears in 23% (41%, employment-weighted) of firms, primarily for writing, document analysis, and information search; 65% restrict use to three or fewer tasks. Evidence suggests both top-down and bottom-up diffusion: worker use can occur without firm adoption, and vice versa. Most firms (66%) use AI for task augmentation, while employment reductions are rare (2%). Regression results show a positive relationship between firm performance and AI integration breadth. However, functional deployment and operational investment are associated with employment declines, while worker-task use is not once these factors are controlled for.

title: Residential Energy Burden: Geographic Variation and Price Responsiveness
affiliations: Concordia College

detail.title: Residential Energy Burden: Geographic Variation and Price Responsiveness
detail.abstract: Residential energy costs consume a larger share of income for lower-income households than for higher-income ones, but the size of that gap varies considerably across the United States. Using Consumer Expenditure Survey microdata from 2005 through 2024 merged with state-level energy prices from the EIA State Energy Data System, I document residential energy burden across all nine U.S. census divisions and the income distribution, and estimate price elasticities by income decile. Energy burden declines sharply with income across all divisions. Price elasticities are inelastic throughout and larger in absolute value at higher income levels, compounding the distributional burden effects.

title: Seeing the Goal, Missing the Truth: Human Accountability for AI Bias
affiliations: Robert H. Smith School of Business, Emory University Goizueta Business School and Lancaster University - Lancaster University Management School

detail.title: Seeing the Goal, Missing the Truth: Human Accountability for AI Bias
detail.abstract:
This research explores how human-defined goals influence the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) through purpose-conditioned cognition. Using financial prediction tasks, we show that revealing the downstream use (e.g., predicting stock returns or earnings) of LLM outputs leads the LLM to generate biased sentiment and competition measures, even though these measures are intended to be downstream task–independent. Goal-aware prompting shifts these intermediate measures toward the disclosed downstream objective, producing in-sample overfitting. Specifically, purpose leakage improves performance on data prior to the LLM’s knowledge cutoff, but provides no advantage after the cutoff. This bias is strong enough that regularization of prompt instructions cannot fully address this form of overfitting. We further show that the bias can arise from users’ unintentional conversational context that hints at the purpose. Overall, we document that AI bias due to “seeing the goal” is not an algorithmic flaw, but stems from human accountability in research design.

title: The Collision Probability: A Two-dimensional Surrogate Safety Measure to Assess Collision Risk under Uncertain Vehicle Movements
affiliations: University of Tennessee Knoxville, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Northwestern University

detail.title: The Collision Probability: A Two-dimensional Surrogate Safety Measure to Assess Collision Risk under Uncertain Vehicle Movements
detail.abstract: Surrogate Safety Measures (SSMs) are widely used for proactive traffic risk assessment. This study proposes collision probability (CP), a novel surrogate safety measure that applies a probability scale to assess collision risk under uncertain vehicle movements. At any time of risk assessment, this approach predicts trajectories of a pair of vehicles over a specified near-future horizon and anticipates the critical time when vehicles reach the minimum relative distance within that horizon. Based on the stochasticity of kinematic parameters given by probability density functions, the probability of a collision is calculated through integrals of the relative distance distribution. While the measure is established in a two-dimensional space for general traffic scenarios, CP can be derived through a simplified one-dimensional version. Based on the uncertainty of vehicle movement calibrated through real-world trajectory observed in Chattanooga, USA, a comprehensive evaluation of CP is conducted across three scenarios: car-following trajectories in stop-and-go traffic, and two types of conflict trajectories at an intersection with turning and through movements. In each scenario, the probabilities are compared with the frequency of collisions from repeated simulations, as well as existing SSMs such as Time-to-Collision. The results indicate that CP provides much more accurate risk assessment and demonstrates strong cross-scenario applicability, even under theoretical and future scenarios.

title: Characteristics of a Sufficient Statistic to Measure City Housing Prices
affiliations: Florida State University, College of Business, Government of the United States of America - Office of Financial Research and George Washington University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Characteristics of a Sufficient Statistic to Measure City Housing Prices
detail.abstract:
Characterizing the level and change of housing prices in cities is central to many empirical questions, whether prices are measured using rents or asset values. The task is complicated by the heterogeneity of the housing stock, the joint consumption of housing and neighborhood, and differences in accessibility. This paper focuses on intra-city location which, based on economic theory, is systematically related to housing prices. The final conclusion is that a sufficient statistic to describe both the level of and change in the average housing price requires that prices be aggregated from relatively homogeneous market areas and weighted by housing quantities such as dwelling units or interior space. Common repeat-sales and hedonic indexes are generally not weighted in this fashion but could be modified to do so.

title: The Annuity Puzzle Revisited: Barriers, Behavior, and Policy Paths to Lifetime Income
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Marketing Area, University of California, Los Angeles - Anderson School of Management, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign - Department of Finance, Hebrew University, Jerusalem Israel, York University - Schulich School of Business,  and 401(k) Annuity Hub

detail.title: The Annuity Puzzle Revisited: Barriers, Behavior, and Policy Paths to Lifetime Income
detail.abstract:
Wealth decumulation decisions, or how to optimize consumption over an uncertain remaining lifespan, are among the most difficult people face. They involve intertemporal tradeoffs, uncertainty, complexity, and emotion, yet many consumers receive little formal guidance. A central challenge is securing lifetime income and avoiding outliving resources, particularly through life annuities that guarantee income for life. Standard economic models predict high demand for annuities, but in practice few individuals purchase them, a gap known as the annuity puzzle. This paper introduces annuities, examines limited adoption among consumers and plan sponsors, reviews leading explanations, and outlines approaches to increase uptake and improve decision quality.

title: Understanding Medicaid Managed Care: The Procured Competition Model
affiliations: Harvard University - Harvard Kennedy School (HKS) and Yale University - School of Public Health

detail.title: Understanding Medicaid Managed Care: The Procured Competition Model
detail.abstract:
Medicaid is one of the largest public programs in the United States — providing health insurance to over 75 million low-income Americans — and over three quarters of its enrollees receive care via private “managed care” insurers. In this summary article, we make three central points about the economics of contracting out Medicaid to private insurers. First, the empirical evidence on Medicaid privatization is mixed: contracting out has not meaningfully reduced public costs or improved quality of care. Second, we propose a framework, which we call “procured competition,” to describe the unique structure of Medicaid managed care as a hybrid of public procurement and regulated competition. Third, we discuss the key policy levers across procurement, competition, and consumer choice in this model. Throughout, we highlight open research questions, arguing that the enormous variation in how states design these programs — combined with limited evidence on what works — represents a promising area for high-impact scholarship.

title: Learning by Mail: The Impact of Correspondence Schools in Early 20th Century America

detail.title: Learning by Mail: The Impact of Correspondence Schools in Early 20th Century America
detail.abstract:
This paper examines correspondence education as an alternative educational pathway in early 20th-century America. Using newly digitized records from the International Correspondence Schools—the largest such institution, with over 4 million students by 1940—linked to census data, I show that enrollment increased the likelihood of skilled employment by 6-10pp within 3-10 years, particularly among younger students who used it as a substitute for high school. I develop a general equilibrium Roy-style model where individuals sort into educational options by ability. Consistent with the model, correspondence education facilitated skill acquisition for lower-ability individuals and improved selection into high school, amplifying its returns.

title: How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Science: Evidence from AlphaFold
affiliations: Kellogg School of Management and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: How Artificial Intelligence Shapes Science: Evidence from AlphaFold
detail.abstract:
We study how a frontier AI model affects scientific discovery by examining the release of the AlphaFold2 algorithm and its impact on structural biology and related fields of science. Structural biology is the field of science concerned with understanding the structure and function of proteins. Researchers in this field historically devoted substantial time and resources to experimentally solving three-dimensional protein structures. AlphaFold can predict these structures without running experiments. In July 2021, researchers gained access to hundreds of thousands of these AI-predicted structures virtually overnight. Yet, to date, we find that the rate of experimental structure determination has remained almost unchanged. Instead, researchers appear to use predicted structures to facilitate and complement experimental structure determination. Looking at downstream science that builds on protein structures, we find that basic research on proteins that had no structure information prior to AlphaFold increases by 15 to 40% relative to proteins that already had a structure, shifting the direction of research toward less-studied proteins. However, we find no evidence so far that more applied, early-stage drug development is targeting these proteins, though such activity may emerge in the future.

title: Influence Capacity Beyond GDP: An Axiomatic Three-Axis Decomposition

detail.title: Influence Capacity Beyond GDP: An Axiomatic Three-Axis Decomposition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was conducted by the author independently.

detail.abstract:
Cross-national comparisons that rest on Gross Domestic Product silently assume one dollar of value added equals one dollar of mobilizable, system-shaping capability. The assumption fails sharply when the comparison spans different industrial structures, state capacities, and network positions in the global production and rule-making system.

This paper develops an axiomatic framework that replaces GDP, in its role as a proxy for national power, with a three-axis influence functional I(S) = PI^a * MU^b * NU^c, where PI is productive capacity (defined via useful work / exergy throughput), MU is mobilizable surplus (a control-theoretic reachability rate over factor allocations), and NU is network position (a percolation-based perturbation rate on the technology sets of other systems).

The Cobb-Douglas form is derived along three converging routes: (i) a representation theorem from five axioms (continuity, monotonicity, zero-axis annihilation, base-point-independent multiplicative scaling, log-additivity); (ii) a Tullock-contest microfoundation across three independent contests with distinct battlegrounds; (iii) a budget-feedback dynamic microfoundation deriving the linear coupled ODE from a capability-evolution principle. A meta-theorem on collapse sequence unifies a strict PI -> NU -> MU ordering for self-productive industrial-era hegemons with an information-era inversion (NU -> PI -> MU) and an administered-external-base regime.

The framework is calibrated against eleven historical cases (Habsburg Spain, Dutch Republic, Pax Britannica, late Soviet Union, Qing China, Ottoman Empire, Mughal India, Tang China, Roman Empire, Mongol Empire, Russia 2014-2024) plus the Saudi-US 1970 static cross-section, with sub-national portability tested against three corporate dyads (Apple/Samsung, Microsoft/Google, TSMC/Intel) and three documented historical firm collapses (BlackBerry, Nokia, Kodak).

Four pre-registered falsifiable predictions for the US-China transition are reported with explicit failure thresholds: (P1) 2028 dollar reserve share >= 52%; (P2) 2030 advanced-semiconductor alliance share >= 80%; (P3) 2032 RMB reserve share <= 8%; (P4) 2045 China/US overall influence ratio in [0.77, 1.18]. Eight Python companion scripts reproduce all numerical claims.

detail.abstract: This document establishes for the first time the conceptual foundations, terminology, and architecture of what the author calls Applied Intelligence Architecture (AIA): an emerging field that radically distinguishes between the use of artificial intelligence tools and the construction of sovereign, personalized intelligence systems. The concept of the Cognitive Router is introduced as the central component of every AIA architecture — the orchestration layer that interprets intent, routes tasks to specialized agents, and maintains systemic coherence across the system. The Cognitive Sovereignty System (CSS) is presented as the first documented implementation of this category. The document defines AIA as a new discipline at the intersection of systems architecture, cognitive design, and applied knowledge management, and establishes four foundational principles: system sovereignty, structural personalization, active institutional memory, and platform independence.

detail.title: Firm Pay, Amenities, and Inequality
detail.abstract:
We estimate firm-specific amenity valuations using discrete choice experiments embedded in a large-scale survey of German workers linked to administrative records. Workers rank hypothetical offers from real firms they would consider joining, with randomized wages identifying money-metric valuations. Valuations vary substantially across firms and demographic groups, yet a single index performs surprisingly well. Valuations are approximately orthogonal to firm wage premia; they therefore do not offset between-firm wage inequality. However, male-female differences in amenity valuations explain part of the gender wage gap.

title: MEASURING SUCCESS IN PLATFORM ENGINEERING: A REVIEW OF METRICS AND KPIS ACROSS LITERATURE
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: MEASURING SUCCESS IN PLATFORM ENGINEERING: A REVIEW OF METRICS AND KPIS ACROSS LITERATURE

keywords: of Computer Science and Software Engineering Platform Engineering

detail.abstract: Platform engineering has become a critical discipline in modern software development, enabling organizations to improve developer experience, accelerate software delivery, and standardize operational practices through internal platforms. As adoption grows, there is an increasing need to evaluate the effectiveness of platform engineering initiatives using measurable outcomes. This study, Measuring Success in Platform Engineering: A Review of Metrics and KPIs Across Literature, examines existing research and industry practices to identify and analyze key performance indicators (KPIs) used to assess platform engineering success. The study highlights that success in platform engineering is multidimensional and cannot be captured through a single metric. Commonly discussed metrics include developer productivity, deployment frequency, lead time for changes, system reliability, platform adoption rates, and developer satisfaction. Additionally, emerging indicators such as cognitive load reduction, self-service usage rates, and internal platform engagement are increasingly being used to evaluate developer experience and platform effectiveness. However, the literature also reveals inconsistencies in how these metrics are defined, measured, and applied across different organizational contexts. A key finding of this review is the lack of standardized frameworks for measuring platform engineering success, which leads to challenges in comparing outcomes across organizations. While some metrics align with DevOps principles such as DORA metrics, others are more qualitative and experience-driven, making them difficult to quantify consistently. The study also identifies a growing shift toward outcome-based and experience-centric measurement approaches that go beyond traditional operational KPIs. In conclusion, the paper emphasizes the need for a balanced, multi-dimensional measurement framework that integrates technical performance, business outcomes, and developer experience. Such a framework would enable organizations to more accurately assess the value of platform engineering initiatives and guide continuous improvement in internal developer platforms.

title: When Does Automating AI Research Produce Explosive Growth? Feedback Loops in Innovation Networks
affiliations: , , Columbia University and

detail.title: When Does Automating AI Research Produce Explosive Growth? Feedback Loops in Innovation Networks
detail.abstract:
AI labs are increasingly using AI itself to accelerate AI research, creating a feedback loop that could lead to an intelligence explosion. We develop a general semi-endogenous growth model with an innovation network, where research and automation in one sector increase the productivity of research in other sectors, and derive a clean analytical condition under which growth becomes superexponential (``explosive''). We find that automating research can offset diminishing returns to ideas by activating two reinforcing channels: a technological feedback loop across research sectors, and an economic feedback loop in which higher output finances further research. Growth becomes explosive if the combined strength of technological and economic feedback loops overcomes diminishing returns. In a simple simulation calibrated to trends in AI progress, fully automating software research and modest (5%) automation in other sectors generates a singularity within six years. Bottlenecks do not overturn the result if task automation advances sufficiently fast.

title: The Proposed Artificial Intelligence Bill (2026): Analyzing the EU Blueprint and the Realities of AI Regulation in Kenya
