detail.title: The Proposed Artificial Intelligence Bill (2026): Analyzing the EU Blueprint and the Realities of AI Regulation in Kenya
detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has threatened the already frail regulatory frameworks in middle and lower middle African Countries. As jurisdictions, like Kenya, rush to regulate the development, deployment, and use of algorithmic systems, some structural, ethical and legal issues have been laid bare. This article attempts analyzes the ongoing discourse surrounding the proposed Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026, contextualizing it against its sister, European Union's regulatory model. This paper functions as a commentary and enlightenment of the practical realities facing the Bill and the regulation of AI in our space. It argues that while the Bill and its models offer Kenya a robust starting point, successful regulation requires highly localized institutional harmonization, specialized judicial training and mitigation of the already existing facets related to data protection and sub-version.

title: COGNITIVE LOAD REDUCTION THROUGH INTERNAL DEVELOPER PLATFORMS: EVIDENCE FROM EMPIRICAL AND GREY SOURCES
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: COGNITIVE LOAD REDUCTION THROUGH INTERNAL DEVELOPER PLATFORMS: EVIDENCE FROM EMPIRICAL AND GREY SOURCES

keywords: of Computer Science and Software Engineering Internal Developer Platforms

detail.abstract: Internal Developer Platforms (IDPs) have emerged as a central component of modern platform engineering, aiming to improve developer productivity by abstracting infrastructure complexity and streamlining software delivery workflows. A key expected benefit of these platforms is the reduction of cognitive load experienced by software engineers during development, deployment, and operational tasks. This study, Cognitive Load Reduction Through Internal Developer Platforms: Evidence from Empirical and Grey Sources, synthesizes findings from both empirical research and grey literature to examine how IDPs influence cognitive load in software development environments. The study explores how internal platforms reduce cognitive burden by providing standardized workflows, self-service capabilities, automated pipelines, and reusable templates that minimize the need for repetitive decision-making. Evidence suggests that by consolidating tooling and abstracting low-level infrastructure concerns, IDPs enable developers to focus more on business logic and less on operational complexity. Empirical sources indicate improvements in developer efficiency and workflow simplification, while grey sources-including industry reports, engineering blogs, and practitioner documentation-highlight real-world implementations where platform engineering has reduced context switching and improved developer experience. However, the findings also reveal that cognitive load reduction is not guaranteed and may vary depending on platform design quality, usability, and organizational context. Poorly designed platforms, overly complex abstractions, or rigid workflows can introduce new forms of cognitive burden, negating intended benefits. Additionally, the lack of standardized measurement techniques for cognitive load in software engineering presents challenges in consistently evaluating platform effectiveness across studies. The study concludes that while Internal Developer Platforms have strong potential to reduce cognitive load, their effectiveness depends on thoughtful design, continuous feedback loops, and alignment with developer workflows. A balanced approach that considers both technical and human factors is essential for maximizing the cognitive and productivity benefits of platform engineering.

title: Towards a New Macroeconomic Architecture: A Foundational Roadmap and Integrated Framework for Testing Cooperativism

detail.abstract:
This working paper serves as a foundational roadmap for the development of cooperativism as a new macroeconomic architecture. It identifies key and often insufficiently addressed challenges in contemporary economic science, summarizes the progress achieved so far, and outlines the future trajectory of this multidisciplinary research program.

The central contribution of the paper is the introduction of a new theoretical and methodological framework designed for the analysis and stress testing of macroeconomic architectures. It is based on the premise that the persistent divergence between the rate of return on capital (r) and the rate of economic growth (g) may stem from the institutional configuration of economic systems themselves, rather than solely from ex post distributive mechanisms. This perspective implies the need for a fundamental expansion of existing approaches to the design and modelling of economic systems.

The proposed methodology integrates four key analytical modules: a stock-flow consistent (SFC) framework ensuring macroeconomic integrity, agent-based modelling (ABM) capturing micro-level interactions, an assessment of financial and digital resilience, and a behavioural analysis of the concentration of power. This synthesis enables the ex ante identification of structural mechanisms through which institutional arrangements shape the dynamics of capital accumulation.

A preliminary application of this framework to the model of cooperativism suggests that increasing the level of macroeconomic democracy—defined as a composite analytical parameter encompassing wealth distribution, the role of inheritance, the degree of participation in firm governance, and the functioning of market mechanisms—may lead to a systematic decline in the rentier component of returns on capital alongside a simultaneous stimulation of productivity. Within this setting, the difference between r − g appears as a decreasing function of the institutional parameter, indicating the existence of a threshold level for wealth convergence.

The model of cooperativism, based on the synergy of sovereign money and cooperative structures, is presented as an analytically tractable configuration enabling the testing of the proposed framework. The results thus provide a starting point for further comparative research on alternative macroeconomic architectures and their impact on long-term stability and the distributive dynamics of economic systems.

title: The Convention on Contracts for the International Sales of Goods ("CISG"): an examination from the European Union Value Added Tax law perspective

detail.title: The Convention on Contracts for the International Sales of Goods ("CISG"): an examination from the European Union Value Added Tax law perspective
detail.abstract: This analysis shall explore and evaluate the effects of the EU VAT rules on CISG transfers of risks or ownership to property in conjunction with the EU VAT formal and procedural requirements and differing views on such place of transactions. As the effects of the EU VAT within the CISG disputes cannot be observed directly, this paper will use several CISG and CJEU VAT rulings to examine their relationships and ramifications. The paper brings to light that there is no common understanding amongst the courts and tribunals of what constitutes the requirement of compliance with formalities under Article 54 CISG, and if non-compliance with the VAT rules caused the aggrieved party to lose money directly from the breach, the burden of the VAT must be an element in the calculation of damages under Article 74 CISG.

title: No Labels, No Problem: Identifying Investment Fund Cohorts through Clustering
affiliations: , European Securities and Markets Authority , European Securities and Markets Authority, European Central Bank (ECB), ,  and

detail.title: No Labels, No Problem: Identifying Investment Fund Cohorts through Clustering
detail.abstract: This paper applies a tailored clustering approach to identify cohorts of investment funds for financial stability assessment. To define clusters, we use regulatory data on asset class exposures reported under the Alternative Investment Fund Managers Directive (AIFMD). We applied our approach to more than 10,000 alternative investment funds (AIFs) holding €3.7 trillion in assets, revealing 12 economically interpretable fund cohorts, including traditional bond and equity funds, liability-driven investment (LDI) funds, and private asset funds. Our cluster-based approach substantially outperforms traditional AIFMD categories in explaining fund return variance and points to material vulnerabilities, notably concentrated leverage in GBP-denominated LDI funds and widespread liquidity mismatches. The dispersion of these cohorts across EU jurisdictions underscores the need for oversight and cross-border coordination in ensuring the macroprudential oversight of the investment fund sector. This framework provides regulators, supervisors and macroprudential authorities with a practical framework for identifying funds whose collective behaviour could amplify systemic risks during periods of market stress.

title: Dynamic Panel Threshold Regression for Unbalanced Panels, with Endogenous Regressors and Continuity-Robust Inference
affiliations: Vietnam National University - Ho Chi Minh City (VNU-HCM) - International University and

detail.title: Dynamic Panel Threshold Regression for Unbalanced Panels, with Endogenous Regressors and Continuity-Robust Inference

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors certify that they have no affiliations with or involvement in any organization or entity with any financial interest or non-financial interest in the subject matter or materials discussed in this manuscript.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors did not receive any funding for this work.

detail.abstract: We introduce xtdpthresh, a Stata command for estimating the dynamic panel threshold model of Seo and Shin (2016) on unbalanced panels. The command supports three transformations — first-difference (FD), forward orthogonal deviations (FOD; Arellano and Bover 1995), and system GMM (Blundell and Bond 1998) — with user control over the instrument set via collapse and maxlag() in the style of xtabond2 (Roodman 2009). Threshold-parameter inference follows the grid-inversion framework of Gong and Seo (2026, §4.1) combined with the fast-bootstrap convention of xthenreg (Seo, Kim, and Kim 2019, the reference Stata implementation of Seo-Shin 2016), which uses unit-level wild residual weights, a fixed first-stage GMM weight matrix, and one-step bootstrap GMM per draw. This scheme is 30-60-fold faster than the exact cluster-resample Algorithm 1 of Gong-Seo and matches what Stata threshold users are already accustomed to from xthenreg; Gong-Seo uniform-validity (Theorem I.1) is proved for the exact algorithm, while we document empirical coverage near nominal in a Monte Carlo on the canonical Seo-Shin Tong-SETAR data-generating process as evidence for the fast scheme's practical validity. The command extends the fast-bootstrap scheme beyond the sup-Wald linearity test of xthenreg to the grid-inversion threshold CI and the continuity test of Gong-Seo, and to the FOD and system GMM configurations for which formal bootstrap validity is not yet established in the literature. We illustrate the command on Hansen's (1999) firm investment data, on an artificially unbalanced variant of that dataset, and on FDIC Call Report data for 500 U.S. commercial banks over 36 quarters, 2015-2023. A small Monte Carlo documents 95% grid-bootstrap coverage between 0.90 and 0.99 across the three transformations on balanced and unbalanced panels, with FD closest to nominal; we treat this as empirical support for, rather than proof of, the validity of the bootstrap under FOD and system GMM. The command fills a gap in the dynamic panel threshold toolkit: to our knowledge, it is the first Stata implementation to combine unbalanced-panel support, an endogenous threshold via user-supplied instruments, Blundell-Bond system GMM, and continuity-robust grid bootstrap inference in a single interface.

title: The Verification Bottleneck: Microeconomics When Intelligence Is Abundant
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Verification Bottleneck: Microeconomics When Intelligence Is Abundant
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has reduced the marginal cost of producing cognitive output to near zero. Standard microeconomic theory therefore predicts that prices should converge toward zero and output should expand rapidly. Yet in practice, organizations consistently report a different pattern: AI systems perform well in pilot environments but fail to scale in high-stakes production settings. This paper provides a microeconomic explanation for this divergence. This mechanism implies that prices are pinned by the cost of reliability rather than the cost of production, breaking the standard prediction that marginal cost collapses under free generation. The model provides a unified explanation for several observed phenomena: the pilot-to-production gap, slower adoption in highliability sectors, persistent price premia for verified outputs, and the emergence of verification as a distinct economic activity. The paper contributes to microeconomic theory by introducing a setting in which output is stochastic, non-contractible, and verification is asymptotically but not perfectly effective, implying a strictly positive lower bound on the cost of usable output. It contributes to the economics of AI by identifying verification, rather than generation, as the binding constraint on value creation.

title: The Influence of Health, Recognition, Obedience, and Willingness to listen on Understanding and Need for Clarification of Interview Questions: Evidence from the European Social Survey 2004 to 2023

detail.title: The Influence of Health, Recognition, Obedience, and Willingness to listen on Understanding and Need for Clarification of Interview Questions: Evidence from the European Social Survey 2004 to 2023
detail.abstract: The art of taking surveys implies designing interview questions which are comprehensible to the average interviewee. If not, clarification ought to be available to the interviewee. In this study, I document the ability to understand interview questions and the subsequent need for clarification relying on approximately 170,000 pooled observations of ten rounds of the European Social Survey from 2004 to 2023. Based on two stereotype logistic regressions, the understanding and need for clarification are explained by individual characteristics and macro-influences. The results reveal that health, age, education, immigration status, and personality traits do matter. Moreover, nationality, zeitgeist, and mode of interviewing appear relevant. Overall, the study documents the factors to consider for safeguarding an interviewee's understanding and need for clarification of interview questions.

title: Beyond the Gulf: Rethinking Stepwise Migration, Citizenship Penalty, and Filipino Nurses in the UAE
affiliations: and Institute for Social & Economic Research - Zayed University

detail.title: Beyond the Gulf: Rethinking Stepwise Migration, Citizenship Penalty, and Filipino Nurses in the UAE
detail.abstract: The Gulf region, especially the United Arab Emirates (UAE), has steadily become a key destination for skilled migrants from the Global South. In the UAE labour market, Filipino nurses constitute the largest segment of the expatriate healthcare workforce and are essential in maintaining hospital systems across the emirates. Despite their strong qualifications, dual licences, and long-standing contributions, they still face structural wage disparities and limited pathways to advancement-issues rooted in nationality-based hierarchies that shape the Gulf labour market. Survey data from 203 Filipino nurses in Dubai, along with 30 in-depth interviews, reveal ongoing disparities in pay and professional mobility compared to Western expatriates with similar credentials. Filipino nurses earned an average of USD 1,569 per month in the UAE, well below what is typically earned in Western countries. Logistic regression analysis shows that expected salaries abroad-and limited long-term integration prospectsare the strongest factors influencing their intent to migrate further. Many respondents view the UAE as a temporary stepping stone to gain experience before moving to Canada or the United States. Recent labour reforms, including long-term residency programmes, are steps toward more inclusive migration policies. However, high salary thresholds and strict eligibility rules still exclude most healthcare workers, reinforcing job insecurity and leading to skilled worker attrition. To improve highly skilled professionals' retention and support the region's healthcare goals, Gulf states must address the citizenship penalty directly. Harmonising wage and promotion systems, expanding skills-based residency pathways, and investing in inclusive leadership and professional growth programmes are vital. Viewing skilled migrants as long-term contributors-not just temporary workers-will strengthen healthcare resilience and support the broader socioeconomic development plans of the region.

title: Does CAPM Accurately Predict Expected Returns of Nifty 50 Stocks? An Empirical Investigation Using 2022-2025 Data

detail.title: Does CAPM Accurately Predict Expected Returns of Nifty 50 Stocks? An Empirical Investigation Using 2022-2025 Data

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), developed by Sharpe (1964) and Lintner (1965), posits a linear relationship between an asset's systematic risk, measured by beta, and its expected return. Despite its foundational status in financial economics, the empirical validity of CAPM has been extensively challenged, with particular scepticism directed at emerging equity markets. This study empirically investigates whether CAPM accurately predicts the expected returns of Nifty 50 stocks using daily return data for ten index constituents over the period January 2022 to March 2025, comprising 804 daily observations per security. Beta coefficients are estimated through Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression using the excess return market model in Gretl, with robustness evaluated through Breusch-Pagan heteroskedasticity tests, Ramsey RESET specification tests, Durbin-Watson autocorrelation diagnostics, and normality of residuals tests. The results indicate that while beta is statistically significant for all 10 sample stocks, CAPM demonstrates limited predictive accuracy, the single market factor explains an average of only 28.42% of return variation, and the model systematically overestimates returns for 6 out of 10 stocks. Heteroskedasticity is detected in 7 out of 10 stocks and model misspecification in 3 out of 10, consistent with the theoretical critique of Lai and Stohs (2015) regarding CAPM's inherent endogeneity. These findings extend the prior Indian evidence of Chaudhary (2016) to the post-pandemic market environment of 2022-2025.

title: When Everyone Upgrades: Replacement Complementarities and Endogenous Growth

detail.title: When Everyone Upgrades: Replacement Complementarities and Endogenous Growth
detail.abstract: A firm's payoff from operating old capital depends on the quality used by productmarket peers. I embed this horizontal replacement complementarity in a vintagecapital model with endogenous innovation in capital goods. Capital users choose when to replace and which vintage to buy, while capital-good producers innovate in response to replacement demand. Peer complementarities alter both the replacement range and the return to innovation. When the complementarity is strong enough, the same fundamentals support multiple balanced-growth paths. Beliefs then select the continuation: shifts in expectations can move the economy between slow-replacement and fast-replacement regimes, generating recurrent replacement waves, growth movements, and consumption dynamics even without shocks to fundamentals.

title: Two-State Mathematics An Axiomatic Foundation for the Mathematics of Dissipative Structures

detail.title: Two-State Mathematics An Axiomatic Foundation for the Mathematics of Dissipative Structures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants and/or animals, therefore ethical approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Taking Prigogine's theory of dissipative structures as its physical foundation, this paper identifies a fundamental limitation in classical mathematical tools: they dissolve "process" into the derivative or probability flow of "states," lacking a primitive characterization of the duality between the two. To address this gap, the paper constructs a new axiomatic framework-Two-State Mathematics (TSM), or the Process-State Duality Language-which elevates irreversible transformation from process to state to a first-class mathematical object. The paper first repairs the evolutionary potential function by embedding four core dissipative mechanisms-entropy production rate, decay of information retention, diffusion asymmetry, and critical slowing down-into a single scalar function Ψ and rigorously proves its global Lyapunov stability. The repaired function satisfies the four core axioms of TSM and admits a faithful embedding. The framework yields three structural advantages: critical slowing down and information loss are unified as dual manifestations of the same irreversible transformation; phase-transition thresholds are derived as geometric consequences of the non-isomorphism of the irreversible natural transformation; and process and state interventions can be jointly optimized.

detail.title: A Complex Systems Ontology of Money
detail.abstract: This paper proposes a unified ontological model of money grounded in a complex-systems framework-dissipative structure theory, synergetics, and information theory-and provides a mathematical formalization of money, credit, and inflation mechanisms within a networked state space.

title:
ICE UN-DOCUMENTED: HOW CAMPOS-CHAVES ALLOWS ICE TO DISOBEY CONGRESS WITH DEFECTIVE NOTICES TO APPEAR

40 Geo. Immigr. L.J. (Winter 2026).
affiliations: and

detail.title:
ICE UN-DOCUMENTED: HOW CAMPOS-CHAVES ALLOWS ICE TO DISOBEY CONGRESS WITH DEFECTIVE NOTICES TO APPEAR

40 Geo. Immigr. L.J. (Winter 2026).
detail.abstract: The issuance of defective Notices to Appear (“NTA”), the charging docu-ment in immigration court, has become a recurrent and systemic failure in the contemporary U.S. immigration system. Under INA § 239(a)(1)(G)(i), an NTA must specify the time and place of removal proceedings. Despite clear statutory language, ICE routinely issues NTAs that omit one or both of these critical details, and thereby undermines the procedural protections Congress intended NTAs to contain as the charging and case-initiating documents for noncitizens in removal proceedings. Courts have recognized that the absence of a statutorily compliant NTA can jeopardize noncitizens’ ability to attend immigration court proceedings. This ICE malfeasance exposes noncitizens to “in absentia” removal orders, which effectively deprive them of notice, due process, and rights guaranteed under federal law and in immigration court. ICE’s practices have generated considerable litigation, including three U.S. Supreme Court decisions in Pereira (2018), Niz-Chavez (2021), and Campos-Chaves (2024). This article examines the consequences of ICE’s failure to comply with the statutory notice requirements mandated by INA § 239, including illustrative case examples from Hofstra Law School’s Deportation Defense Clinic, demonstrating how defective NTAs prejudice noncitizens. One clinic client is “Maria,” whose story was previously described in The ICE Trap: Deportation Without Due Process, published in the UCLA Law Review. Another clinic client, “Oscar,” is introduced in this article. Oscar’s case was described in an amicus brief filed with the U.S. Supreme Court in Campos-Chaves. This article concludes with pro-posed solutions to address the pervasive problem of ICE disobeying Congress by issuing defective NTAs.

title: Nowcasting Kuwait's IMF ARA Reserve Adequacy Coverage Without Short-Term Debt or Other Liabilities Data

detail.title: Nowcasting Kuwait's IMF ARA Reserve Adequacy Coverage Without Short-Term Debt or Other Liabilities Data
detail.abstract: The IMF's Assessing Reserve Adequacy (ARA) framework computes a coverage ratio whose denominator combines short-term external debt (STD), other liabilities (OPL), broad money, and exports. For Kuwait, the IMF itself notes that "the absence of a decomposition of external debt into short-term versus long-term components hampers the assessment of FX reserve adequacy" (International Monetary Fund, 2026, p. 49), and the same constraint applies to OPL. We propose a nowcasting methodology that combines a quarterly Balance of Payments goods-and-services trailing-four-quarter proxy for exports with a damped Holt's exponential smoothing one-step-ahead forecast of the combined STD+OPL contribution back-solved from labeled IMF Article IV K values. Applied to Kuwait 2014-2025 under a pseudo-out-of-sample expanding-window backtest, the methodology nowcasts IMF first-published labeled coverage with mean absolute error of 5.04 percentage points (5.31 against the latest revisions), beating a same-cutoff persistence benchmark by 4.4 percentage points against first publications (2.6 percentage points against latest revisions) on the eleven scoreable years. In live forward operation the methodology runs in real time and is available on average 11 months ahead of IMF's first labeled actual.

title: HOW TO MAKE RIGHT CHOICE CONCERNING ELECTIVES
affiliations: Osun State University, College of Law, Ifetedo

detail.title: HOW TO MAKE RIGHT CHOICE CONCERNING ELECTIVES

detail.abstract: This paper examines the critical process of selecting elective courses within the university system, with particular focus on law students. It underscores the importance of informed decision-making in course selection, noting that electives play a pivotal role in shaping students’ academic trajectories and future professional specializations. The study outlines the diverse range of elective courses available within the Faculty of Law and emphasizes the need for students to adopt a strategic and personalized approach that aligns with their strengths, interests, and career aspirations. It further explores the advantages of electives, including intellectual diversification and skill development, while identifying key factors that influence students’ choices, such as career goals, academic performance, and perceived course difficulty. Additionally, the paper highlights common pitfalls students encounter during the selection process, including poor planning and reliance on external opinions without adequate self-assessment. The discussion culminates in practical recommendations designed to guide students toward making well-informed and balanced elective choices. Ultimately, the paper contributes to a better understanding of how thoughtful course selection can enhance both academic success and professional preparedness among law students.

reference: Center for the History of Political Economy (CHOPE) Workshop Paper No. 2026-3
title: Henry Manne, Pareto in the Pines, and the Origins of the Law and Economics Movement
affiliations: University of Warwick - Warwick Law School and Duke University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Henry Manne, Pareto in the Pines, and the Origins of the Law and Economics Movement

publicationDetails.detailsText: Center for the History of Political Economy (CHOPE) Workshop Paper No. 2026-3

detail.abstract: Law and economics—or the application of economic reasoning and methods to the study of law—was a niche topic of study at Chicago and Yale in 1950s and 1960s, before coming out of the wilderness in the early 1970s and becoming an institutionalized feature of American legal education by the late 1980s. Relying on archival material, the paper shows how this remarkable transformation was driven by an academic entrepreneur, Henry Manne, who in 1971 started a summer school in economics for law professors. This program prepared the ground for, and gave shape to, the intellectual and geographical spread of law and economics. But Manne's enterprise would not have succeeded had there not been a widespread demand for the inclusion of social science research in the law school curriculum, combined with the failure of the alternative law and society movement—which sought to apply sociological concepts and methodologies to the study of legal phenomena—to establish a real toehold in the law school world.

title: Demographics and Sovereign Risk: Do Markets Price Population Aging?

detail.title: Demographics and Sovereign Risk: Do Markets Price Population Aging?
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether sovereign credit markets price demographic structure, and through which channels. Using a panel of 81 rated countries from 1970 to 2024, we find that the Higgins (1998) demographic polynomial Z₁ predicts sovereign credit ratings unconditionally (Z₁ = 14.3, p < 0.05), but this effect is absorbed once we condition on income (Z₁ = 8.0, p = 0.18, N = 2,202). The demographic-rating relationship is not a universal phenomenon-it is concentrated in advanced economies: the OECD subsample retains a strong, significant effect (Z₁ = 35.6, p < 0.05, N = 1,021), while the non-OECD coefficient is null (6.6, NS). Income itself dominates: log GDP per capita enters at +3.81 (p < 0.001) on ratings and-3.49 (p < 0.001) on spreads, absorbing much of what previously appeared as a demographic effect. The most novel finding is the Z₁ x income interaction on sovereign spreads:-1.71 (p < 0.05). Aging widens spreads disproportionately for richer countries-the demographic penalty on borrowing costs is income-conditional. This interaction survives the addition of debt controls (-1.80, p < 0.01) and year fixed effects (-0.62, p < 0.05), and is dramatically amplified within the eurozone (Z₁ x income =-6.68, p < 0.001). On sovereign spreads, the contemporaneous Z₁ effect is not significant (15.9, p = 0.23), and the previously significant 5-year lagged result (23.5, p < 0.05 in the unconditional specification) is fully absorbed by income conditioning (4.8, NS). The country + year FE rating result, which was a headline finding at 11.4 (p < 0.01) in the unconditional specification, attenuates to 5.6 (NS, p = 0.20) once income is controlled. Year FE spreads provide the one robust specification: Z₁ = 16.7 (p < 0.05). The Z₁ x debt interaction on spreads remains significant (+0.53, p < 0.05), but income conditioning reveals that much of the debt amplification operates through the income channel. The suppression pattern documented in the unconditional specification reverses to mediation: Z₁ attenuates by 22.5% when fiscal controls are added, from 8.37 (no fiscal) to 8.01 (with fiscal balance), consistent with demographics operating partly through the fiscal channel. Rolling window analysis continues to reveal dramatic temporal instability in the spread channel, with the eurozone crisis driving a massive sign flip (Z₁ =-90 in the 2002-2011 window), but this confounding event does not alter the income-conditioning conclusion.

title: Pension Systems, Demographic Aging, and the Home Bias Puzzle: Global Evidence

detail.title: Pension Systems, Demographic Aging, and the Home Bias Puzzle: Global Evidence
detail.abstract: This paper tests whether pension system growth mediates the relationship between demographic aging and cross-border portfolio diversification. Using a panel of up to 188 countries from 1990 to 2024, we find that demographic aging robustly predicts pension system growth (Z₁ = +69.2***, p = 0.0002, N = 1,225, 42 countries), establishing the first stage of the mediation chain. However, pension fund growth does not uniformly translate into changes in external portfolio allocation: the second stage (pension spending → gross external assets) is positive but insignificant (+6.22, p = 0.304), and the income-conditioned full-sample relationship between demographics and gross external assets is null (Z₁ = +441, p = 0.405, N = 5,583). The pension-to-diversification channel is contingent on institutional context. Two subsample findings are robust across all specifications. First, the eurozone provides the clearest case where the full mediation chain operates: the Z₁ × eurozone interaction is-385*** (p < 0.001), indicating that monetary union with free capital mobility and regulatory harmonization channels demographic pension growth into cross-border allocation. Second, low-income countries show the strongest demographic effect on external assets (Z₁ =-4,715***, p = 0.005), where institutional capacity for cross-border investment is the binding constraint. Portfolio composition effects (debt and equity levels) are null under income conditioning, rejecting a pension-theoretic debt tilt.

title: Intelligent Guide Systems for Digital Heritage: A Systematic Review of AR-AI Integration in the Era of Generative Cognition
affiliations: , Faculty of Computers and Information, Faculty of Computers and Information, Faculty of Computers and Information, Faculty of Computers and Information and Faculty of Computers and Information

detail.title: Intelligent Guide Systems for Digital Heritage: A Systematic Review of AR-AI Integration in the Era of Generative Cognition
detail.abstract: Digital transformation in cultural heritage institutions has increasingly prioritized immersive technologies to enhance visitor engagement and knowledge delivery [8]. However, traditional Augmented Reality (AR) solutions remain constrained by the scalability bottlenecks of marker-based tracking and the pedagogical limitations of static content delivery [1]. This work uses the Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM) as a primary case study to validate a consolidated system-level perspective of recent advancements in the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with AR [6]. By synthesizing existing research through the lens of GEM's large-scale operational challenges-such as an expected annual volume of 5-8 million visitors-this study identifies recurring architectural patterns. It evaluates how robust perception capabilities, achieved through mobile-optimized Convolutional Neural Networks such as YOLOv8 and EfficientNet [2, 15], and intelligent cognition, powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) grounded in historical Knowledge Graphs [4, 19], address critical technical challenges including lighting sensitivity and occlusion [9]. The findings indicate that the convergence of adaptive vision and generative storytelling transforms the museum visit from passive observation into an active, dialogue-driven exploration [25]. The study concludes that applying this framework to the Grand Egyptian Museum establishes a new benchmark for 'Generative Cognition' in high-traffic heritage sites, providing a scalable model for transforming visitor interaction globally.

title: BEATS TO DEALS: THE ROLE OF IP LAW AND INNOVATION POLICY IN ADVANCING THE MUSIC INDUSTRY 1
affiliations: Osun State University, College of Law, Ifetedo

detail.title: BEATS TO DEALS: THE ROLE OF IP LAW AND INNOVATION POLICY IN ADVANCING THE MUSIC INDUSTRY 1
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the role of intellectual property (IP) law and innovation policy in advancing the music industry, with particular emphasis on the challenges and opportunities presented by the digital age. It underscores the economic and cultural significance of the music industry and highlights the need for robust legal frameworks to protect the rights of creators, producers, and distributors of musical works. The study provides a conceptual clarification of key terms, including intellectual property, copyright, neighbouring rights, and innovation policy, and explores their intersection within the music industry.

The paper analyses the importance of copyright, trademarks, and licensing systems in ensuring fair compensation, protecting creative works, and fostering sustainable growth within the industry. It further examines the impact of digital technologies, noting both their innovative potential—such as blockchain and digital tracking systems—and the heightened risks of infringement through piracy, unauthorized streaming, and artificial intelligence-generated content.

Focusing on Nigeria as a case study, the paper evaluates existing innovation policies and regulatory measures aimed at curbing digital infringement and promoting creativity. It concludes that while significant progress has been made, continuous legal and policy adaptation is essential to effectively address emerging technological challenges and ensure the long-term growth and sustainability of the music industry.

title: From Transactions to Reasoning: Architecting AI for Institutional Portfolio Decisions

detail.title: From Transactions to Reasoning: Architecting AI for Institutional Portfolio Decisions

declarations.funderStatement: gradientcio.com

detail.abstract: Institutional debate around AI in asset allocation has focused on models-machine learning techniques, optimization methods, predictive frameworks. This emphasis misses the true constraint. Most portfolio systems were built to record what happened, not to provide AI with the information required to reason about what might happen next. AI effectiveness in portfolio analysis is determined less by model sophistication than by context quality. Even the most advanced model will underperform if it is forced to infer portfolio structure, assumptions, and constraints from narrative text or transaction records. Conversely, simpler models can deliver materially better analysis when provided explicit, machine-readable context describing portfolio entities, forward-looking assumptions, relationships, and governance constraints. The opportunity is significant. AI can evaluate tens of thousands of scenarios, assess regime-dependent behavior, optimize across complex constraints, and quantify probabilistic outcomes at scales infeasible for manual analysis. Realizing this potential, however, requires architecture designed for decision support rather than accounting. Transaction-centric systems remain essential for compliance and reporting, but AI-enabled analysis requires entity-based architecture in which assumptions are primary data, relationships are explicit, and constraints are formally specified rather than embedded in prose. This paper argues that context architecture-not algorithm choice-is the foundational requirement for effective AI in institutional portfolio management, and outlines the architectural principles needed to support forward-looking, multi-asset decision-making.

reference: China Accounting & Finance Review, volume 28, issue 2, 2026
title: Firm-level regulatory intensity and corporate strategic change
affiliations: University of Texas at Tyler, East Carolina University and Coastal Carolina University

detail.title: Firm-level regulatory intensity and corporate strategic change

publicationDetails.detailsText: China Accounting & Finance Review, volume 28, issue 2, 2026

detail.abstract:
Purpose-We empirically examine the impact of firm-level regulatory intensity, an external force or context, on corporate strategic change (i.e. changes in a firm's financing, investing and operating decisions to boost its competitive advantage and performance). 

Design/methodology/approach-Using a sample of 78,523 firm-year observations of US firms from 1995-2019, we model firm strategic change as a function of firm-level regulatory intensity and other firm characteristics. We estimate the model using OLS regression with standard errors clustered at the firm level to generate statistical inference, controlling for firm-and year-fixed effects. Robustness tests include various methodologies, including propensity score matching, entropy balancing and instrumental variable approaches. We also employ alternative measures of firm-level regulatory intensity and corporate strategic change to further validate our results. 

Findings-Regulatory intensity decreases the extent of corporate strategic change, providing evidence that managers become more cautious and conservative in undertaking strategic changes when facing a greater regulatory burden. This finding is robust to various model specifications and alternative proxies for strategic change, suggesting that regulations may hinder firms from making strategic changes in a timely manner. Delayed strategic changes can lead to negative effects on a firm's performance in the short run and growth in the long run. Further analysis shows that regulatory intensity reduces strategic changes in resource allocations but induces more strategic changes in corporate capital structure. 

Originality/value-We enrich the literature on corporate strategic change and the association between regulatory intensity and corporate decision-making. The finding that corporate managers are more cautious in implementing strategic changes when facing a high level of regulatory compliance provides important implications to regulators and managers. To mitigate the unintended effects of regulations on businesses, policymakers should be more prudent in initiating and passing new regulations by adopting a more evidencebased and transparent approach and regulators and regulation implementing agencies should provide sufficient compliance support. Corporate managers need to proactively engage in the rule-making process to turn intensified compliance into business strategy drivers and undertake timely changes to enhance performance and long-term competitiveness.

title: CMAs in Context: Building AI-Ready Investment Frameworks

detail.title: CMAs in Context: Building AI-Ready Investment Frameworks

declarations.funderStatement: gradientcio.com

detail.abstract: Asset allocators make decisions across multiple horizons at once. Strategic policy rests on long-term capital market assumptions that change slowly under formal governance. Implementation, by contrast, responds to nearer-term realities: quarterly rebalancing, tactical tilts driven by valuations and regimes, and pathdependent liquidity from private market capital calls and distributions. Most institutions already hold this multi-horizon view, but they maintain it through periodic memos, committee discussions, and analyst spreadsheets rather than through a unified analytical framework.

detail.abstract:
RESUMEN

Durante más de siete décadas, la inflación crónica argentina —con tasas anuales de dos o tres dígitos en cuatro de cada cinco años desde 1950— hizo estructuralmente inviable el crédito hipotecario de largo plazo. Tras la crisis de 2001-2002 el mercado hipotecario se contrajo a niveles marginales y, hacia 2024, representaba apenas el 0,36% del PBI, una fracción del 30% de Chile, del 10-15% de Brasil y México y del más del 70% de Estados Unidos. La consecuencia es un déficit habitacional estructural estimado en 3,5 millones de viviendas y un mercado inmobiliario operado casi enteramente en efectivo y en dólares, accesible solo a quienes ya disponen de ahorro previo en moneda dura. La introducción en 2016 de la Unidad de Valor Adquisitivo (UVA) —unidad de cuenta indexada al Índice de Precios al Consumidor— resolvió parcialmente el problema de deterioro real de la cartera bancaria al permitir aplicar tasas reales bajas sobre capital ajustable, pero no resolvió el obstáculo estructural restante: el descalce de plazos entre depósitos bancarios de 30 a 90 días y créditos hipotecarios de 15 a 30 años.

El presente trabajo propone un marco regulatorio integral para superar dicho obstáculo mediante la securitización de cartera hipotecaria UVA en valores de corto plazo. La arquitectura propuesta articula tres componentes: (i) cesión temporal y secuencial de flujos hipotecarios a fideicomisos financieros hipotecarios, comenzando siempre por la primera cuota a vencer; (ii) hipoteca divisible funcional sobre créditos ya originados; y (iii) regla legal imperativa de distribución del producido de ejecución entre titulares parciales de la garantía. El documento detalla el paquete de reformas legislativas, prudenciales, registrales y tributarias necesario, incluyendo textos normativos sugeridos para una ley o decreto de necesidad y urgencia, una Comunicación del BCRA, una Resolución General complementaria de la CNV y cláusulas mínimas del contrato de fideicomiso, junto con un régimen tributario que equipare estos valores fiduciarios con los títulos de deuda pública nacional. El diseño preserva el tratamiento de venta verdadera (true sale), evita los excesos del mercado subprime estadounidense pre-2008 mediante criterios estrictos de elegibilidad y tutela estructural del deudor, y aspira a desencadenar el multiplicador económico de la construcción residencial sin recurrir a expansión monetaria ni a subsidios fiscales directos.

ENGLISH ABSTRACT

For more than seven decades, Argentina's chronic inflation —with double- or triple-digit annual rates in four out of every five years since 1950— has rendered long-term mortgage lending structurally unviable. Following the 2001-2002 crisis, mortgage credit collapsed to marginal levels and, by 2024, stood at roughly 0.36% of GDP, a fraction of Chile's 30%, Brazil's and Mexico's 10-15%, and the United States' 70%-plus. The introduction of the Unidad de Valor Adquisitivo (UVA) in 2016 partially solved the bank-side problem of real-value erosion of mortgage portfolios, but did not address the remaining structural obstacle: the duration mismatch between bank deposits of 30 to 90 days and mortgage loans of 15 to 30 years.

This paper proposes an integrated regulatory framework to overcome that obstacle by securitizing UVA mortgage portfolios into short-duration instruments. The proposed architecture articulates three components: (i) temporary and sequential assignment of mortgage cash flows to mortgage-backed financial trusts; (ii) functionally divisible mortgages over already-originated loans; and (iii) a statutory waterfall rule governing the distribution of foreclosure proceeds among partial collateral holders. The document details the required legislative, prudential, registral and tax reform package, together with a tax regime that grants these securities parity treatment with Argentine sovereign debt. The design preserves true-sale treatment, avoids the excesses of the pre-2008 U.S. subprime market, and aims to unleash the economic multiplier of residential construction without resorting to monetary expansion or direct fiscal subsidies.

title: Passive Demand but Active Pay: The Effect of ETF Flows on CEO Compensation Design

detail.title: Passive Demand but Active Pay: The Effect of ETF Flows on CEO Compensation Design
detail.abstract: ETF flows generate non-fundamental demand for stocks, reducing price informativeness and amplifying return co-movement. I examine the implications for CEO compensation design. I find that ETF flows prompt boards to substitute stock options for stock awards, with total compensation unchanged: a pure compositional shift. The convex payoff of options makes them well-suited to tracking the CEO's market-determined outside options, which flow-driven co-movement raises (the retention channel). Cross-sectional tests confirm this channel: the substitution is strongest for firms in thin CEO labor markets, for firms with more powerful CEOs, and for firms with sector-driven ETF flow. I also test an informativeness channel but do not find independent support for it; however, analyst coverage attenuates the substitution in a pattern consistent with retention being the overarching constraint. A fire-sale pressure measure isolating the non-fundamental component of ETF flows confirms the substitution pattern.

detail.abstract: The SEC’s Item 1.05 cybersecurity-incident disclosure mandate provides a new setting for testing whether cyber-incident disclosure effects survive once disclosure is standardized and mandatory. Using 82 cybersecurity-related Form 8-K filings from June 2021 through April 8, 2026, including 66 Item 1.05 filings, I conduct a pre-registered event study of post-disclosure abnormal returns. The primary test is post-mandate Item 1.05 disclosures, measured over T+5 trading days against the Russell 2000 ETF. I add official EDGAR acceptance timestamps and measure returns from the first NYSE close after public acceptance. The primary test yields alpha of -0.03% with a two-way firm-by-month clustered t-statistic of -0.02. The result is a sharp null: I cannot reject zero tradeable T+5 abnormal return. Matched non-cyber 8-K controls show that cyber-event windows underperform the same issuers’ ordinary non-cyber 8-K windows, but this relative result is not driven by a negative absolute cyber-event alpha. Intraday trade and minute-bar evidence shows negative returns over the first 5–30 minutes after feasible entry, but this immediate repricing does not survive as reliable T+5 close-to-close drift. The paper’s main contribution is methodological: event studies of mandatory disclosures should distinguish price reactions around the disclosure date from returns available to a strategy entering after public release.

title: Recovery, Specification, and Consistency
affiliations: Finance Dept., Pamplin College of Business, Virginia Tech, City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Economics and Finance and Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: Recovery, Specification, and Consistency
detail.abstract: Recovering market beliefs, time and risk preferences from asset prices requires specifying a subjective state space for the pricing model. Recovery results are unique to each specification but differ cross specifications and can only be mutually consistent when each specification extracts identical price information. Finer specifications do not improve the recovery consistency because they require more price information, and hence, are also more sensitive to information distortion. Using option price data, analytical methods and neural network analysis, we show that recovery inconsistencies are common and economically significant. Our findings suggest that a fully consistent recovery framework remains difficult to achieve.

title: Are Banks and Private Credit Complements or Substitutes?

detail.title: Are Banks and Private Credit Complements or Substitutes?
detail.abstract: This paper examines how the rapid growth of private credit alters bank functions in credit intermediation, using variation in exposure to private debt and the deregulation that relax leverage constraints for private credit lenders. As private credit specializes in relationship lending and supplies credit to opaque firms, small banks respond by lowering loan rates, loosening underwriting, increasing geographic presence, and expanding small business lending to defend their core markets. In contrast, large banks retreat from direct lending and instead fund private credit intermediaries, benefiting from lower regulatory risk weights and higher returns on capital. Banks with weaker balance sheets have stronger incentives to exploit this regulatory advantage, while those operate in concentrated banking markets face weaker incentives to compete for borrowers.

detail.abstract: This white paper examines the fundamental shifts in organisational work, innovation, and workforce capability triggered by the COVID-19 pandemic. Drawing on survey data and analysis from McKinsey, the World Economic Forum, and Salesforce Research, the paper argues that the pandemic accelerated a reskilling emergency requiring organisations to develop three forms of agility — cognitive, emotional, and learning. It proposes a five-step transformation agenda addressing digital acceleration, hybrid work culture, remote workforce management, cognitive agility development, and navigating operational complexity. The paper has particular relevance for knowledge-intensive service organisations and public-sector institutions in emerging market contexts undertaking post-pandemic workforce reinvention.

detail.abstract: When the supply chain system suffers a disruption, the consequences ripple outward across the entire industrial landscape. Standard on-time delivery metrics reduce supplier performance to simplistic binary metrics and are structurally incapable of recording the depth, severity, or operational consequence of delivery failures in advanced manufacturing sectors. This paper introduces the Supplier Stability Framework (SSF), a field-deployable composite risk scoring methodology that integrates four measurable performance dimensions- late arrival frequency, open-late exposure, commitment integrity, and delay severity into a single composite index called the Friction Index (FI). The framework further incorporates a parallel Material Discrepancy (MD) Fault Attribution system that differentiates supplier-responsible quality events from transit and handling noise. The methodology is designed to be industry and ERP-agnostic, requiring only standard fields available in any Purchase Order export. A fully functional open-source implementation is publicly available at supplier-stability-metrics.streamlit.app, demonstrating the framework's portability to the broader U.S. manufacturing sector. The framework's scoring behavior was validated against a live procurement dataset in the semiconductor fabrication equipment manufacturing sector, with supplier rankings cross-referenced against documented production disruption events.

title: Innovative Complements and Substitutes for Contracts in U.S. Law

detail.title: Innovative Complements and Substitutes for Contracts in U.S. Law
detail.abstract: The displacement of traditionally negotiated contracts by technological substitutes-smart contracts, decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs), platform-governed gig arrangements, and AI-generated agreements-poses foundational challenges to U.S. contract law that existing doctrine is ill-equipped to resolve. This article examines how code-and algorithm-based governance restructures contractual relationships, analyzing fragmented legal responses at both the federal and state levels. It further distinguishes between complements (mechanisms that enhance contractual efficiency and enforceability) and substitutes (instruments that displace contractual governance functions altogether). The article argues that U.S. federalism generates a characteristic problem: the same jurisdictional competition that enables rapid regulatory experimentation simultaneously produces temporal fragmentation, interpretive divergence, and compliance asymmetries, imposing disproportionate costs on smaller commercial actors. The staggered state adoption of the 2022 U.C.C. amendments exemplifies this structural tension. The analysis contends that distinctive features of the U.S. civil litigation system-including broad discovery, the American Rule on attorney fees, and opt-out class actions-create an enforcement gap that drives endogenous market demand for self-executing substitutes and automated complements as alternatives to costly formal adjudication. Critically, this litigation-driven technological innovation is not normatively neutral: while it enhances efficiency and reduces transaction costs, it simultaneously erodes public accountability and renders large portions of state-made law practically ineffective. Unresolved questions of worker classification, platform accountability, and AI-generated intellectual property ownership reveal the outer limits of a legal order confronting technologies indifferent to territorial boundaries, necessitating a deeper reassessment of assent, unconscionability, fairness, and accountability in modern U.S. contract law.

title: Rolling with the Punches: The European Commission's Approach to the Sharing of Search Data under Article 6(11) DMA
affiliations: University Villanueva

detail.title: Rolling with the Punches: The European Commission's Approach to the Sharing of Search Data under Article 6(11) DMA
detail.abstract:
Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act obliges Google, as the sole designated gatekeeper for online search engine services, to share ranking, query, click and view data with thirdparty undertakings on fair, reasonable and non-discriminatory terms, whilst ensuring that any personal data is duly anonymised. Google's successive compliance efforts fell short of the European Commission's enforcement expectations, prompting the latter to trigger specification proceedings under Article 8(2) DMA and publish Implementation Measures addressing five core pillars: eligibility, data scope, anonymisation, FRAND pricing and dataset acquisition. 

This article critically examines each pillar in turn, arguing that whilst the EC's shift from frequency thresholding to entity and length-based thresholding represents a meaningful technical improvement, residual vulnerabilities remain unaddressed. The extension of the provision's scope to AI chatbots, the incremental cost-based pricing methodology and the auditing requirements for dataset access each raise further questions that the Implementation Measures leave, at best, partially resolved.

title: Structural Lag and Small Business Failure: An Empirical Stress Test of Stage-Based Enterprise Architecture Using U.S. Longitudinal Cohort Data

detail.title: Structural Lag and Small Business Failure: An Empirical Stress Test of Stage-Based Enterprise Architecture Using U.S. Longitudinal Cohort Data
detail.abstract:
This article examines whether broad patterns in U.S. small business performance are directionally consistent with the developmental logic of the 4-Stage Growth Model (Sloan, 2026). That model proposes that growth unfolds through a sequence of integrated enterprise architectures, and that growth instability arises when these architectures fail to evolve in parallel with increasing organizational complexity. The companion paper establishes the theoretical architecture; this article examines its consistency with observable patterns of small-business survival, failure, and scaling dynamics using publicly available U.S. and international data. Together, they constitute a two-part research program: the first establishing the design theory, the second assessing its inferential alignment with empirical evidence.

The analysis is inferential rather than causal. It does not measure enterprise architecture directly or test the model econometrically. Instead, it evaluates whether macro-level performance patterns—survival clustering, failure dynamics, and transition volatility—are consistent with the model’s core mechanism: that as firms grow, coordination demands increase, and sustained performance requires corresponding evolution in integrative capacity across eight interdependent enterprise dimensions. When this evolution does not occur, structural lag accumulates and multi-domain misalignment emerges.

Three contributions follow. First, observed failure patterns are more accurately characterized as multi-domain strain than isolated deficiencies, with volatility concentrating at key developmental transitions—particularly the Growth → Take-Off stage. Second, international comparisons indicate that institutional environments moderate outcomes without eliminating the requirement for architectural evolution. Third, boundary condition analysis clarifies that the model’s explanatory power increases with enterprise complexity and is less applicable to intentionally non-scaling firms. While the evidence does not establish causality, its consistency with the model’s mechanism supports the framework as a foundation for future empirical investigation of stage-based enterprise development.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates why Nepal's strong macroeconomic buffers in early FY2026 have not translated into durable economic transformation. Drawing on a multi-source data framework that triangulates Nepal Rastra Bank monetary and financial data, National Statistics Office national accounts, Ministry of Finance budget execution data, the Department of Foreign Employment migration statistics, and projections from the World Bank Nepal Development Update (April 2026) and the International Monetary Fund Extended Credit Facility reviews, the paper examines six interconnected structural paradoxes that constrain Nepal's growth. Core findings are: (i) gross foreign exchange reserves of USD 22.5 billion and a current account surplus of 6.7 percent of GDP coexist with GDP growth projected to moderate to 2.3 percent in FY2026, driven by the economic fallout of the September 2025 Gen-Z protests; (ii) capital expenditure execution reached only 12.1 percent of the annual budget in the first half of FY2026, while public debt servicing exceeded capital expenditure by 2.2 percentage points of GDP; (iii) the Middle East conflict, which escalated from February 28, 2026, poses high transmission risk through remittances and energy imports given that 77.3 percent of Nepali migrant workers are based in the region; and (iv) the new single-party majority government formed after the March 5, 2026 snap election carries a credible reform mandate but faces institutional durability constraints. The paper argues that converting Nepal's current macroeconomic stability into structural transformation requires fiscal federal reform, NPL resolution, a proactive LDC graduation strategy, and governance reforms capable of outlasting the current political moment.

detail.abstract:
This paper argues that Florida's behavioral health crisis is consistent with historically recurring patterns of structural exclusion rather than isolated policy failures. Drawing on historical trauma scholarship, emerging epigenetic research, current behavioral health data, legislative analysis, and autoethnographic lived experience, this analysis suggests that documented gaps in Florida's care infrastructure reflect patterns traceable across multiple policy eras. Florida's per-capita state mental health agency expenditure of $36.05 ranks last among all 50 states (SAMHSA State Mental Health Agency Expenditure Data). The state's behavioral health workforce supply meets approximately 24% of estimated population need (HRSA, 2024). Florida conducted an estimated 120,955 involuntary psychiatric examinations between July 2025 and April 2026, with a disproportionate number involving minors (USF Baker Act Reporting Center). In Collier County and the Immokalee farmworker community, these patterns intersect with documented healthcare avoidance attributable to Florida SB 1718 (USF Im/migrant Well-Being Research Center, 2024), behavioral health service gaps at Healthcare Network of Southwest Florida (HPCSWF, 2023), and racial and economic disparities in Adverse Childhood Experience burden (CDC, 2023). 

This paper proposes the Golden Horizon Healthcare System, administered by She Is Us United Inc. in partnership with Taylord Healthcare Solutions LLC, as a community-sovereignty response to these intersecting patterns. Scenario-based cost modeling, using published state unit cost data, suggests a potential $3.55 return per $1.00 invested over five years, though results vary significantly depending on assumptions (see Section 7).

detail.abstract: The proliferation of artificial intelligence across public administration, healthcare, financial services, education, and critical infrastructure has generated a global discourse on AI ethics, responsible AI, trustworthy AI, and the conditions under which publics extend or withhold trust in algorithmic systems. Yet this discourse has remained fragmented: AI ethics operates primarily as a normative philosophical enterprise; responsible AI has been colonised by corporate self-regulatory frameworks with limited enforcement; trustworthy AI has been partially operationalised through the EU AI Act but remains contested in its practical implementation; and public trust in AI-arguably the foundational social condition upon which all other governance objectives depend-has been treated as an outcome of technical design rather than as a socio-political phenomenon requiring its own governance architecture. This paper argues that the fragmentation of these four concepts represents a structural governance failure with practical consequences: it allows organisations to adopt the language of ethical AI while evading the institutional accountability that genuine ethical commitment demands. The paper develops an integrated conceptual framework-the Ethics-Trust Architecture (ETA)-that situates AI ethics, responsible AI, trustworthy AI, and public trust within a single analytical structure. Drawing on Floridi et al.'s (2018) foundational AI ethics principles, the HLEG's (2019) trustworthy AI requirements, the EU AI Act's compliance architecture, socio-technical systems theory, and the author's prior governance frameworks-the Integrative Governance Framework (IGF), the Ethical Delegation Matrix (EDM), and the Perceived Delegation Readiness (PDR) construct-the paper maps the relationships between these four concepts and proposes institutional design principles for closing the gap between ethical principle and governance practice. The paper concludes with a research agenda directly relevant to the qualitative and interdisciplinary PhD positions emerging across Scandinavian universities in 2026, which represent the most concentrated institutional investment in non-technical AI governance scholarship in Europe.

detail.abstract: Cotard's syndrome, a rare neuropsychiatric condition characterized by nihilistic delusions of nonexistence, presents a uniquely destabilizing challenge to theories of moral agency and ethical responsibility. While traditionally examined within psychiatry, its implications for moral philosophy, bioethics, and neuroethics remain insufficiently developed. This thesis offers a comprehensive interdisciplinary analysis of Cotard's syndrome through the framework of Principlism, while engaging deeply with Kantian deontology, utilitarianism, virtue ethics, and contemporary philosophical accounts of personhood and responsibility. It argues that Cotard's syndrome constitutes not merely a pathological belief but a structural collapse of the conditions necessary for moral agency, including selfhood, affective engagement, and rational deliberation. Drawing on neurobiological models and case studies, the thesis demonstrates that ethical decision-making is inseparable from neurocognitive integrity. title: Who Thrives in Collaboration with AI? Dispositional and Cognitive Predictors of Human-AI Augmentation
affiliations: , , , ,  and UCL School of Management, University College London

detail.title: Who Thrives in Collaboration with AI? Dispositional and Cognitive Predictors of Human-AI Augmentation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used as a collaborator in knowledge work, yet individuals could vary substantially in how much they benefit from collaboration with AI. This study examines the dispositional and cognitive predictors of human-AI augmentation. In a laboratory experiment with 219 university students in South Korea, participants completed analytical and creative tasks first without generative AI and then with access to an AI assistant. Results show that AI collaboration improved both analytical and creative task performance both in terms of quality and reduced time. Individual differences also predicted these gains: action orientation, leadership, perseverance, and linguistic comprehension were positively associated with stronger performance gains in analytical tasks, while internal locus of control showed a negative association. For creative tasks, cooperativeness and learning agility emerged as positive predictors for performance gains, whereas trustingness showed a negative association. These findings indicate that the benefits of generative AI depend to an extent on individuals’ psychological and cognitive profiles. The study contributes to research on human-AI collaboration by identifying who is most likely to thrive when working with AI, and offers practical implications for AI training, talent development, and organizational selection.

detail.abstract: This study examined forensic auditing mechanisms and financial performance of Cadbury Nigeria Plc covering the period 2015-2024. Specifically, the study investigated the effect of forensic audit independence, litigation support services, and forensic audit remuneration on financial performance measured by Return on Assets (ROA), while firm size was introduced as a control variable. The study adopted an ex-post facto research design and relied on secondary data obtained from the annual reports of the company. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) unit root test, diagnostic tests, and multiple regression analysis. The empirical results were further supported using SWOT and PESTEL assessments. The findings revealed that forensic audit independence (β =-0.041312, p = 0.2179), litigation support services (β =-0.040546, p = 0.1146), and forensic audit remuneration (β =-0.445458, p = 0.1550) had negative and statistically insignificant effects on return on assets. However, firm size exhibited a negative and statistically significant effect on ROA (β =-0.371394, p = 0.0185). The overall regression result showed that the explanatory variables jointly had a significant effect on ROA (F-statistic = 91.62436; p = 0.0108). Diagnostic tests further confirmed that the model was free from heteroskedasticity, multicollinearity, and autocorrelation. The study concluded that forensic auditing improves governance and fraud prevention rather than immediate profitability. It recommended strengthening forensic audit independence and adopting cost-effective forensic auditing practices.

detail.abstract:
A stark narrative dominates the business press. High-profile technology companies are flattening hierarchies, carving out middle management, and framing AI as the ultimate replacement for human orchestration. The 'unbossing' trend paints a grim picture for the future of work. The reality across the broader Australian economy is far more complex. 

AI disruption is not a homogeneous force – it moves at different speeds and takes fundamentally different shapes across sectors, companies, and individual roles. For much of the real economy, AI will not drive workforce elimination. It will drive workforce transformation. That transformation places a new mandate on HR and Learning and Development (L&D) leaders-one that extends far beyond traditional hiring and capability planning. HR and L&D must now equip their organisations for a shift that is redefining the very nature of management and the capabilities it demands. Leaders consistently ask how to build capability for a future that remains unsettled. 

This paper addresses that challenge by drawing on interviews with Institute of Managers and Leaders (IML) members leading AI adoption firsthand across health and aged care, resources and energy, community services, and state government. Ground-level evidence shows the answer is not technical software proficiency. Navigating the AI shift demands adaptive skills-the judgement, contextual thinking, and human capability that determine whether an organisation thrives or fractures under pressure.

detail.abstract: Interest and involvement in corporate social responsibility (CSR) have surged among several stakeholders such as investors and corporations, notwithstanding the ambiguity surrounding how CSR participation translates into financial gains. Consequently, numerous research studies have scrutinized integration between social responsibility and financial performance, yielding inconclusive findings. There is insufficient empirical documentation for a direct interconnection between CSR and financial results. Consequently, the aim of this investigation is to examine, whether engagement in corporate social responsibility directly influences financial results. In this study, a sample of 10 prominent Indian companies spanning various sectors was randomly chosen from the list of top CSR spending companies. Corporate social responsibility expenditure was designated as the independent variable, while several indicators such as Return on Assets, return on Equity and Net Profit were selected for gauging financial performance. Additionally, control variables including Firm Size, Firm Age, Ownership Type, and Leverage were incorporated. Employing a regression model for examination, the results indicated a positive correlation between social initiatives and financial outcomes spanning from 2017-18 to 2024-25.

title: Negotiating at a Distance: The Impact of Communication Media and Negotiator Traits

detail.abstract:
Purpose – Prior research has yet to provide a coherent theoretical framework explaining how communication media hinder or advance negotiation success, and many dated studies are unlikely to be relevant. This study aims to examine the impact of four communication media on negotiation outcomes. It also examines the potential moderating effects of the following negotiator characteristics: conflict management style, personality traits and indirect communication style. 

Design/methodology/approach – A total of 400 participants formed 200 dyads to negotiate a mixed- motive relational conflict through face-to-face (FTF) interaction, videoconferencing, audio call or synchronous text messaging. Linear mixed regression was used to assess the impact of communication media on non-economic outcomes of the individual negotiator and the moderating effect of negotiator traits. One- way and two-way analyses of variance were used to examine the impact of economic outcomes, as well as the moderating effect of negotiator traits, on negotiation dyads. 

Findings – The study found the synchronous text-based negotiations yielded poorer negotiation outcomes than other media. However, there were no significant differences in negotiation outcomes across FTF, video and audio negotiations, except for higher trust levels in FTF negotiations than video and audio negotiations, and higher value creation in audio than FTF negotiations. Importantly, the study revealed the moderating effect of conflict management style, indirect communication style and the personality traits of extraversion, conscientiousness, agreeableness and emotional stability. Specifically, dyads in which both negotiators had high assertiveness achieved lower joint value creation in FTF than audio and video negotiations. Furthermore, for dyads characterized by mismatched levels of extraversion, joint value creation was significantly lower in FTF negotiations than video and audio negotiations. 

Research limitations/implications – Greater statistical power for negotiator traits’ effects on economic outcomes could have been achieved with a higher number of dyads. 

Practical implications – When choosing the most appropriate medium for negotiating a complex matter with no prior familiarity with one's counterpart, it is prudent to rely on FTF interaction if it is crucial to establish trust. On the other hand, synchronous text messaging is a poor fit in terms of both economic and non- economic outcomes. When economic outcomes such as joint value creation are important, audio communication may surpass FTF communication due to the potential for negotiators to focus better on the content of their negotiation. With regard to other economic and non-economic outcomes, FTF, video and audio modes are likely to lead to comparable outcomes. The choice of communication mode does matter for certain outcomes, but the most optimal mode may differ across negotiators. It is more crucial to understand the characteristics of the negotiators as they have been shown by this study to influence the impact of communication media on negotiation success. For instance, the FTF setting, while conducive for trust- building, may not lead to positive economic outcomes if the negotiators have mismatched extraversion levels or are both assertive in their conflict management styles. Leaner media, such as video or audio communication, may be more appropriate in this regard.
