detail.abstract: Accounting practices evolve in response to changing historical, economic, and institutional contexts, particularly during periods of social and political transformation. Previous studies have typically framed accounting change as a consequence of external institutional pressures, while overlooking the internal dynamics and resource dependencies that can lead to resistance to change. This study addresses this gap through a historical case analysis of a major charitable organization in pre-unification Italy, using process tracing and a mixed institutional and resource-dependence framework. The paper offers three main contributions. First, it suggests that conflicting external reforms and internal demands can generate active resistance, and that the pressure-and-resistance process can be cumulative. Second, it expands accounting historiography by examining the understudied context of pre-unification Italy and showing public-sector accounting spillover into private nonprofit organizations. Third, it offers insights for policymakers and standard-setters, emphasizing that reform effectiveness depends on its alignment with organizational identity, legitimacy, and stakeholder expectations.

title: Big Data-Driven Early Warning Model for Safety Risk Management in Tobacco Enterprises

detail.title: Big Data-Driven Early Warning Model for Safety Risk Management in Tobacco Enterprises
detail.abstract: In the current digital transformation, it is essential to immediately ensure the safety and stability of production to address the increasing complexity brought by the development of industrial automation and the diversification of system data transmission networks. A comprehensive tobacco enterprise safety risk early warning system based on big data analysis and advanced machine learning technology to provide scientific evidence for decision-makers. Develop an application capable of real-time danger detection and alerting; traditional methods have not yet addressed this flaw. The proposed system includes a scalable distributed data processing pipeline for collecting and normalizing data from environmental sensors, high-frequency sensors, and operator logs. In highdimensional datasets affected by noise, novel feature engineering and dimensionality reduction methods are employed to extract key data. Boosted decision trees, kernel networks, and deep residual networks are important components of the ensemble learning system. The system's adaptability to anomalous events and the interpretable anomaly models can accurately identify changes in risk conditions. Identify instances of false negatives or missed reports in traditional monitoring systems; based on retrospective empirical evidence from actual production data, the accuracy of event occurrence predictions has significantly improved. The data-based modular early warning system has improved decision-making capabilities and operational safety in the tobacco industry environment. In order to expand its scope, we plan to promote it in more areas and enhance its preventive maintenance capabilities.

title: Trade Shocks, Reshoring, and the Green Transition - Micro–Macro Perspectives on Fragmented Globalization

detail.title: Trade Shocks, Reshoring, and the Green Transition - Micro–Macro Perspectives on Fragmented Globalization

detail.abstract: Trade wars, pandemics, and geopolitical rifts have turned "supply chain resilience" and "reshoring" into core elements of national economic strategies. Yet the implications of these trade disruptions for the global green transition remain poorly understood. This paper asks: How do contemporary trade shocks and the resulting reshoring and rewiring of global value chains (GVCs) affect the pace and distribution of decarbonization? Methodologically, we synthesize macro models of supply-chain reorientation, firm-level evidence on trade policy uncertainty and sourcing decisions, and case-based analyses of sustainability-oriented reshoring, combining them with a life-cycle and structurally grounded conceptual framework. We argue that fragmented globalization generates a new "green trilemma" among resilience, efficiency, and global environmental justice, in which reshoring can be either a catalyst for low-carbon structural change or a vehicle for spatially selective environmentalism. Our contribution is threefold: we bridge micro and macro perspectives on trade disruptions, reinterpret reshoring as a political allocation of global carbon space, and propose a Resilient Green Trade Compact that aligns trade, industrial, and climate policy across blocs. The paper concludes that the question is not whether to reconfigure trade, but whether we can do so without derailing a globally coherent green transition.

detail.abstract: This manuscript reconstructs an axial discipline that historically circulated in fragments across corporeal geometry, Vatican architectural frameworks, Renaissance proportional sciences, and archaic cosmology. Using the analytical architecture of UNC sYstEm L, the study identifies a set of structural constants 33 vertebrae, 284 elliptical columns (4×71 = 280+4), three global functional tiers, and the axial nodes C2, T6, S1/Co1 that exhibit stable proportional continuity across domains. A central finding is the emergence of the ratio: 28433=8.606 which recurs in vertebral distribution, thoracic symmetry (T6), rib-spine ratios (24/33), gestational cycles (280+4), and elliptical architectural modules. These alignments suggest a fractal axial mechanism underlying corporeal, spatial, and cosmological systems. The manuscript introduces a coded structural expression, the Axial Structural Invariant (ASI-Δ7): ASI-Δ7=(28433)712⋅C2+T6+S13 This invariant functions as a structural signature rather than a disclosed algorithm. Several computational steps and continuity operators have been intentionally omitted to preserve the integrity of the discipline. This work positions the axial discipline referred to here as Pre-Canonical Ars Axialis as the structural substrate underlying the author's previous SSRN contributions on continuity, rupture, tension fields, and high-field systemic stability.

title: ORGANIZATIONAL CULTURE AS A SOURCE OF COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE IN THE IMPLEMENTATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

detail.title: ORGANIZATIONAL CULTURE AS A SOURCE OF COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE IN THE IMPLEMENTATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
detail.abstract: With the exponential growth of artificial intelligence adoption, it is becoming more difficult for companies to maintain technological leadership, and therefore they are forced to adapt to changing market conditions in a timely manner. In this article, organizational culture plays a special role as a tool and source of competitive advantage in the implementation of artificial intelligence in the company's work processes. The research methodology includes the identification of the main functions of management, their analysis through the prism of aspects and types of management, as well as highlighting the role of artificial intelligence. The article examines the cases of the high-tech company Amazon, which demonstrate that organizational culture is a critical prerequisite for successful management and integration of artificial intelligence into the company's business processes, as well as the main source of competitive advantage for companies.

detail.abstract: This study proposes a conceptual model of human decision-making by reframing it as a process of response generation rather than mere selection among alternatives. While conventional theories define decision-making as choosing what to do, this study focuses on how action emerges and is expressed in relation to others. It identifies three fundamental sources of human action: Instinctive, Analytical, and Relational. The study introduces Response Intelligence as the integrative capacity that synthesizes these three sources and enables the generation of appropriate response. In addition, the concept of EPA (Entry Point for Awareness) is proposed as the precondition for response, conceptualized not as a boundary but as a continuous field in which awareness and meaning emerge. This framework shifts the understanding of decision-making from choice to response, offering a new perspective on human behavior.

title: Prosecuting a President

detail.title: Prosecuting a President

publicationDetails.detailsText: 23 Ohio State Journal of Criminal Law 267 (2026)

detail.abstract: In the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, many commentators treated the prosecutions of Donald Trump as critically important—bulwarks against authoritarianism and reminders that no one is above the law. Yet despite prosecutions and convictions, Trump was elected president once again. It’s hard not to view the prosecutions as failures across many dimensions. In this essay, I argue that the Trump prosecutions have important lessons to teach us about the limitations of both the criminal system and—more broadly—liberal legalism. I contend that the Trump prosecutions should serve as important reminders that criminal law is culturally contingent and that a prosecution cannot serve as a magic wand to do away with objectionable conduct. More broadly, I argue that the Trump prosecutions should serve as important illustrations of the limitations of liberal legalism as a response to authoritarianism. Criminal legal institutions—like all legal institutions—are culturally embedded. They depend on the judgment of discretionary actors, on public perception, and on politics. The Trump prosecutions show that law can’t be divorced from politics. Law and legal institutions might be important components of an attempt to combat Trumpism or advance justice. But they are only components. Arguments and tactics that rest on a hope that Trumpian politics can be defeated by some sort of apolitical, liberal law miss the reality that Trumpian politics can only really be defeated by politics.

title: Demographics and the Resource Economy: How Commodities Amplify the Lifecycle

detail.title: Demographics and the Resource Economy: How Commodities Amplify the Lifecycle
detail.abstract: The conventional wisdom that commodity revenues "mask" or "confound" demographic effects on external balances is wrong. Using a 140-country panel (N = 4,893) with World Bank natural resource rents interacted with demographic principal components and conditioning on income level (log GDP per capita and Z₁ × log GDP per capita), we find that commodity revenues amplify the demographic lifecycle mechanism rather than suppressing it. The Z₁ × Resource Rents interaction on the current account is +0.124 (p = 0.0002), attenuated 19% from an unconditional specification (+0.154) but still highly significant, confirming that commodity amplification is real and not an artifact of income differences between commodity and non-commodity economies. Income itself carries a large independent effect (log GDP per capita = +5.28, p < 0.01; Z₁ × log GDP per capita = +1.41, p < 0.01), indicating that richer countries have steeper demographic slopes irrespective of commodity status. The amplification is entirely hydrocarbon-driven, though income conditioning reveals that gas amplification was substantially overstated in unconditional specifications: oil Z₁ × Oil = +0.152 (p < 0.001, attenuated 39% from +0.248), gas Z₁ × Gas = +0.343 (p = 0.022, attenuated 51% from +0.702 and weakened from 1% to 5% significance), minerals =-0.078 (not significant). Gas-rich economies are disproportionately high-income, explaining the large gas attenuation. We do not find evidence that rents amplify the demographic effect through savings or investment beyond additive contributions; the interaction appears at the current account level (Z₁ × Resource on savings = +0.039, not significant). The interaction has weakened from 0.288 (p = 0.023, 1980-1999) to 0.035 (not significant, 2010-2024). A post-2000 era dummy interacted with the Z₁ × Resource term confirms a statistically significant structural break (-0.183, p = 0.016), consistent with sovereign wealth fund maturation and capital account liberalization, though the specific institutional mechanism is suggestive rather than identified. Commodity dependence disrupts FDI patterns-the Z₁ × Resource interaction on FDI is negative (-0.232, p < 0.01), indicating that extractive investment follows geology rather than demographics-while portfolio allocation is unaffected. Aging commodity exporters, particularly Iran (rents 29%, old-age dependency ratio tripling from 10% to 35% by 2050), face a "double cliff" of simultaneous demographic and depletion pressure, amplified by the energy transition.

title: Innovación como derecho fundamental y cultura de la integración / Innovation as a fundamental right and the culture of integration
affiliations: and Universidad de Guayaquil

detail.title: Innovación como derecho fundamental y cultura de la integración / Innovation as a fundamental right and the culture of integration

contentFormat.other: Working paper, preliminary theoretical framework for the Culture of Integration and Innovation as a Right

detail.abstract:
This article proposes a normative framework in which innovation, conceived as a fundamental right -understood as “the right of every person to access, create, adapt, and transform knowledge under conditions of equity, freedom, and sustainability”- is articulated with a culture of integration as a condition for its effective exercise.


It argues that a right to innovate cannot exist without social structures that integrate cultural, social, and cognitive diversity. From this perspective, the article develops the concept of “innovative integration”, understood as the set of practices and institutions that enable the effective participation of all individuals in the creation and transformation of knowledge.


The paper connects this framework with the notion of “guaranteed innovation”, emphasizing that state obligations must ensure not only access but also structural integration. It concludes that a culture of integration is the mechanism through which the right to innovation becomes effective in diverse contexts.

title: Attention-Risk-GNN: An Explainable Graph Neural Network for Systemic Risk Propagation
affiliations: Morehouse College and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Attention-Risk-GNN: An Explainable Graph Neural Network for Systemic Risk Propagation
detail.abstract: Systemic risk in interbank networks is very difficult to quantify and explain. Current approaches produce either opaque risk scores with no justification, or explanations not relating to the underlying model scores. AttentionRisk-GNN, a graph neural network framework, is introduced in this paper to address both limitations simultaneously. The architecture performs multihead attention on directed exposure graphs, whereby rather than adding explainability to the model after-the-fact, it takes Shapley attribution during the forward pass such that each risk score is provided with a list of the counterparty that actually caused it, ranked. On the 500-node benchmark, the model has F1 = 0.91 and AUC = 0.96, outperforming DebtRank and the three GNN baselines. The runtime scales linearly with respect to the number of institutions on sparse graphs and convergence is guaranteed by standard nonconvex stochastic gradient descent theory.

title: The Impact of Isomorphic Mimicry, Economic Opaqueness, and Depoliticization of Public Servants on Public Sector Performance in Sub-Saharan Africa
affiliations: Independent, National Assembly Budget Office, Ministry of Economic Planning and Development, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Nairobi, affiliation not provided to SSRN, UNIVERSITY OF THE GAMBIA and University of Somalia

detail.title: The Impact of Isomorphic Mimicry, Economic Opaqueness, and Depoliticization of Public Servants on Public Sector Performance in Sub-Saharan Africa
detail.abstract:
This study examines the impact of isomorphic mimicry, economic opaqueness, and depoliticization of public servants on public sector performance in Sub-Saharan Africa. Using a fixed effects panel model covering 30 countries over the period 2005–2023, the analysis investigates how institutional design, transparency, and bureaucratic arrangements shape governance outcomes. The findings show that isomorphic mimicry is consistently associated with lower public sector performance, indicating that the adoption of externally prescribed institutional models without corresponding improvements in administrative capability undermines effectiveness. Economic opaqueness emerges as the most significant determinant of weak performance, highlighting the critical role of transparency and accountability in public sector efficiency. Depoliticization exhibits a weaker and less consistent effect, suggesting that bureaucratic insulation alone does not guarantee improved outcomes in the absence of robust accountability systems. Interaction effects further reveal that institutional constraints reinforce one another, particularly where mimicry coexists with weak transparency. Overall, the results suggest that public sector performance in Sub-Saharan Africa is driven more by functional institutional capacity and transparency than by formal institutional design. The study contributes to debates on governance reform by emphasizing capability-building and context-sensitive institutional development over symbolic policy adoption.

Keywords: Isomorphic Mimicry, Economic Opaqueness, and Depoliticization of Public Servants, Public Sector Performance, Sub-Saharan Africa economies.

detail.abstract: This report is a field-based socio-economic study of the Mathabhanga village in Batiaghata, Khulna, under the Live-in-Field Experience (LFE) program. The research uses the techniques of Participatory Rural Appraisal (PRA), questionnaire surveys, observation, and village mapping to analyze the demographic makeup of the village, living patterns, agriculture, health, environment, and the local infrastructure. The results indicate that agriculture is the major livelihood, while income diversification is not high, and seasonality greatly impacts economic stability. The paper also puts into the limelight some critical problems in healthcare access, sanitation, education, and environmental management, such as the water quality issues and the waste disposal practices. In spite of these adversities, the village demonstrates promise in the use of natural resources, cooperation of communities, and the presence of NGOs. The report also outlines significant development gaps and gives viable recommendations to alleviate the rural livelihoods, health services, and environmental sustainability in the study area.

title: A Mathematical Framework for Sequence Risk

detail.title: A Mathematical Framework for Sequence Risk
detail.abstract: Sequence risk refers to the dependence of terminal wealth on the order in which a fixed set of returns is realized. It is present whenever an investor contributes to or withdraws from a portfolio during the investment horizon and is absent when there are no intermediate cash flows. This paper derives a second-order approximation for the expected value and variance of terminal wealth under uniform permutations of a fixed return multiset. Both moments reduce to closed-form expressions involving two quantities: the within-multiset variance of returns and a measure of how capital exposure is distributed across time. The ratio of the two moments gives a Sequence Sensitivity Index that summarizes path dependence in a single coefficient of variation and does not require enumerating permutations. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the approximations in decumulation, accumulation, and zero-cash-flow regimes, and indicate the horizons and dispersion levels at which the second-order truncation loses accuracy.

detail.abstract: For nearly three decades, the 1995 Bank Merger Guidelines shaped how federal regulators analyzed bank mergers in the United States. The Biden administration broke with this tradition, undertaking a significant overhaul of bank merger oversight as part of its comprehensive pro-competition agenda. This chapter examines that reform effort, the Trump administration's partial dismantling of these changes, and the path forward for future policymakers. The Biden-era reforms deserve careful study despite their mixed fate, as they could provide a blueprint for reinvigorating bank merger enforcement in a future administration.

title: Increasing Transparency in Digital Music Markets: Regulatory Pathways Beyond Copyright Law?

detail.title: Increasing Transparency in Digital Music Markets: Regulatory Pathways Beyond Copyright Law?

declarations.funderStatement: This paper explores results from the comprehensive study ‘Roles of EU competition law and platform regulation across online music platforms’, conducted for the project Fair MusE (Promoting Fairness of the Music Ecosystem in a Platform-Dominated and Post-Pandemic Europe), funded by the programme Horizon Europe (Grant agreement ID: 101095088) to investigate and promote fairness for music creators and stakeholders in digital music markets.

publicationDetails.detailsText: NIR Nordiskt Immateriellt Rättsskydd nr 1 2026

detail.abstract:
Music markets have long been criticised for a lack of adequate and transparent information on the exploitation of musical works and concerns regarding the working conditions for music creators. Initial hopes that the rise of online music consumption might bring a significant change to this data transparency problem have not sufficiently materialised. In the European Union (EU), one of the main legislative reactions to the radical changes that digitisation and the rise of online platform has brought to music and other creative sectors, and the resulting impact for the exploitation of copyright and related rights, has been the Directive for Copyright in the Digital Single Market (DSM Directive). 
One of the novelties of the DSM Directive is contained in Article 19. Article 19 enshrines a transparency obligation to the benefit of authors and performers to receive, at least once a year, “up to date, relevant and comprehensive information on the exploitation of their works and performances from the parties to whom they have licensed or transferred their rights”, including from sub-licensees. This article examines whether and how other areas of EU law regulating digital platform markets, in particular EU competition law and EU platform regulation, could support the effective implementation of the transparency obligations set out under Article 19 DSM Directive.

detail.abstract: This paper looks at something most NGO leadership discussions tend to avoid , what happens to employees when the salary doesn't add up. Through conversations, questionnaires, and field observations, data was gathered from NGO employees working across different regions and roles. What emerged wasn't surprising, but it was sobering: 85% of respondents were dissatisfied with what they earn, and a large majority reported either no increment at all or one so small it barely registers. What makes this more than just a salary complaint is the profile of the people involved. These are educated, qualified, often highly experienced individuals, people who chose this sector knowing it wouldn't make them rich, but perhaps not expecting to feel this invisible. The paper explores how financial stress slowly chips away at motivation, creates a quiet but steady disengagement, and eventually threatens the very work these organizations exist to do. At the same time, the data also tells a more layered story. People aren't staying simply because they have no choice. Many stay because of a genuine, deeply felt sense of service. Others because of religious conviction, the flexibility their role offers, or because the work is close to home and community. These are real and meaningful reasons. They deserve to be understood, not just used as justification for keeping salaries low.

title: Interventions du FMI face aux crises financières: Réformes économiques et impacts sociaux–le cas du Liban en perspective
affiliations: and Notre Dame University

detail.title: Interventions du FMI face aux crises financières: Réformes économiques et impacts sociaux–le cas du Liban en perspective
detail.abstract:
Objective: To analyze the impact of International Monetary Fund (IMF) interventions in countries facing financial crises, with a particular focus on the case of Lebanon. The study aims to identify the economic and social factors determining the effectiveness of IMF-imposed austerity programs, while providing specific recommendations for the Lebanese context.

Design/methodology/approach: This research is based on an in-depth analysis of secondary sources, including IMF reports, academic studies, and economic data, in order to compare outcomes across different countries and apply these findings to Lebanon.

Findings: The results show that the success of IMF interventions largely depends on the coherence of economic reforms and their adaptation to national specificities. However, austerity policies often have significant negative impacts, such as worsening social inequalities and deterioration of public services. In the case of Lebanon, the study highlights that interventions are likely to fail without transparent governance, effective coordination, and measures tailored to the country’s socio-economic characteristics.

Originality/value: This article stands out through a detailed analysis of IMF programs within a global framework, while offering practical recommendations specific to Lebanon. The study explores the necessary balance between economic reforms, social equity, and governance in order to maximize the effectiveness of interventions.

title: Computational Macrohistory: Structural Stress and Political Instability in the MENA Region - A Computational Macrohistory Analysis of the Arab Spring

detail.title: Computational Macrohistory: Structural Stress and Political Instability in the MENA Region - A Computational Macrohistory Analysis of the Arab Spring
detail.abstract: We extend the Computational Macrohistory (CMH) framework to an eleven-country analysis of structural preconditions for political instability in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region during 2000-2012, with particular reference to the Arab Spring uprisings of 2010-2011. Building on the three-country proof of concept presented in WP-2026-003, we construct a five-component Systemic Stress Index(SSI) for Algeria, Bahrain, Egypt, Jordan, Kuwait, Morocco, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Tunisia, and Yemen, drawing on variables capturing demographic pressure, income inequality, youth unemployment, regime type, and internet penetration. The SSI should be understood as a reduced empirical proxy designed to test whether core structural signals hypothesised by the CMH framework appear in historical data; it does not implement the full CMH dynamic system. Our results indicate that the SSI correctly classifies eight of eleven countries at the pre-event benchmark year of 2010, achieving a descriptive accuracy of 72.7% against a binary outcome variable distinguishing severe instability (revolution or civil war) from all other outcomes. This analysis is retrospective classification, not out-of-sample prediction. Group-level analysis reveals a mean separation of 0.290 standard deviation units between instability and stability clusters. Robustness analysis across six alternative weighting schemes demonstrates that the Base specification is among the most stable, with the Regime-focused scheme achieving marginally superior pairwise discrimination. Leave-one-component-out analysis identifies youth unemployment (E₄) and anocracy stress (derived from P₁) as the most discriminatively critical components. Three misclassified cases—Jordan, Egypt, and Syria—are discussed in detail; each reveals theoretically informative limits of the current five-variable specification rather than random error. The paper concludes by specifying the conditions under which the expanded research programme—targeting N ≥ 30 validated country-cases—would constitute genuine statistical validation of the framework.

title: Asynchronous Compliance in AI Governance: Rules in Multiple Legal States
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Asynchronous Compliance in AI Governance: Rules in Multiple Legal States
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence governance increasingly requires organizations to make design, procurement, and deployment decisions under rules that are neither fully settled nor fully absent. Existing accounts often describe this environment in terms of regulatory lag, fragmented standards, or generalized uncertainty. This Article advances a narrower claim. It identifies a distinct governance conditiondescribed here as asynchronous compliance-in which organizations build and deploy systems under rules distributed across multiple legal states at once: proposed but not final, finalized but not yet in force, in force but not yet enforced in any stable pattern, enforced but not yet interpreted consistently, and active elsewhere under jurisdictionally non-fungible compliance logics. Once obligations are distributed across these overlapping states, compliance can no longer be treated as a singular point-in-time status. Organizations instead optimize for optionality under legal incompletion. The practical result is not merely uncertainty, but a recognizable pattern of organizational behavior: architectural conservatism, documentary branching, procurement caution, segmented release, and the movement of governance authority upstream into design and deployment decisions. In that environment, governance tractability becomes a competitive variable, and technically stronger systems can lose to weaker systems that are easier to defend administratively. The contribution is intentionally diagnostic. It does not propose a harmonization strategy, a preferred enterprise compliance architecture, or an institutional reform agenda. Its narrower objective is to clarify why the contemporary governance difficulty lies not simply in incomplete rules, but in the fact that incomplete rules already govern.

title: Informed Predictive Maintenance Modeling

detail.title: Informed Predictive Maintenance Modeling

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced this work.

detail.abstract: Explainable predictive maintenance requires not only accurate models but problem formulations that are legible to engineers, operators, and decision-makers who may pursue different goals on the same task. This study addresses that challenge by grounding the failure-prediction problem in an axiomatic probability framework, using the empirical outcome distribution to inform class imbalance handling, bias initialization, and multilabel stratification. Physics-informed feature engineering encodes domain knowledge directly into the feature space, making model explanations accessible across technical backgrounds. A tuned multilabel neural network achieves a macro-average F1 of 0.98, with LIME analysis confirming that predictions are driven by physically meaningful interaction terms. The results suggest that bringing the right domain expertise to both data preparation and model interpretation is essential for producing explanations that are operationally accountable.

detail.abstract: Purpose: Analysing the impact of the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) interventions in countries facing financial crises, with a particular focus on the case of Lebanon. How-ever, austerity policies often have significant negative impacts, such as worsening social inequalities and deteriorating public services. Regarding Lebanon, the study highlights that

title: Filling the Gaps with MICE: Addressing Missing Data in Real Estate Price Indices
affiliations: University of Graz and

detail.title: Filling the Gaps with MICE: Addressing Missing Data in Real Estate Price Indices
detail.abstract:
Missing data are a common feature of micro-level transaction data used to construct hedonic real estate price indices. Missingness typically occurs in the descriptive characteristics required for quality adjustment rather than in transaction prices. Since these characteristics are central to hedonic quality adjustment, complete-case analysis can skew measured price dynamics through sample-selection and composition effects. This paper proposes multiple imputation as a way to handle missing characteristic values in index construction. The aim is not to recover individual missing values, but to restore incomplete observations and reduce variability in the estimation sample. We employ multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE) as a flexible imputation framework. Since conventional aggregation rules for multiple imputation, Rubin’s rules, do not align with the multiplicative chaining structure of price indices, we introduce an alternative aggregation method based on pooled growth rates. Empirical evidence from two applications, a large dataset of Vienna apartment transactions and a smaller, more heterogeneous Austrian office market, shows that index estimates are relatively robust to missing data in large, homogeneous settings. In contrast, in thinner and more heterogeneous markets, imputation can materially affect index dynamics. In both settings, flexible MICE specifications with rich predictor sets perform better than simpler imputation methods.

title: Executive control of labour rights: the dangerous path of the Employment Rights Act 2025
affiliations: School of Law, King's College, London; Centre for Business Research, University of Cambridge

detail.title: Executive control of labour rights: the dangerous path of the Employment Rights Act 2025
detail.abstract:
Instead of 'making work pay', the Employment Rights Act 2025 paves a dangerous path of 'making rights options'. A future hostile government could, through Regulations, without an Act of Parliament, destroy new rules regarding zero hours contracts, gagging contracts, equality action plans, limits to 'fire and rehire', the sector negotiating body remits, electronic balloting, and the Fair Work Agency. This vast scope of executive control in the Act adds to a long list of existing labour rights that can be switched on or off with Regulations, including who gets any employment rights, how many holidays we have, dismissal and redundancy procedures, who controls workers' pension money, whether listed companies have worker directors, and whether the Treasury and Bank of England pursue full employment or smother real wages under a guise of 'price stability'. 

There is a very high risk of an extremist government in the near future, namely one led by Farage's Reform or the post-Truss Conservatives. The destruction of labour rights could be on a bigger scale than even the 2010 Conservative-Liberal coalition's measures. To recall, this included neutering most rights through Tribunal fees, destroying fair dismissal for a third of the workforce with a 2 year qualifying period, tying a million people into zero hours contracts via Jobcentre benefits, and halting collective bargaining across the public sector and universities with pay freezes. Then there were the anti-union Acts. 

To protect social democracy, a new Labour Rights Act is needed that solidifies workers' rights (without discretion of governments to change them) and that meets international standards. This means creating the rights that Labour originally promised to roll out in its first 100 days, and adding rules found in a majority of wealthy democracies: a single worker status, a sector-bargaining action plan to achieve at least 80% cover, creating worker directors and giving workers control of their pension money, and a statutory duty for full employment at fair wages and hours. This will change people's lives. But crucially it will also change the reality of political power bases, and make it harder for fascist-lite parties to exist and get votes.

title: Causal Discovery via Simultaneous DAG Recovery Using the Angles Space of Directional Dependence Measures
affiliations: DataMineit, LLC

detail.title: Causal Discovery via Simultaneous DAG Recovery Using the Angles Space of Directional Dependence Measures
detail.abstract: Most causal discovery algorithms utilizing a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) framework execute sequentially (e.g. constraint-based models) or iteratively (e.g. score-based or functional causal models). In contrast, we develop a new method-Angles-based Directional Dependence (ADD)-that executes over the entire DAG space simultaneously, based on only two matrix estimations. We apply dual orderings on any (positive definite) directional dependence measure for all pairwise relationships, identify statistically significant directional dependence in the angles space (where angles are independent random variables), and then enforce acyclicality to make proper causal interpretations. Potential benefits of the approach include increased coherence, due to simultaneous edge-calling within a positive definite space; increased power, due to the ability to use any directional dependence measure and thus, opportunistically adapt to different or varying data conditions; and increased speed/scalability, due to the need for only two matrix estimations, and two (fast) simulations to define empirical confidence bounds under independence (regardless of the size of the DAG space). We conduct a preliminary empirical study evaluating directional dependence marginally, effectively identifying directed reachability under nonlinear, heavy-tailed data conditions and thus, indicating applications to feature selection in quantitative finance. The promising results justify and encourage a more extensive follow-up study to benchmark against competing algorithms to more fully test the above-mentioned potential benefits of ADD.

title: Integrating User Trust and Social Filtering into a Hybrid Recommendation Model for Urban Transportation Mode Selection
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: Integrating User Trust and Social Filtering into a Hybrid Recommendation Model for Urban Transportation Mode Selection
detail.abstract: Traditional recommendation systems for urban transportation have largely relied on collaborative filtering based on historical trip patterns or on content-based filtering using static user preferences. While hybrid approaches have been proposed for transportation transaction platforms, few attempts have been made to incorporate social trust information into mode selection recommendations. This paper presents a hybrid recommendation model that integrates collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, and trust-based social filtering to suggest optimal transportation modes-car, bus, metro, bicycle, or walking-for urban travelers. Trust relationships are derived from explicit user declarations as well as implicit cooccurrence patterns in travel histories. Evaluation on a mobility dataset containing travel diaries from 210 urban commuters demonstrates that the inclusion of trust propagation improves recommendation precision by 12.4% compared to a hybrid model without social filtering, with particular gains for cold-start users who have limited personal trip histories. The results suggest that trust-aware social filtering offers a viable direction for enhancing transportation recommendations beyond conventional similarity-based methods.

title: The CLARITY Act in Motion: What the Senate Debate Reveals About Digital Asset Regulation
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: The CLARITY Act in Motion: What the Senate Debate Reveals About Digital Asset Regulation
detail.abstract: The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act of 2025, or CLARITY Act, represents one of the most consequential efforts by the United States Congress to establish a unified regulatory framework for digital assets. After passing the House of Representatives with bipartisan support in July 2025, the bill entered a more complicated Senate process marked by parallel committee consideration, sustained banking-industry opposition, and a prolonged dispute over stablecoin yield. As of May 2026, a bipartisan compromise on the yield question has reopened the path toward Senate Banking Committee markup, though important legislative and political obstacles remain. This paper examines the bill's core regulatory structure, the Senate committee process, the stablecoin reward controversy, and the remaining steps required for enactment. It argues that the CLARITY Act may ultimately reshape the U.S. digital asset landscape, but only if lawmakers can preserve a workable coalition and resolve remaining concerns about banking substitution, ethics language, and legislative timing.

title:
La soutenabilité des startups féminines
dans un Liban en période de crise
The sustainability of women ’ s startups in Lebanon
in times of crisis

detail.title:
La soutenabilité des startups féminines
dans un Liban en période de crise
The sustainability of women ’ s startups in Lebanon
in times of crisis
detail.abstract:
Purpose: This study aims to analyse the factors influencing the viability of women ’ s startups in Lebanon, particularly in the context of multiple crises. The goal is to understand how these factors impact the financial autonomy of women entrepreneurs and their role in the emancipation of women in a society beset by economic, political, and social challenges.
Design/methodology/approach: The methodological approach is based on a literature review and econometric analysis using the Elastic Net model to identify and assess the impact of different factors on the performance of women ’ s startups. The study considers variables such as product innovation, economic stability, and ongoing crises.
Findings: The findings reveal that product innovation is the most decisive factor in the financial success of female startups, while multiple crises, particularly economic and political, exert negative pressure on their viability. A stable socio-economic context is crucial to ensure the development of these companies.
Originality/value: This research stands out for its consideration of women ’ s entrepreneurship in an environment marked by a series of crises. Thus, it offers an innovative perspective on the unique challenges faced by women entrepreneurs in Lebanon. It also highlights the
importance of supporting these initiatives to foster women ’ s economic emancipation in
a difficult context.

reference: Chicago Booth Accounting Research Center Research Paper No. Forthcoming
title: Optimizing the AI Data Supply Chain: A Framework for Strategic Sourcing and Risk Management
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Optimizing the AI Data Supply Chain: A Framework for Strategic Sourcing and Risk Management

publicationDetails.detailsText: Chicago Booth Accounting Research Center Research Paper No. Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Chicago Booth: Chookaszian Accounting Research Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: The AI data supply chain plays a fundamental role in the development of high-performing and compliant machine learning models. However, current data sourcing, quality assurance, processing, regulatory compliance, cost management, and risk mitigation strategies exhibit significant inefficiencies. Drawing from traditional supply chain management principles, this study identifies key capability gaps in AI data supply chains and proposes a structured framework for optimization. The analysis highlights critical deficiencies, including reactive and ad hoc data sourcing, insufficient quality control mechanisms, inefficient batch-based processing, fragmented compliance tracking, unstructured cost management, inadequate risk mitigation strategies, and limited scalability. The study outlines core challenges, including fragmented sourcing strategies, reactive quality control, batch-oriented processing inefficiencies, inconsistent regulatory compliance, unstructured cost management, and insufficient risk mitigation. To address these limitations, the proposed Dynamic Adaptive Sourcing Framework (DASF) integrates facility location modeling, supplier evaluation scorecards, network optimization, Little's Law for processing efficiency, and continuous improvement mechanisms. This structured approach enables AI providers to strategically balance public, proprietary, and synthetic datasets, optimize costs, and reduce compliance risks while maintaining high data quality and fairness. A case study applying decision tree modeling and linear programming optimization to AI fraud detection demonstrates the framework's effectiveness in enhancing sourcing efficiency, reducing regulatory exposure, and improving data quality. The results highlight how systematic data sourcing models can replace ad-hoc decision-making with structured, quantifiable, and adaptive methodologies, ensuring sustainable AI development. By integrating supply chain best practices, this research provides a scalable, regulatory-compliant, and cost-efficient approach to AI data supply chain optimization, offering a competitive advantage to AI providers navigating an increasingly complex landscape.

title: A Hybrid Data Mining Approach for Real-Time Ride-Sharing Recommendations in Urban Transportation Networks
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, and

detail.title: A Hybrid Data Mining Approach for Real-Time Ride-Sharing Recommendations in Urban Transportation Networks
detail.abstract: The rapid urbanization observed in the early 2010s has intensified traffic congestion and environmental concerns, making efficient ride-sharing a critical component of sustainable transportation systems. Existing ride-matching platforms often rely on static user preferences or simple geographic proximity, failing to adapt to dynamic travel patterns and individual behavioral nuances. This paper proposes a hybrid data mining approach for real-time ridesharing recommendations in urban networks. The method integrates collaborative filteringbuilding on user trip history and similarity metrics (Herlocker et al., 2004)-with association rule mining from spatiotemporal trajectory data (Lee et al., 2008). A lightweight real-time matching engine processes streaming GPS probes and trip requests, applying a sliding window model to capture short-term demand fluctuations (Yuan et al., 2010). Evaluation using three months of taxi trip records from Chicago (2013) and a simulated user study with 500 participants shows that the hybrid approach achieves a 23% improvement in ride acceptance rates and a 31% reduction in detour overhead compared to baseline distance-only methods. Furthermore, computational latency remains under two seconds for up to 1,000 concurrent requests, meeting real-time operational constraints. These results suggest that combining historical preference mining with live traffic pattern detection offers a practical path toward more responsive and effective ride-sharing recommendations in dense urban settings.

title: Working Paper Series: Full Paper-Future Warfare Readiness -Article 6 Triangulated Acceptable Engagement (TAEM): A Practitioner Framework for ASEAN-AUKUS-China Diplomatic Practice

detail.title: Working Paper Series: Full Paper-Future Warfare Readiness -Article 6 Triangulated Acceptable Engagement (TAEM): A Practitioner Framework for ASEAN-AUKUS-China Diplomatic Practice
detail.abstract: Heightened great power rivalry between AUKUS partners and China presents a structural challenge to Southeast Asian states. Existing analytical frameworks to an extent elide bilaterally beneficial Pareto-optimal solutions that present themselves in multilateral form even as idealisation is confounded by three irreducible forces: ASEAN states' preference for bilateral over multilateral commitments; AUKUS partners' need for concrete rather than symbolic strategic payoff state for participation anyway; and China's active counterengagement around the region designed to preserve its rights. The Triangulated Acceptable Engagement Model (TAEM)-an operationalisation of the existing hedging literature into a desk-officer-usable workflow. It replaced Pareto optimisation by a triangulated tolerance, which is a structured heuristic where each party accepts an engagement design because the realistic alternatives would do worse for it. It has three main components: a National Capacity layer that applies to the functional-domain level rather than at the whole-of-state level (acknowledging that capacity portfolios are uneven across cyber, maritime, and other domains); an Engagement Channels layer to distinguish functionally among bilateral, ASEAN-led multilateral, and hybrid arrangements; and an Acceptability Test applied separately from each of the three parties' perspectives, aided by a 0-3 scoring rubric for identifying binding constraints. The design of particular engagement activities involves explicit exit triggers and follows a five-step allocation algorithm, which is applied to four stage conditional scenarios corresponding to the Ukrainian, Singaporean, and Korean/Turkish stages of national capacity. Through these scenarios, existing ASEAN arrangements (ASCCE; Singapore's Information Fusion Centre; Indonesia-Australia Defence Cooperation Arrangement) are used as illustrative anchors in three success scenarios, while the AUKUS announcement of September 2021 and a counterfactual Indonesian response serves to retrospective apply the framework in failure scenario to show how TAEM would have indicatored features of structural failure patterns that subsequently emerged. The TAEM's contribution is transforming established hedging knowledge into an auditable, operational tool. This framework is targeted to ASEAN engagement designers and conditionally a tool for AUKUS expectation management; its relevance to China-led engagement is illustrated as a functional extrapolation.

title: The State-Contingent Debt Premium: Evidence from French Public Bonds
affiliations: Santa Clara University - Leavey School of Business - Economics Department and ESCP Business School

detail.title: The State-Contingent Debt Premium: Evidence from French Public Bonds
detail.abstract:
State-contingent debt (SCD) instruments have been proposed as an improvement to sovereign debt markets, but their issuance costs are not well understood. We estimate the SCD premium at issuance and for more than a decade thereafter, employing a quasi-twin bond strategy that uses two very similar French government bonds issued in 1956: one conventional bond and one state-contingent bond with coupons linked to industrial production. At issuance, the expected yield on the SCD bond was 77 basis points higher than its twin. Due to robust growth in the French economy ex-post, the realized SCD premium at issuance was roughly twice as large (146 basis points). However, rising market prices of the state-contingent bond reduced both spreads to zero by 1964. They rose again in May 1968 following an unexpected general strike, which significantly reduced French industrial production; however, by 1970, the SCD premium had fallen to values close to zero.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title:
The Collapsed Pyramid:
A CFO's Reflections on Justice, Power, and Structure in Multinational Corporations

detail.title:
The Collapsed Pyramid:
A CFO's Reflections on Justice, Power, and Structure in Multinational Corporations

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial, personal, or professional conflicts of interest related to this study. The observations presented are drawn from the author's own executive career and do not involve any current commercial, consulting, or advisory relationships that could be perceived to have influenced the content.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author as a reflective practitioner contribution.

detail.abstract:
This reflective paper introduces and develops the concept of The Collapsed Pyramid, a framework describing a recurring structural pathology observed across multinational corporations. Drawing on more than two decades of executive experience as a Chief Financial Officer and Senior System Architect in eight countries, and through professional engagement with colleagues of more than thirty nationalities, this paper documents how the classical managerial pyramid, in which authority, responsibility, and rewards are vertically aligned, frequently collapses in practice. In the collapsed configuration, authority concentrates at the top, responsibility is displaced downward, and benefits are extracted upward, producing a structural inversion of organizational justice. 

The paper examines six interrelated dimensions in which this collapse manifests: (1) company policies, (2) budgeting processes, (3) the asymmetry between power and responsibility, (4) staffing structures, (5) bonuses and remuneration, and (6) employee benefits. For each dimension, the paper contrasts the normative ideal with field observations, offers anonymized illustrative vignettes, identifies the mechanism of collapse, and considers who ultimately bears the cost. The analysis is anchored in established management scholarship, including Fayol's principle of parity between authority and responsibility, agency theory, and social identity theory.

 The paper concludes that the collapsed pyramid is not primarily a failure of individual ethics but a structural failure rooted in weak board independence, ineffective compensation committees, conflicts of interest in policy-making, and the absence of functioning accountability mechanisms for senior executives. The paper is offered as a practitioner contribution to the literature on corporate governance and organizational justice, and as a cautionary reference for newly appointed executives who may encounter these patterns early in their tenure.

title: Information Overload? The Impact of Algorithmic Routines on Organizational Performance
affiliations: Tilburg University, Kühne Logistics University, Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management and Kühne Logistics University

detail.title: Information Overload? The Impact of Algorithmic Routines on Organizational Performance
detail.abstract: Firms are increasingly adopting digital technologies, such as robotic process automation and artificial intelligence, to automate organizational routines with the aim of enhancing organizational performance. However, such adoption is not guaranteed to result in performance improvements. A priori, it is not always fully clear what the organizational performance impact of adopting algorithmic routines will be. We analyze the digital traces of algorithmic and human-enacted routine instances in a replenishment process at a large international manufacturing company. Our analysis employs novel object-centric process mining techniques, which enable the complete identification of routine instances. In contrast, conventional process mining approaches would obscure mutually related deletions and insertions. Our results show a substantial increase in the share of algorithmic routine instances following adoption, thereby reducing the share of human-enacted routine instances, resulting in productivity gains. However, through econometric analysis, we demonstrate that algorithmic routines can negatively affect a key organizational metric (replenishment lead time), thereby adverse impacting organizational performance. Furthermore, our findings indicate that human-enacted routine instances tend to outperform algorithmic routine instances and positively affect replenishment lead time. Given that suppliers primarily need to respond manually to these routine instances, we attribute these findings to information overload, a concept originating from organizational information processing theory (OIPT).

title: Agentic AI in Procurement Software: A Neutral Market Whitepaper
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Agentic AI in Procurement Software: A Neutral Market Whitepaper

keywords: and transformation leaders Publication style Structured whitepaper with abstract

detail.abstract: Procurement software is moving from digitized workflow management to AI-assisted and increasingly agentic operating models. In practical terms, agentic AI means software agents that can understand a procurement objective, gather context from enterprise systems, reason through a sequence of steps, take or recommend actions, and escalate to humans when judgment, authority, or risk demands it. This whitepaper examines how agentic AI is emerging across procurement software, including source-to-pay suites, intake and orchestration platforms, sourcing specialists, supplier management platforms, contract and AP automation tools, and ERP-native procurement systems. The paper compares leading and widely available procurement software providers based on publicly available information as of May 2026. It does not endorse any one vendor. Instead, it evaluates the market through neutral criteria: functional coverage, AI maturity, agentic workflow depth, governance, data foundation, integration approach, enterprise fit, and implementation risk. The central finding is that no single procurement platform is universally best. Suite vendors tend to provide breadth, governance, and ERP alignment; orchestration platforms tend to provide speed and user adoption; sourcing specialists tend to offer sharper autonomous sourcing capability; and AP or contract specialists tend to deliver deep automation in narrower domains. The right choice depends less on brand reputation and more on procurement maturity, data quality, governance appetite, supplier complexity, existing ERP landscape, and the degree of autonomy the organization is ready to accept.

title: Constituent Interests in SEC Rules: Evidence from Voluntary Comment Letters *
affiliations: MIT Sloan School of Management, University of Florida and Dartmouth College - Tuck School of Business

detail.title: Constituent Interests in SEC Rules: Evidence from Voluntary Comment Letters *
detail.abstract: We provide large-scale descriptive evidence on how the SEC's rulemaking process relates to constituent interests expressed in voluntary comment letters. Using large language models, we construct a comprehensive dataset linking constituents' stated preferences across more than 65,000 comment letters addressing 417 rules proposed between 1995 and 2024. We find that proposed rules more frequently align with firms' stated interests than those of other constituents, while this advantage attenuates at adoption. Conversely, retail investors' preferences are more often associated with dropped provisions. Within-group agreement amplifies these patterns, while cross-group disagreement disproportionately disadvantages retail investors and experts.

title: The Institutional Collapse Predictor A Forward-Looking Framework for Corporate Failure Risk Assessment
affiliations: Consciousness Gradient Theory Group Ltd

detail.title: The Institutional Collapse Predictor A Forward-Looking Framework for Corporate Failure Risk Assessment
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Institutional Collapse Predictor (ICP), a quantitative framework for assessing corporate collapse risk within a 12-24 month window. The ICP integrates five analytical dimensions: incident severity, market perception, financial trajectory, leadership stability, and narrative integrity, into a composite risk score that maps to a seven-tier classification system from STABLE to CRITICAL COLLAPSE. The framework has been retrospectively validated against nine major corporate collapses with complete distributional separation between collapsed and surviving institutions. A prospective validation study of 19 companies (October 2025) is currently maturing, with early results showing the highest-risk prediction (Beyond Meat) tracking strongly toward collapse. An 18-company dual-track blind scoring study demonstrated inter-rater reliability between a human scorer and an AI scorer, with average divergence of approximately 4.5 points (excluding two outliers attributable to pre-v2.9 methodology) on a scale where meaningful classification changes require movement of 15-35 points. The ICP addresses a gap in existing corporate risk assessment by combining real-time incident tracking with contrarian sentiment analysis, treating positive market sentiment as a risk amplifier rather than a reassurance signal.

title: Dirac Blocks for Sensitivity Engines: Boundary Calculus and Likelihood-Ratio Reweighting for Boundary-Sensitive Monte Carlo Greeks

detail.title: Dirac Blocks for Sensitivity Engines: Boundary Calculus and Likelihood-Ratio Reweighting for Boundary-Sensitive Monte Carlo Greeks
detail.abstract: Distributional Sensitivity Engine (DSE) and Numeraire-Based Distributional Sensitivity Engine (NDSE) express option values and sensitivities through a small collection of conditional digital blocks under pricing measures matched to the relevant numeraire. A central numerical difficulty is that these objects are boundary functionals of the form E_t^M[1_{X<m}], so differentiation generates distributional terms and standard pathwise Monte Carlo becomes unstable near the exercise boundary. This paper examines that boundary layer. It formulates a generic moving-boundary calculus for digital blocks, records the first- and second-order Dirac structure through weighted δ- and δ′-terms, and then specializes the resulting formulas to the NDSE shell under fixed and parameter-dependent numeraire measures. The paper also records the corresponding Monte Carlo implementation layer through mollifier estimators, one-dimensional bias–variance guidance, and likelihood-ratio reweighting. Accordingly, the paper isolates the boundary-calculus and Monte Carlo consequences of those digital blocks for boundary-sensitive Greeks in DSE and NDSE.

title: Enhancing Sustainable Supply Chain Practices in Bangladesh's Manufacturing Sector: A Strategic and Operational Analysis

detail.title: Enhancing Sustainable Supply Chain Practices in Bangladesh's Manufacturing Sector: A Strategic and Operational Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or sensitive data requiring ethical approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Sustainable supply chain management (SSCM) has become a critical priority for manufacturing industries worldwide, particularly in developing economies such as Bangladesh. This study examines the challenges and opportunities of implementing sustainable practices across Bangladesh's manufacturing supply chains. The research identifies key issues, including inefficient logistics systems, limited supplier compliance with environmental standards, and low adoption of digital technologies. Using a qualitative approach grounded in industry observations and secondary data, the study proposes a three-pillar framework focused on digital transformation, green logistics, and integrating supplier sustainability. The findings suggest that adopting sustainable supply chain practices can significantly enhance operational efficiency, reduce environmental impact, and improve global competitiveness. This paper offers practical insights for industry practitioners and policymakers seeking to transition toward sustainable and resilient supply chain systems.

title: The Strengths and Limitations of Qualitative and Quantitative Research Methods: A Systematic Review
affiliations: Universitas Muhammadiyah Palopo

detail.title: The Strengths and Limitations of Qualitative and Quantitative Research Methods: A Systematic Review
detail.abstract: This study aims to analyze the strengths and limitations of qualitative and quantitative research methods through a systematic review approach. The purpose of this research is to provide a comprehensive understanding of how both methods are applied in social science research and how they contribute to research outcomes. The study uses secondary data obtained from scientific journals, academic books, and relevant publications published within the last ten years. The findings indicate that qualitative research methods are effective in exploring social phenomena in depth, providing rich, detailed, and contextual insights. However, these methods tend to have limitations in terms of objectivity and generalizability. On the other hand, quantitative research methods are capable of producing measurable, objective, and generalizable results through statistical analysis, but they often lack depth in explaining complex social contexts. The study concludes that both methods have complementary strengths and limitations, and researchers are encouraged to select or combine methods based on research objectives, data characteristics, and the nature of the problem being studied.

title: The Labor Market as an Equilibrium Newsvendor Problem
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: The Labor Market as an Equilibrium Newsvendor Problem
detail.abstract:
I study hiring under uncertainty when firms can either hold permanent labor as a buffer or hire from a spot market after demand is realized. I build a model where the spot market is endogenously determined such that when one firm relies more on spot labor, it thickens the market that other firms use as well. Individual firms do not internalize that contribution, so the competitive equilibrium involves too much buffering. I evaluate the model in the market for registered nurses using the universe of daily time sheet records from skilled nursing facilities. The data support the model’s general equilibrium predictions. Markets with thicker agency markets have less rationing conditional on total nursing hours, and thicker agency markets have compressed upper tails of permanent staffing and higher overall hours in the lower part of the distribution. Estimating a facility-level newsvendor model with heterogeneous spot market frictions and rationing costs I find that the nursing labor market was more efficient post-COVID, there are substantial welfare gains from lower spot market frictions, and that the marginal external benefit for a firm that participates in the spot market instead of hiring an employee as buffer averages 7 percent of wages. This labor market underprovides flexibility because the value of availability is not fully priced.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: The Sound of Drones is the Sound of Death: Human Rights Violations and Supply Chain Disruptions
affiliations: Kelley School of Business

detail.title: The Sound of Drones is the Sound of Death: Human Rights Violations and Supply Chain Disruptions
detail.abstract: Drones have become an increasingly integral part of twenty-first century warfare. This Article examines human rights violations and the supply chain disruptions resulting from drone warfare. Three case studies are analyzed: the Russia/Ukraine war, the Israel/Palestine war, and the Sudanese civil war. Modern warfare tactics can be seen in actions taken by the Houthis in West Yemen in response to the Israel/Palestine war, in which unmanned surface vessels, cruise missiles, unmanned underwater weapons, and drones are being used to stop, damage, and sink ships. Such conflicts result in supply chain disruptions. The Russia/ Ukraine war has resulted in significant disruptions to the supply chains for energy, wheat, and oil. In addition, it is a basic tenet of international humanitarian law that innocent civilians should not be targeted, yet fully autonomous robots may not be able to distinguish military targets from civilians. There is an urgent need for intervention. This Article provides five recommendations for how to address human rights violations and supply chain disruptions.

title: Gender Bias in the Resistance to Feedback
affiliations: Autonomous University of Barcelona, , University of Florida and University of Florida

detail.title: Gender Bias in the Resistance to Feedback
detail.abstract: Responses to performance feedback play a critical role in shaping future outcomes in educational and professional contexts. This paper examines whether evaluator gender influences the likelihood that individuals contest feedback. Using data from large introductory economics courses, we exploit the random assignment of evaluators with randomly assigned male- or female-sounding names to identify a systematic gender bias: individuals are significantly more likely to contest feedback when it is delivered by an evaluator with a female-sounding name than when similar feedback comes from a male-sounding evaluator. This gender disparity is most pronounced when evaluations fall below students’ performance expectations, are more ambiguous, yet are scored neutrally relative to a "fair" assessment. These findings suggest that women in evaluative positions face disproportionate resistance when delivering negative assessments and have implications for their authority, credibility, and career advancement in both educational and workplace settings.

title: Beyond Borders, Within Societies: Inequality and the Global Transmission of US Monetary Policy
affiliations: and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Beyond Borders, Within Societies: Inequality and the Global Transmission of US Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: This paper provides novel evidence on how income inequality shapes the heterogeneity of US monetary policy spillovers to GDP across foreign economies. Using state-dependent local projections and exploiting variation in disposable income inequality across 87 countries over 1966-2020, we show that household heterogeneity influences how foreign GDP responds to a US monetary tightening. GDP contracts up to one and a half times more when inequality is above average. However, while higher inequality amplifies negative spillovers in advanced economies, it mitigates them in emerging markets. To rationalise this finding, we use a three-country open economy Two-Agent New Keynesian (TANK) model, which suggests this divergence is driven by differences in participation in international financial markets. Households in emerging markets face greater barriers to international investment, limiting their ability to re-balance portfolios towards higher-return foreign bonds after the shock.

title: Democratic socialism and the law
affiliations: School of Law, King's College, London; Centre for Business Research, University of Cambridge

detail.title: Democratic socialism and the law
detail.abstract: Are democracy and socialism compatible? Does democratic socialism work? And what is its relation to the law? This paper shows that democratic socialism is the dominant political model in wealthy democracies, overwhelmingly popular among voters, and the chief driver of human progress. It explains how democratic socialism was built through the understanding of capitalism's failures, especially the shape-shifting legal forms of 'private' property in the means of production, 'freedom' of contract, and 'competitive' corporations. It identifies the three core features of 21 st century democratic socialism: more public and common ownership, economic democracy on a floor of social rights, and fair taxes. These policies have been spreading, are the prevailing practice in most wealthy countries, and are overwhelmingly popular among voters. It is a myth that the shape-shifting rules of capitalism lead to more innovation, productivity, less waste, or are good for democracy. The evidence is clear that the reverse is true. Democratic socialism is humanity's greatest hope.

title: A Systematic Review of Empirical Research on the Economic Impact of Peer-to-Peer Short-term Rental Accommodation on Tourist Destinations
affiliations: University of the Aegean and

detail.title: A Systematic Review of Empirical Research on the Economic Impact of Peer-to-Peer Short-term Rental Accommodation on Tourist Destinations
detail.abstract: This chapter provides a review of the quantitative empirical literature on the economic impact of short-term rental accommodation (STRs) on tourist destinations. The review identifies three main research themes relating to hotel industry performance, tourism industry employment, and housing prices and rents, and reveals a consensus on the effects of the latter two themes. In addition, a framework for research on the impact of STRs is provided, particularly regarding the investigation of its effect on hotel industry performance. The review also reveals gaps in the literature regarding the effect of increased compliance on government revenue and STRs market growth.

title: CONSUMO CONSPICUO Y SEMIOSIS SOCIAL: UNA INTERPRETACIÓN HERMENÉUTICA DEL VALOR RELACIONAL EN LOS BIENES VEBLEN CONSPICUOUS CONSUMPTION AND SOCIAL SEMIOSIS: A HERMENEUTIC INTERPRETATION OF RELATIONAL VALUE IN VEBLEN GOODS

detail.title: CONSUMO CONSPICUO Y SEMIOSIS SOCIAL: UNA INTERPRETACIÓN HERMENÉUTICA DEL VALOR RELACIONAL EN LOS BIENES VEBLEN CONSPICUOUS CONSUMPTION AND SOCIAL SEMIOSIS: A HERMENEUTIC INTERPRETATION OF RELATIONAL VALUE IN VEBLEN GOODS
detail.abstract: Investigador independiente Colombia RESUMEN El presente artículo analiza el consumo de bienes Veblen desde un enfoque de economía política estructural, integrando economía conductual, teoría de la identidad y semiótica del consumo. Se plantea como hipótesis que el valor de estos bienes no es intrínseco, sino relacional, emergente de procesos de significación social mediados por narrativas económicas y estructuras simbólicas. Metodológicamente, se adopta un enfoque cualitativo hermenéutico basado en el análisis del discurso publicitario de marcas globales, utilizando fuentes primarias como informes de valor de marca (Interbrand, Kantar) y gasto publicitario (Statista, WARC). El marco teórico articula los aportes de Akerlof sobre economía e identidad, Shiller sobre narrativas económicas y Baudrillard y Barthes sobre el consumo como sistema de signos. Los resultados evidencian que la publicidad configura dispositivos simbólicos que transforman bienes en signos de distinción, reproduciendo jerarquías económicas y culturales. Se concluye que el consumo conspicuo constituye un mecanismo estructural de reproducción social, con implicaciones críticas para la teoría del consumidor contemporánea.

detail.abstract: The space research scene in India is on the rise, and this study takes a closer look at what's Abstract: The purpose of this article is to investigate how employee engagement (EE) can improve organizational effectiveness (OE). In order to do this, a fictitious model that depicts the relationship between EE and OE in terms of both individual characteristics and total impact is presented. Due to the substantial changes in job responsibilities and workforce diversity brought about by the globalization of firms, managing employee engagement is essential for success in a dynamic and competitive environment. The aims and objectives of the organization are closely in line with this engagement. The purpose of this article is to provide an exploratory analysis of employee engagement, covering its changing definitions and ideas, the drivers or elements that affect it, its metrics, and its importance for improving business outcomes. A review of a few pieces of employee engagement literature is part of the technique. According to the study's findings, employee engagement is a continuous process that varies greatly depending on the firm. Employee engagement is generally understood to be the integration of different behavioral components, such as commitment, involvement, attachment, discretionary effort, energy, positive attitude, and psychological presence, that together turn employee potential into performance and positively impact organizational success, even though there isn't a universally accepted definition for the term.

title: Does the informal economy determine inward foreign direct investment?

detail.title: Does the informal economy determine inward foreign direct investment?
detail.abstract: The relatively small literature on the relationship between inward FDI and the size of the informal economy has not reached a consensus and country-level data indicates that the correlation of these variables differs across countries with different levels of development. This chapter uses panel cointegration to estimate the relationship between inward FDI and the size of the informal economy in the destination country and the findings provide evidence in favor of a long-run relationship.
