detail.abstract:
This study examines nurse retention in U.S. hospitals through the lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT), a motivational framework that explains how workplace conditions shape employee retention and outcomes in healthcare settings. Despite widespread retention initiatives, many hospitals lack formalized strategies to effectively retain nursing staff.

This quantitative study examines the relationship between key workplace factors and nurse retention through the lens of self-determination theory (SDT). Using secondary data from the 2016 Texas Hospital Nurse Staffing Survey, the study analyzes whether (1) length of residency/internship/fellowship programs, (2) duration of new employee training, and (3) the number of frozen direct-care RN positions predict nurse turnover rates.

Multiple linear regression analysis revealed statistically significant relationships among variables; however, the predictive strength of individual factors was limited. While training duration and staffing constraints demonstrated directional relationships with turnover, none emerged as strong standalone predictors of retention outcomes.

These findings suggest that employee retention is influenced by a broader system of motivational and organizational factors rather than isolated structural interventions. The study contributes to the growing body of research on intrinsic motivation in the workplace and offers practical insights for healthcare leaders seeking to improve retention strategies.

Improving nurse retention has implications for organizational performance, healthcare quality, and community well-being, highlighting the importance of aligning workforce strategies with human-centered motivational frameworks.

title: Five "Blockades" and One Legal Problem: Naval Enforcement in the U.S.-Iran Conflict

detail.title: Five "Blockades" and One Legal Problem: Naval Enforcement in the U.S.-Iran Conflict

keywords: UN Convention on the Law of the Sea

publicationDetails.journalName: Emory University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
There are not one, but five distinct blockade-style operations underway in the U.S.-Iran armed conflict. Each has different legal authorities, and each raises different legal issues and operational risks. The central problem is not simply that there are multiple blockade-like operations—it is that the United States is collapsing distinct legal authorities into a single “blockade” framework, obscuring the legal basis for each. These operations draw from distinct legal paradigms that are increasingly being blurred.

First, Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz on March 2—an illegal blockade that has been remarkably effective, bringing maritime traffic in the Strait to a standstill.

Second, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) responded on April 13 with a naval blockade applicable to all vessels transiting to or from Iran.

The United States began the third, fourth, and fifth blockades on April 16. CENTCOM dramatically expanded the initial blockade by asserting a belligerent right to visit and search (1) all Iranian vessels; (2) vessels suspected of carrying contraband; and (3) vessels with active Treasury Department Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctions—regardless of location. The Pentagon is characterizing all these enforcement actions as a wartime blockade – that’s problematic. This global enforcement expansion beyond the Strait raises a set of legal questions that should be clarified. Each visit, board, search, and seizure must rest on a sound legal foundation. These operations draw from three distinct legal frameworks: (1) the law of naval warfare; (2) peacetime maritime law enforcement authorities; and (3) hybrid regimes such as the Proliferation Security Initiative.

We may well be entering the most legally surreal moment of the conflict. The United States is simultaneously observing a ceasefire with Iran while enforcing a naval blockade—a belligerent wartime operation that has no legal basis in peacetime.

title: CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF DANGEROUS GOODS DOCUMENTATION AND ITS IMPACT ON AIR CARGO SAFETY: An Empirical Study of Documentation Practices and Error Patterns

detail.title: CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF DANGEROUS GOODS DOCUMENTATION AND ITS IMPACT ON AIR CARGO SAFETY: An Empirical Study of Documentation Practices and Error Patterns
detail.abstract: This study investigates the role of dangerous goods (DG) documentation in air cargo safety. Dangerous goods-including flammable liquids, gases, toxic substances, radioactive materials, and lithium batteries-must be documented in accordance with ICAO Technical Instructions (Doc 9284) and IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR). In spite of these well-established rules, documentation errors continue to be a recurring problem in day-today cargo operations. Data were gathered through a structured questionnaire administered to 50 respondents-cargo staff and MBA aviation students in Chennai-along with interviews with seven cargo documentation practitioners. The results indicate that only 24% of respondents have full knowledge of IATA DGR; 62% come across documentation errors on a regular basis; just 44% consistently follow the mandatory DG checklist; and 56% point to time pressure as a direct reason for mistakes. Based on these findings, the study calls for wider adoption of digital documentation tools, more frequent and structured training, and tighter internal audit routines.

title: Reimagining Identity Management with Blockchain: A Business and Technical Analysis of Decentralized Identity for Oracle and Formula 1
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Quinnipiac University and Quinnipiac University

detail.title: Reimagining Identity Management with Blockchain: A Business and Technical Analysis of Decentralized Identity for Oracle and Formula 1
detail.abstract: This paper examines how a blockchain based decentralized digital identity system can transform identity management for organizations like Oracle and Formula 1 by addressing the weaknesses of traditional centralized systems, where sensitive data is stored in one place and becomes vulnerable to breaches and inefficiencies. The proposed solution allows individuals to control their own digital identities through a distributed ledger, eliminating the need for organizations to store passwords or large amounts of personal data. It explains how smart contracts can automate identity verification, making access faster and more reliable, especially in fast paced environments like Formula 1 where thousands of credentials must be managed across multiple countries. The paper also explores how this system reduces administrative work and operational costs while improving security and trust between users and organizations. In addition, it outlines how the system could be integrated with existing cloud infrastructure, the roles of key stakeholders, and the overall business impact, including potential new revenue opportunities. Overall, it shows that decentralized identity is a practical solution that can turn identity management from a major risk and cost into a more efficient and valuable system.

title: Regulating Romance: Australia's Dating App Safety Governance And Its Implications For The U.S.
affiliations: Duquesne University School of Law

detail.title: Regulating Romance: Australia's Dating App Safety Governance And Its Implications For The U.S.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Thomas R. Kline School of Law of Duquesne University School of Law Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Thomas R. Kline School of Law of Duquesne University Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The use of dating apps for financial and physical harm, as shown in the mainstream media in documentaries such as The Tinder Swindler 1 and Dating App Horrors: The Untold Story, has raised concerns about platform accountability. Some scholars suggest that government regulation is a means to stop the harm, but due to legislative delays and the rapid evolution of technology, self-regulation is a more effective approach. Self-regulation involves industry participants establishing and enforcing standards to protect consumers and foster trust, with approaches ranging from voluntary policies enforced by the industry to coregulation (or joint industry-government oversight), which is often considered the most effective. While many scholars discuss the issue of a lack of legal remedies for harms stemming from dating apps, few explore the idea of self-regulated codes for such platforms. Even fewer countries have tried implementing a comprehensive regulatory framework that requires dating app companies to provide solutions for reported harms and to track their effectiveness by recording data on these incidents and responses. However, recently, Australia created its new Online Dating Code of Conduct, a pioneering industry-led standard that requires transparency, safety standards, and regular reporting from dating platforms. This online code was pioneered by the Industry leaders (Match Group, Bumble, Grindr, The Meet Group, eHarmony, RSVP, and Spark) with collaboration from “the Australian Government, safety advocates, and other stakeholders.” This article argues that by using the Australia Dating Code of Conduct as a benchmark, the United States could better prevent harms stemming from online dating.

title: The Meaning of AI and Its Implications for Antitrust Law
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: The Meaning of AI and Its Implications for Antitrust Law

declarations.funderStatement: The author has received financial support from Innovators Network Foundation. No funding source influenced the arguments expressed in this article or stands to benefit from them.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an integral part of our daily life and has already reshaped competition dynamics, prompting renewed debate within the antitrust community. Grounds for reconsideration include a disruption of antitrust fundamental principles, such as its consumer welfare goal, and possibly leaving room for alternative forms of regulation. Surprisingly, the scholarly conversation lacks a clear definition of AI. This Article fills this void by examining AI’s goals and scope during key historical moments. It defines intelligence in AI to assess whether contemporary AI might be capable of undermining antitrust pillars and a change of antitrust core values is required.

This Article makes two important contributions to contemporary literature: First, it lays out a comprehensive historical framework of the meaning of AI and its intelligence property. Second, it applies this framework to the current antitrust debate. AI will not disrupt antitrust pillars. However, AI will require adapting antitrust core values to a changed technological framework.

title: Reconceptualizing Law Firm Ownership
affiliations: Indiana University - Kelley School of Business and

detail.title: Reconceptualizing Law Firm Ownership
detail.abstract:
Who should own law firms? A defining feature of the American legal profession for over a century has been that only lawyers can own law firms. Within the past few years, however, that bedrock principle has come under pressure. Specifically, Arizona and a handful of other states have initiated reforms to American Bar Association Rule 5.4, which prohibits non-lawyers from owning shares in firms that are engaged in the practice of law. Some commentators argue it will improve access to justice, while others claim that non-lawyers will create perverse incentives in legal representation. Yet this back-and-forth has seemingly reached a dead end.

 This article reframes this debate in a way that carries novel implications for law firm ownership and management structure. We do this by making both theoretical and empirical claims regarding the recent paradigm shift in law firm ownership. First, we argue that the normative merits of non-lawyer ownership cannot be understood outside of a theoretical corporate governance framework. Specifically, we argue that a classic legal principle—the separation of ownership and control—is a critical overlooked variable.

 Second, we show as an empirical matter, that transformation of the traditional law firm ownership paradigm is already broader and more complex than is generally understood. To support this claim we present a qualitative field study drawing on structured interviews with law firms in Arizona and leading industry participants around the world. Taken together, the contributions of this article establish a research agenda and conceptual toolkit that goes beyond familiar tradeoffs that have been overly rehearsed in previous scholarship. Ultimately, this will allow regulators and scholars to better analyze the policy implications of recent fundamental shifts in law firm ownership.

title: A Falsifiability-First Investigation Across Classical Physics, Quantum Mechanics, Biology, Computation, Cognition, and the Full Mechanics of Perception
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Falsifiability-First Investigation Across Classical Physics, Quantum Mechanics, Biology, Computation, Cognition, and the Full Mechanics of Perception

keywords: A Falsifiability-First Investigation Across Classical Physics
and the Full Mechanics of Perception

detail.abstract:
If everything follows the lightest path according to its own Perception, then the only question remaining is: how does Perception work?

This paper investigates one of the most consistently rediscovered principles in the history of science: that every system — from a photon to a protein, from an electron to an economy — moves in the direction of least geometric resistance relative to its own perceptual capacity. The Architecture of Freedom Intelligence calls this the lightest-path law. It is not asserted axiomatically. It is tested.
The paper proceeds in seven movements. First, we state the governing asymmetry: Distortion is observer-independent while Perception is irreducibly observer-dependent, and this asymmetry is the structural reason Freedom cannot be collapsed into any prior physics equation. Second, we construct the complete master equation and its four empirically validated levels of Perception. Third, we trace the historical record — 2,400 years of independent convergence from Hero of Alexandria through Feynman — to show that the principle is not a modern conjecture but the most repeatedly rediscovered pattern in natural philosophy. Fourth, we enumerate 35 concrete falsifiability tests and report their outcomes. Fifth, we examine every major class of apparent violation and explain precisely why each is a Perception failure rather than a gradient violation. Sixth, we draw out implications for physics, biology, cognition, and engineering. Seventh, and most distinctively, we provide a full Glossary: every technical term in the Architecture of Freedom Intelligence defined with the precision and specificity its use requires.
The conclusion is methodological: the lightest-path principle is not a philosophical claim about the universe. It is a structural claim about movement. A system that consistently moved against its own perceptual gradient would exhaust itself and cease. The principle is falsifiable, has been tested, and has not been falsified. The open questions are precisely located and honestly stated.

title: Organizational Diagnosis As Phase Space: Attractor Classes, Observer Bias, And Intervention Logic In Autopoietic Systems
affiliations: and

detail.title: Organizational Diagnosis As Phase Space: Attractor Classes, Observer Bias, And Intervention Logic In Autopoietic Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a conceptual framework employing formal notation as structural scaffolding rather than claiming numerical computation — an epistemological design decision consistent with the model’s constructivist foundations. We present a dynamic systems-theoretic model for diagnosing organizational states — the Systemic Organizational Diagnosis as Phase Space (SODP). The model formalizes organizational dynamics as movement in a four-dimensional phase space: three coordinates deductively derived from Luhmann’s (1984) canonical dimensions of meaning (Sinndimensionen), one operationalizing his constitutive system-environment distinction (the epistemic status is addressed in Section 4): Meaning↔Function (SF1), Order↔Vitality (SF2), Internal↔External (SF3), and Continuity↔Transformation (SF4). We identify six organizational dynamic states — Homeostasis, Edge of Chaos, Torus, Rigidity, Strange Attractor, and System Failure — each requiring qualitatively different intervention logic. The model introduces the Paralysis Overlay L(t), a transversal overlay state activated by power polarization that overrides all attractor dynamics. A hybrid architecture explicitly separates formal structural description (Level 1) from AI-supported operative execution (Level 2), epistemically avoiding pseudo-precision. Core contributions include: the first operationalization of six organizational dynamic states as a complete diagnostic instrument; the formalization of observer bias as a structural model element (β-vector, eight components); the non-monotone attractor stability function with dkrit as separatrix, formalizing two qualitatively different pathways to attractor change; and the ∆-level operator distinguishing symptom level from solution level. We address a central gap in systems-theoretic organizational research: despite decades of theoretical development, no operational instrument has located organizational states in a formally defined state space with unambiguous intervention logic per organizational dynamic state. Three open research questions with proposed empirical designs frame the validation agenda.

title: The Instability of Less Discriminatory Credit Models

detail.title: The Instability of Less Discriminatory Credit Models
detail.abstract: Algorithmic debiasing ("AD") of credit scoring models is increasingly promoted as a means to improve a lender's fair lending performance, yet little is publicly known about the robustness and stability of the resulting Less Discriminatory Alternative ("LDA") Models. Using a simple synthetic credit scoring model estimated on publicly-available Home Mortgage Disclosure Act ("HMDA") data, I evaluate the structural and performance stability of LDA Models derived using various degrees of fairness regularization across 100 random training samples. I find that the resulting LDA Models are inherently brittle, exhibiting substantial instability in their estimated credit risk relationships, AIR-based fairness performance, and Area-Under-the-Curve ("AUC")-based accuracy performance in response to relatively small random training data variations. This instability grows as larger fairness weights are used, distorts the conceptual soundness of the LDA Models' estimated risk profiles, and injects material statistical bias into the models' estimated risk coefficients and aggregate performance metrics. The specific "disparate impact factors" selected by the AD process to drive fairness improvement also vary widely both across training samples (for a given Fairness Weight) and within a training sample (across Fairness Weights), calling into question whether the AD process is truly remediating illegal disparate impact under the governing legal framework, or simply implementing a latent reverse disparate impact to achieve approval-rate equity. Beyond these safety-and-soundness and compliance concerns, I document significant intra-group unfairness, ECOA Adverse Action Notice complications, and other risks that lenders should evaluate carefully before deploying algorithmically-debiased credit models.

title: Agentic Leadership and the Limits of Scale: How Managing a Multi-Agent AI Ensemble Reveals New Theory
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Agentic Leadership and the Limits of Scale: How Managing a Multi-Agent AI Ensemble Reveals New Theory
detail.abstract: Managing a heterogeneous multi-agent AI ensemble-where different agents bring distinct stylistic dispositions, calibration habits, and compliance tendencies-requires a form of human leadership competency that has no established name, no systematic theory, and no dedicated treatment in the governance, AI literacy, or prompt engineering literatures. This paper identifies and theorises that gap, names it agentic leadership, and offers a first theoretical sketch of what the competency entails. It does so through an empirical account of an operational deployment: approximately six weeks of live Maestro protocol production (late February to mid-April 2026), in which a structured AI-assisted crisis sensemaking protocol was deployed against a fast-moving international security crisis and encountered three documented failure modes.

title: Captured Conscience: Organisational Silence and the Safety Deficit at Frontier AI Labs

detail.title: Captured Conscience: Organisational Silence and the Safety Deficit at Frontier AI Labs
detail.abstract: Frontier AI labs are uniquely positioned to cause civilisation-scale harm and uniquely ill-equipped to hear internal warnings about it. This paper argues that the safety deficit emerging across OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta AI is a predictable structural outcome, not an accidental cultural one. As these organisations grow and their commercial value rises, the cost of internal dissent rises with it. I define this dynamic as the Silence Gradient: the ratio of voice-suppressing mechanisms, including equity-contingent non-disparagement clauses, broad NDA scope, and governance structures embedded inside commercial reporting lines, to voice-enabling ones, including whistleblower protections, anonymous reporting channels, and independent safety boards. Drawing on organisational theory, the historical record of high-risk industries, and a dataset of 48 publicly documented departures from frontier AI labs between 2019 and 2025, I make three claims. First, that the suppression of internal safety dissent is measurable and has been rising. Second, that it is produced by specific financial, legal, and governance structures rather than individual moral failure. Third, that without institutional intervention, the compounding effect of a rising silence gradient will increase the probability of catastrophic outcomes. To operationalise the first claim, I develop the Silence Gradient Index, a six-component scoring instrument applied using publicly available evidence. Across the four labs in this study, SGI scores range from 40 to 72.5 out of 100. No lab scores zero on any component. I close by proposing three concrete reforms: independent safety boards with statutory employee reporting rights, a mandatory incident reporting framework modelled on the Aviation Safety Reporting System, and restrictions on the use of unvested equity as leverage for non-disparagement agreements.

title: Positive Career Shocks and Employees' Career Change Intention: The Mediating Role of Career Exploration
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Positive Career Shocks and Employees' Career Change Intention: The Mediating Role of Career Exploration
detail.abstract: This study examines whether and how positive career shocks are associated with employees' career change intention. Drawing on the unfolding model of voluntary employee turnover and career self-management research, we argue that positive career shocks may prompt career exploration, which is associated with stronger career change intention. We further examine career stage as a boundary condition of the relationship between positive career shocks and career exploration. Using survey data from 371 employees in China, the results show that positive career shocks are positively associated with career change intention. A bootstrap mediation analysis further indicates that career exploration serves as a significant mediating mechanism in this relationship. The moderated mediation analysis shows that the indirect effect is stronger among employees at higher career stages. This study contributes to the career shocks literature by showing that positive career shocks may have double-edged implications and by identifying career exploration as a key mechanism linking positive shocks to career change intention.

detail.abstract: Purpose: The LGBTQ+ community is side-lined and under-researched. The present study aims to analyze prominent global research trends and activities related to the LGBTQ+ community. This bibliometric research will help academic researchers know the nuts and bolts of LGBTQ+ community research and recognise the significant areas that need further exploration. Research Approach: The current academic research comprises a bibliometric review of 1737 documents (including articles, books, book chapters, conference papers, editorial, letter, note, review, short survey) (Refer Table no. I) available in the Scopus database during 1983-2024. Using the Biblioshiny tool for Bibliometric analysis, it finds out the dominating countries of LGBTQ+ research, prominent authors, influential globally cited documents, dominating research publications, top supporting LGBTQ+ research institutions, and emerging research themes. Major Findings: The major findings highlight a significant growth in publications post 2006, dominance of a leading author (Baral, SD: 25 documents), country (USA: 10084 publications), most supporting institution (University of Toronto, Canada: 300 documents) in the LGBTQ+ research. Value: This research further highlights the requirement for an increase in participation in LGBTQ+ research globally, particularly from unrepresented regions (Global South) and bisexual & non-binary identities. A more inclusive and collaborative approach between different countries, authors, and research institutions has been recommended and expected in the future, addressing a wide scope of social inclusivity of the LGBTQ+ community.

title: When Does Corporate Philanthropy Pay? An Information Perspective
affiliations: European Corporate Governance Institute (ECGI), Indiana University - Kelley School of Business and

detail.title: When Does Corporate Philanthropy Pay? An Information Perspective
detail.abstract: We examine corporate philanthropy as a signal of firm product quality under limited attention. Linking local charitable donations to sales, we find no average effect but a strong fourth-quarter (Q4) lift, especially for firms with Q4-seasonal product mixes. The Q4 effect is also larger when the signal is likely more valuable: in weaker local economies where product quality matters more for consumers' purchase decisions; in more competitive markets where differentiation relies more on non-price signals; for firms with more geographically concentrated sales where attribution is clearer; and after negative product incidents when uncertainty about quality is higher. Overall, the results highlight an informational role of charitable donations, but only when consumers attend to and value such information.

title: ENERGY EFFICIENCY IN WATER INFRASTRUCTURE
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: ENERGY EFFICIENCY IN WATER INFRASTRUCTURE
detail.abstract:
Energy consumption across pumping, treatment and wastewater process infrastructure remains one of the largest controllable operating cost drivers within regulated utilities. While long-term capital investment is important, the most immediate and scalable savings opportunities lie in how existing assets are operated day to day.

The most significant energy levers are concentrated within a relatively small set of operational domains. Across most utilities, the highest-value reduction opportunities typically sit within:

• abstraction and transfer pumping
• booster pressure optimisation
• storage-led network balancing
• wastewater aeration systems
• sludge recirculation and digestion transfer
• wet-well and lifting station controls
• UV, ozone and membrane treatment processes
• filtration backwash frequency and trigger logic

Among these, pumping and aeration consistently emerge as the dominant first-wave value pools, often accounting for the majority of controllable site electricity demand.

This paper presents a field-ready delivery methodology for translating these opportunities into safe, repeatable and scalable operational performance gains.

title: Organizational Culture and Enduring Impact
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Organizational Culture and Enduring Impact

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract: This article examines the central role of culture in enabling organizations to achieve and sustain enduring impact over time. Culture functions as an "invisible infrastructure" that shapes decision-making, behavior and relationships, and must be intentionally designed and continuously reinforced to remain aligned with mission and responsive to evolving external conditions. The article identifies and analyzes a set of interdependent cultural elements including purpose, stakeholder orientation, learning, integrity, collaboration, inclusion, accountability and resilience, that collectively form an integrated system supporting long-term impact. It further explores how culture performs under conditions of stress to serve as a "shock absorber" that stabilizes organizations during disruption and allows them to adapt to the changing conditions and emerge stronger. Organizations seeking enduring impact must invest proactively in both structural capabilities and cultural foundations, recognizing that resilience and effectiveness are ultimately products of sustained cultural alignment and intentional design.

title: Innovation as a fundamental right: towards a new generation in human rights  / La innovación como derecho fundamental: hacia una nueva generación de derechos humanos
affiliations: and Universidad de Guayaquil

detail.title: Innovation as a fundamental right: towards a new generation in human rights  / La innovación como derecho fundamental: hacia una nueva generación de derechos humanos

contentFormat.other: Working paper, preliminary theoretical framework for the Culture of Integration and Innovation as a Fundamental Right

detail.abstract:
This article develops the thesis of innovation as a fundamental right in contemporary societies. Innovation as a fundamental right is defined as the right of every person to access, create, adapt, and transform knowledge, as well as to participate in the ecosystems that enable it under conditions of equity, freedom, and sustainability.


Building on this definition, the article argues that innovation is not merely an economic driver, but a structural condition for the effective exercise of rights such as education, freedom of expression, and development.


Through a comparative law analysis and international standards review, the paper proposes its explicit incorporation into constitutional frameworks as part of a new generation of human rights. It introduces the concept of *“guaranteed innovation”*, understood as the set of positive state obligations aimed at ensuring equitable access to resources, technology, and creative ecosystems.


The article concludes that recognizing innovation as a fundamental right reshapes the social contract in the knowledge era.

title: AN EVALUATION OF THE CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY PROGRAMMES OF THE OGUN-GUANGDONG FREE TRADE ZONE IN IGBESA COMMUNITY, OGUN STATE, NIGERIA.
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: AN EVALUATION OF THE CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY PROGRAMMES OF THE OGUN-GUANGDONG FREE TRADE ZONE IN IGBESA COMMUNITY, OGUN STATE, NIGERIA.
detail.abstract:
In examining the corporate social responsibility programmes of the Ogun Guangdong Free Trade Zone in Igbesa Community, Ogun State Nigeria, triangulation method of research which uses a combination of twin research instruments – in-depth interviews for representatives of the FTZ and questionnaire for the residents of Igbesa – were used in this study. For the in-depth interviews, the Corporate Communication and Chief Information Officers of FTZ were interviewed. Copies of questionnaire were distributed to three hundred and seventy six (376) respondents, drawn across Ogona, Igbe, Idomo & Osi Communities which make up the Igbesa Township. 355 copies of the questionnaires were duly filled and returned for analysis. Based on the returned copies of questionnaire and the interviews conducted with communication executives at Ogun Guangdong FTZ, result of the study shows that one major CSR project completed by the Ogun Guangdong Free Trade Zone is the Model Primary School known as Nigeria-China Friendship Primary Model School. The study also shows that the impact of CSR programmes executed by Ogun Guangdong Free Trade Zone is perceived to be low because some people believe that the projects barely have impact on the general populace. It was concluded that it is important to point that amidst other evolving facts, there is no gain saying that CSR has been a very good Public Relations strategy used by organizations to keep host community loyal. However, it was recommended that as a matter of urgency, stakeholders forum should be called so that the basic needs of the community would be the focus of the Ogun FTZ’s CSR programme; furthermore, Ogun Guangdong FTZ should do a total overhaul of its approach to the use of corporate social responsibilities in building synergy with the host community and a proper channel of communication should be established, before undertaking any further projects.

 

Keywords: CSR, Public Relations, Ogun Guangdong FTZ, Community Relations.

detail.abstract: Export documentation is essential for international trade, ensuring legal compliance, secure payments, and smooth goods movement. This study examines key documents and processes involved. Accuracy is critical. The role of artificial intelligence is also analyzed. AI enhances automation, reduces errors, and improves efficiency, making export documentation faster, reliable, and globally competitive.

title: DATA SOVEREIGNTY AND UPSTREAM PETROLEUM DATA: WHO OWNS THE SEISMIC RECORD?
affiliations: NBA Section on Legal Practice Technology Law Committee

detail.title: DATA SOVEREIGNTY AND UPSTREAM PETROLEUM DATA: WHO OWNS THE SEISMIC RECORD?

keywords: Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Data Management Regulations 2024

detail.abstract: Seismic data is the lifeblood of upstream petroleum exploration. Acquired at enormous cost by international oil companies (IOCs), it encodes detailed knowledge of a nation's subsurface geology which is its "underground map." Yet the legal character of that data is deeply contested. Is a seismic record a creative work protected by copyright? A trade secret protected by the Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS)? Or does it belong to the state by virtue of the doctrine of permanent sovereignty over natural resources (PSNR)? This paper interrogates the tripartite tension between intellectual property law, national data sovereignty, and the commercial imperatives of the petroleum industry. Drawing on primary legislation from Nigeria, Norway, the United Kingdom and Brazil, and examining emerging frameworks of data governance in the cloud era, the paper argues that the current global regime is characterised by productive ambiguity-a constructive uncertainty that serves neither IOCs nor host states well. The paper concludes with concrete recommendations for a balanced legal architecture, with Nigeria's Petroleum Industry Act 2021 and National Data Repository Regulations 2024 serving as both an anchor case study and a template for reform.

title: Reserves as Insurance: International Buffers and Inward FDI in Emerging Markets
affiliations: Universidad Torcuato Di Tella - School of Business,  and

detail.title: Reserves as Insurance: International Buffers and Inward FDI in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: Emerging markets have accumulated large reserve buffers, but whether these buffers causally affect inward foreign direct investment (FDI) remains an open question. Using an unbalanced panel of emerging market economies over 2001-2020, we estimate twoway fixed-effects models of net inward FDI inflows with a rich set of lagged controls. We address the endogeneity of reserve accumulation by instrumenting lagged reserves with the two-year-lagged log of each country's commodity import price index-a source of balance-of-payments pressure orthogonal to export-driven profitability shocks, conditional on a country-specific commodity export price index. The IV estimates imply that a 10% increase in reserves raises FDI inflows by about 18.5% (an elasticity of 1.85), more than four times the fixed-effects OLS estimate of 0.4. The effect is amplified during global stress episodes: the IV elasticity is 1.85 in the full sample but falls to 1.34 when crisis years (2008-2009, 2020) are excluded, consistent with reserves functioning as insurance that matters most when downside risks are salient.

title: Impact Is Not Enough
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Impact Is Not Enough

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract: The concept of impact has fundamentally reshaped the definition of success for many organizations, expanding their ambitions beyond financial performance to include measurable contributions to social and environmental well-being. However, this shift has not been accompanied by sufficient attention to a critical structural limitation: while many organizations are designed to achieve impact, they are not set up to sustain it. This article argues that institutional fragility, often obscured by the illusion of stability, undermines the long-term effectiveness of even highly successful organizations. The result is recurring patterns of decline, including overdependence on key individuals, uneven organizational development, financial vulnerability, mission drift and reactive responses to crisis. The lesson is that impact without endurance is inherently limited and organizations must be intentionally designed for durability, adaptability and long-term resilience. Reframing success to include endurance alongside impact requires a fundamental shift in organizational design, leadership and strategy, recognizing that in a volatile world the true measure of impact lies not only in what is achieved, but in what can be sustained over time.

title: Intermediate Input Prices and the Labor Share
affiliations: and Stanford University

detail.title: Intermediate Input Prices and the Labor Share
detail.abstract: We argue that the relative price of materials is an important determinant of the labor share of income. When materials and primary inputs are complements and the profit share is positive, a higher price of materials lowers the labor share and raises the profit share of value added, without requiring markups or returns to scale to change. We show that materials-price fluctuations align with U.S. labor-share trends, provide causal evidence on this mechanism across industries and commuting zones, and quantify its importance in a dynamic quantitative model. Finally, we use our mechanism to rationalize differential labor-share trends across countries.

title: Policy Paper: Engineering Sovereign Balance in the Gaza Strip Between the Mechanics of Functional Replacement and the Philosophy of Geopolitical Stability
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Policy Paper: Engineering Sovereign Balance in the Gaza Strip Between the Mechanics of Functional Replacement and the Philosophy of Geopolitical Stability
detail.abstract: This policy paper analyzes the two-decade-long "Sovereign Imbalance" in the Gaza Strip through a structural lens, based on the statistical outcomes of Fatah's 8th General Conference. The paper posits that the new leadership weight distribution (70% for the West Bank vs. 30% for Gaza) represents a "Structural Repositioning" rather than marginalization, aiming to break the cycle of "Sovereign Obstruction" and isolated "Field Control". Utilizing the Functional and Engineering Dissection Analysis (FEDA) methodology and the Sovereign Stability Theory (SST), the research proposes a "Sovereign Balance" model operating under UN Resolution 2803 and the Egyptian geopolitical buffer. The model aims to fill the functional vacuum and transcend factional deadlock through a field-testable "Functional Sovereignty" framework.

title: Does s.69 Arbitration Act 1996 include mixed questions of law and fact? The strong case for codification
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill

detail.title: Does s.69 Arbitration Act 1996 include mixed questions of law and fact? The strong case for codification
detail.abstract:
Section 69 of the Arbitration Act 1996 provides the means of appeal against arbitration awards, but it must be based on a ‘question of law’. However, does this include mixed questions of law and fact? Looking at s.69 alone, it is not possible to ascertain this. Furthermore, the interpretive provision s.82 unhelpfully defines ‘question of law’ as a ‘question of law’ in England and Wales and Northern Ireland. While statutory provisions fail to provide a clear guideline, the following case law supports that s.69 does cover mixed questions of law and fact.

It is quite common to encounter mixed questions, indicating their practical
significance. Different jurisdictions have adopted varying approaches to whether mixed questions are included. In the Canadian provinces of Ontario and British Columbia, it is not possible to appeal against a mixed question of law and fact. Similarly, in Australia, only pure questions of law can be appealed, but not mixed questions.

For example, in New Zealand, the judiciary has complained that there were conflicting decisions: some have held that leave to appeal will only be granted for a pure question of law; whilst others allowed leave for mixed questions.Though not as problematic as New Zealand, one could argue that there are already some early signs of the same inconsistency in England and Wales. This could make the English position less instinctive for international practitioners, with there already being early signs of potential inconsistency in English law.

The operational equations, however, must change. Perception was previously underspecied conated with topology, post-hoc improving fractions, or structural alignment which made the framework partially unfalsiable. This paper reformulates AFI so that Perception is clustering of the possibility: a system-relative, prechoice map from logic-admissible options to actionable path-clusters. The FLRP loop becomes an explicit operating-system pipeline: Ω → Ω L → Π S → C S → F S → ChosenCluster → PhysicsUpdate. We map the loop onto PlantaOS, a physical-AI building operating system, and onto phase-change architecture (water/ice, transformable materials), where α acquires real meaning as a phase-solidication and irreversibility regime. title: When Algorithms Scale: Spatial Spillovers in Automated Underwriting
affiliations: Michigan State University and Michigan State University - The Eli Broad College of Business and The Eli Broad Graduate School of Management

detail.title: When Algorithms Scale: Spatial Spillovers in Automated Underwriting
detail.abstract: Automated underwriting systems (AUS) are widely deployed in modern credit markets, standardizing how lenders evaluate borrower risk and process loan applications at scale. While prior research primarily examines automated underwriting at the level of individual loan decisions, it offers limited insight into how these systems reshape credit allocation at the market level. This paper studies how the expansion of automated underwriting relates to mortgage approval outcomes across local credit markets. Using a tract-level panel of U.S. mortgage applications and an instrumental-variables design based on lagged changes in county-level conforming loan limits, we estimate how policy-induced changes in exposure to automated underwriting relate to local approval outcomes. The IV estimates indicate that policy-induced increases in AUS exposure are associated with lower mortgage approval rates. We further document that neighboring AUS exposure predicts lower local approval rates, consistent with spatial spillovers in standardized underwriting environments. Together, these findings suggest that automated underwriting operates not only as a loan-level screening tool, but also as a market-level digital infrastructure whose adoption and diffusion are associated with changes in the distribution of credit access across interconnected markets.

title: Scarce Attention and Platform Design: Evidence from an Anti-Ghosting Intervention
affiliations: Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management, Nova School of Business and Economics and Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University

detail.title: Scarce Attention and Platform Design: Evidence from an Anti-Ghosting Intervention
detail.abstract: Digital peer-to-peer platforms often operate in environments where users manage multiple simultaneous interactions and must allocate limited attention across them. In such settings, one common breakdown is ghosting, where one user stops responding to an ongoing conversation. To address this issue, some platforms have introduced "anti-ghosting" features designed to prompt re-engagement with delayed interactions. In collaboration with a large dating platform, we examine how exposure to such a feature affects user behavior across the broader interaction portfolio. We find that exposure increases reply activity not only in overdue conversations, the feature's direct target, but also in other ongoing conversations. This pattern suggests that the intervention operates beyond task-specific compliance, generating spillovers consistent with a reallocation of attention. Consistent with this mechanism, exposed users shift activity away from browsing for new matches and toward engaging with existing ones. This shift from breadth to depth improves downstream outcomes: users become more likely to form offline matches and, conditional on doing so, form more of them. At the platform level, exposure is associated with higher subscription probability, increased subscription starts, and lower churn. Taken together, these findings show that targeted platform interventions can reshape user behavior beyond their immediate target by reallocating scarce attention across concurrent interactions.

title: Attention as Currency: Measuring the Economic Value of Human Focus
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Attention as Currency: Measuring the Economic Value of Human Focus
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of the digital economy has transformed human attention into a valuable economic resource. This paper examines the concept of attention as a form of currency, arguing that it is scarce, measurable, and actively traded in modern markets. By analyzing digital platforms, behavioral economic principles, and market structures, the study highlights how attention is captured and monetized by major technology firms. The paper further explores the implications of the attention economy on productivity, income inequality, and social well-being. It concludes that managing attention is increasingly important in a world where economic value is closely tied to human focus.

title: The Danish Robotics Ecosystem: Strategic Trajectories, Cluster Dynamics, and Global Competitiveness
affiliations: Novo Nordisk

detail.title: The Danish Robotics Ecosystem: Strategic Trajectories, Cluster Dynamics, and Global Competitiveness
detail.abstract: The Danish robotics, automation, and drone industry has established itself as a premier global cluster, demonstrating robust growth ($4.6$ billion EUR revenue in 2023) despite global macroeconomic headwinds and an asymmetrical reliance on key export markets  like Germany, and theUSA. This paper analyzes the unique structural resilience of the Danish ecosystem, tracing its origin not to traditional heavy industry, but to the pioneering of collaborative robotics (cobots) and autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) in the post-2000 era. The industry's success is predicated on the "Odense Model," a highly integrated national cluster strategy led by Odense Robotics. This strategy fosters intense public-private-academic collaboration across five specialized regional hubs: Funen (hardware/cobots), Greater Copenhagen (deeptech/healthcare AI), Central Jutland (outdoor mobile robots/agritech), Northern Jutland (UAS/drones), and Southern Jutland (mechatronics/industrial control). While facing critical constraints, particularly a severe human capital deficit in advanced software engineering, the cluster is strategically pivoting into counter-cyclical sectors (healthcare, agriculture) and aligning with green transition mandates. Supported by a hybrid financial architecture—combining stable state subsidies (EIFO, Innovation Fund Denmark) with highly targeted private venture capital—the ecosystem continues to generate lucrative global acquisition targets. The paper concludes that maintaining global competitiveness through the 2025-2030 horizon hinges upon solving the acute talent shortage and aggressively executing the strategic transition from mechanical kinematics to AI-driven, interoperable systems.

title: FraudRAG: Knowledge Graph-Augmented Retrieval for Real-Time Financial Statement Fraud Detection Using a Domain-Driven Medallion Architecture
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: FraudRAG: Knowledge Graph-Augmented Retrieval for Real-Time Financial Statement Fraud Detection Using a Domain-Driven Medallion Architecture
detail.abstract: Financial statement fraud-encompassing document forgery, balance manipulation, amount substitution, and entity fabrication-imposes losses exceeding $5.38 trillion annually on global financial institutions. Existing detection systems analyze documents in isolation, failing to leverage the rich relational context inherent in customer-institution networks and prior fraud histories. This paper presents FraudRAG, a novel knowledge-engineering architecture that addresses this limitation through three original contributions: (1) the first Graph-RAG pipeline for financial document forensics, combining Neo4j knowledge graph multi-hop traversal with ChromaDB dense vector retrieval to provide Claude 3.5 Sonnet with dynamically retrieved customer-specific context at inference time; (2) a Domain-Driven Medallion architecture with formally specified Bronze, Silver, and Gold data quality contracts, including a deterministic accounting arithmetic validator at the Silver layer that constitutes a high-precision, submillisecond fraud pre-filter; and (3) a risk propagation mechanism enabling passive fraud ring detection through graph neighborhood scoring without explicit ring labels. Experiments on a reproducible synthetic benchmark of 2,400 annotated financial statements spanning six document types demonstrate AUC=0.943, Precision=0.891, Recall=0.876, and F1=0.883, outperforming rule-based, LLM-only, RAG-only, and graph-only baselines by 18-24 percentage points. Ablation studies confirm the independent contribution of each pipeline component. The system achieves sub-3-second end-to-end latency and scales to petabyte workloads via Apache Spark and AWS EMR. An open-source implementation is publicly available.

title: A CBT-based Psychodiagnostics Workflow for Enhancing the Professionalism of Large Language Models in Mental Counseling
affiliations: , , Shantou University and

detail.title: A CBT-based Psychodiagnostics Workflow for Enhancing the Professionalism of Large Language Models in Mental Counseling
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate significant potential for digital mental counseling. However, existing studies focus primarily on response quality, domain adaptation, and theoretical consistency, neglecting the clinical workflow essential for professional counseling. To address this gap, this study proposes a cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)-based psychodiagnostics workflow for LLMs and develops a counseling system named ListenEase based on this workflow. The workflow organizes counseling into four modules and combines stage-specific prompting with a multi-agent interaction mechanism. Comparative and ablation experiments are conducted on 24 case tasks across four counseling scenarios. The results show that ListenEase outperforms both general and psychology-oriented LLMs on helpfulness, guidance, professionalism, and output stability. The CBT-based workflow improves structured counseling progression and intervention quality, and the multi-agent mechanism enhances emotional tracking and response stability. This study shifts attention from response quality to workflow-level counseling professionalism and provides a lightweight and scalable path for improving psychology-oriented LLMs.

title: Recursive Epistemic Fragility: Intergenerational Transmission of Error in AI-Mediated Knowledge Systems

detail.title: Recursive Epistemic Fragility: Intergenerational Transmission of Error in AI-Mediated Knowledge Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests. All proceeds from the author's published works are committed to DEBRA UK in perpetuity.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This manuscript is a theoretical synthesis and does not report research involving human participants or animals.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for the research reported in this manuscript.

detail.abstract: Generative AI is typically framed as a problem of unreliable outputs: hallucinations, fabricated citations, confident errors. That framing is too narrow. The more consequential risk is that generative AI disrupts two reproduction pipelines simultaneously. Model training pipelines reproduce the technical system. Professional verification pipelines reproduce the human judgement needed to audit it. Both draw on the same raw material: independently produced, independently verified human work. When the technology that depends on that material also displaces it and displaces the conditions under which practitioners form the judgement to verify it, the two pipelines degrade in parallel. The delay between exposure and detectable damage allows degradation to accumulate before the cohorts who could identify it have been shaped by the conditions that would have taught them to do so. This paper develops the argument as a theoretical synthesis across three converging literatures: formal results on recursive training and model collapse, information quality and provenance research, and learning sciences and human-factors work on professional judgement formation. Three mutually reinforcing loops, not three separate concerns, constitute Recursive Epistemic Fragility. The developmental category that matters here is never-skilling: practitioners who never acquire foundational competence because AI performed the cognitive work that would have built it. The full coupled loop is a synthetic inference from converging mechanisms rather than a phenomenon observed at system scale. That evidential gap is itself a finding: the measurement infrastructure needed to detect system-level epistemic fragility has not been built.

title: Governing the Agentic Enterprise: Guardrails for Autonomous AI Agents in B2B Financial Transactions
affiliations: University of Illinois at Chicago

detail.title: Governing the Agentic Enterprise: Guardrails for Autonomous AI Agents in B2B Financial Transactions
detail.abstract: The emergence of autonomous ("agentic") artificial intelligence systems capable of independently executing financial decisions represents a fundamental shift in enterprise operations. In B2B financial environments, such agents are increasingly deployed for payments, liquidity management, and transaction optimization. However, their ability to operate without continuous human oversight introduces significant risks, including financial loss, regulatory non-compliance, and systemic instability. Existing AI governance frameworks and financial control systems are not designed for real-time, adaptive, decision-executing agents. This paper proposes FASTRAC (Financial Agent Safety, Trust, Risk, and Compliance), a control-theoretic governance framework that models autonomous financial agents as bounded, risk-scored actors operating within dynamically enforced constraints. FASTRAC introduces a formal governance function G(A) = {C, V, R, M, L} integrating constraints, validation, risk scoring, monitoring, and learning into a closedloop system. By defining execution as a constrained optimization problem under risk thresholds, the framework ensures that agent actions remain compliant, auditable, and controllable. Through formal modeling and a B2B payment execution scenario, this study demonstrates how adaptive governance mechanisms-such as dynamic risk thresholds and trust-calibrated autonomy-can mitigate risks while preserving operational efficiency. The findings suggest that effective deployment of agentic systems in finance requires a hybrid governance paradigm combining AI intelligence with deterministic control structures.

title: From Generative Bits to Industrial Atoms: A Sensorium-Simulation-Actuation Framework for Physics-Informed AI in Cyber-Physical Systems

detail.title: From Generative Bits to Industrial Atoms: A Sensorium-Simulation-Actuation Framework for Physics-Informed AI in Cyber-Physical Systems
detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems has produced substantial advances in natural language processing, creative content generation, and knowledge synthesis. However, the architectural assumptions underlying these systemsnotably, tolerance for probabilistic error and hallucinated outputs-render them fundamentally unsuitable for direct deployment within industrial cyber-physical systems (CPS), where operational failures carry consequences ranging from economic loss to physical harm. This paper identifies a critical gap in the literature: the absence of an integrated, deployment-ready framework that reconciles AI's probabilistic nature with the deterministic reliability demands of brownfield industrial infrastructure. To address this gap, the paper proposes the Sensorium-Simulation-Actuation (SSA) framework, a three-layer architectural model for reliable industrial AI deployment. The Sensorium layer addresses data acquisition from heterogeneous industrial sensors and legacy protocols within electromagnetically hostile environments. The Simulation layer centers on Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and bidirectional Digital Twins, which constrain AI inference within thermodynamic and physical law boundaries, eliminating physically impossible outputs. The Actuation layer translates validated intelligence into physical interventions including predictive maintenance, generative engineering, and autonomous process control. Drawing on a practitioner-informed synthesis of industry case studies, systems analysis, and comparative framework development, the paper further examines the organizational and cultural barriers-collectively termed 'Pilot Purgatory'-that prevent industrial AI from scaling beyond proof-of-concept deployments. Key findings indicate that IT/OT convergence, physics-constrained modeling, and augmented human-machine collaboration are necessary conditions for industrial AI viability. The paper contributes a structured, actionable framework for scholars, practitioners, and policymakers engaged in the strategic deployment of AI across manufacturing, energy, supply chain, and critical infrastructure domains.

title: Bidirectional Capture with Parallax-Enforced Liveness and Public Time Anchoring A Theoretical Framework for Closing Part of the Analog Hole in Controlled Capture Scenarios

detail.title: Bidirectional Capture with Parallax-Enforced Liveness and Public Time Anchoring A Theoretical Framework for Closing Part of the Analog Hole in Controlled Capture Scenarios
detail.abstract:
As generative video models approach photorealism, verifying the authenticity of recorded footage has become a pressing societal concern. Existing approaches fall into two broad categories. Post-hoc deepfake detection analyzes content for synthetic artifacts and faces a structurally disadvantaged arms race against ever-improving generators. Content-provenance frameworks such as C2PA establish that a given device signed a given pixel stream and document its edit history; this is a valuable and by now industry-standard transparency layer. C2PA is, however, explicitly not a statement about the veridicality of the depicted scene, as its designers have openly acknowledged. The gap between signed pixels and real scenes is commonly referred to as the analog hole.

This paper sketches a theoretical framework that aims to close part of the analog hole for controlled capture scenarios, and to do so as a complementary layer on top of existing provenance infrastructure rather than as a replacement. The framework combines three components: (i) two mutually filming devices whose displays continuously render coupled surrogates, forcing both devices to be physically co-present and in direct mutual observation; (ii) mandatory unpredictable device motion, which forces any scene-substitution attack to re-render the substituted content in real time with geometrically correct parallax; and (iii) time anchoring via public distributed randomness beacons (e.g., drand, NIST Randomness Beacon), which precludes retrograde timestamping and thereby enforces the real-time constraint that underpins component (ii).

The central security claim is not that the framework makes scene substitution impossible, but that it raises the adversary’s cost by orders of magnitude under a stated latency assumption, and that the magnitude of this increase is quantifiable and can be tracked as generative and rendering technology evolve. The framework is offered as a theoretical starting point. Several limitations are open, including reduced security margin against sufficiently capable light-field display hardware, the requirement for two coordinated devices, and inapplicability to spontaneous capture scenarios. The author hopes that others will identify further weaknesses and develop the concept further.

detail.abstract: Three working papers published on SSRN in April 2026 describe a spectral-stability framework for diagnosing post-merger integration health in four state variables. The framework's operational realization-an 8-indicator diagnostic instrument validated on 76 public M&A transactionsdiffers from the published theoretical object along four axes: state dimensionality, classifier architecture, stability semantics, and empirical grounding. Without the trajectory that connects them, the papers read as adjacent but partially incompatible mathematical objects. This paper reconstructs that trajectory from contemporaneous computational artifacts (47 Jupyter notebooks dated March 2 to March 31, 2026) and a git-versioned operational codebase, and documents the methodological pivot of April 16, 2026, at which the ODE-based spectral classifier was superseded by an empirical logistic-regression classifier. The classifier pivot was not a philosophical reversal but an empirical response: the convergence of a 3.9 percentage-point performance gap in favor of logistic regression and a dominant one-factor empirical structure (PC1 = 90.6% of state-vector variance on N = 76) made direct spectral classification operationally less defensible than the empirical alternative. The paper's methodological argument is that hybrid research programs spanning formal theory and operational instrumentation should be evaluated by the visibility of their trajectory, not by the polished appearance of their final artifact.

title: From Invisible to Cited: A Case Study of Generative Engine Optimisation for AI Search Recognition Among Indian Student Founders

detail.title: From Invisible to Cited: A Case Study of Generative Engine Optimisation for AI Search Recognition Among Indian Student Founders

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human subjects, clinical trials, or sensitive personal data. The research is based on publicly available information and self-conducted digital experiments; therefore, formal ethical approval was not required.

detail.abstract:
The emergence of AI-powered generative search platforms, including ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Meta AI, and Perplexity AI, has introduced a new dimension of digital visibility that conventional Search Engine Optimisation (SEO) frameworks were not designed to address. Generative Engine Optimisation (GEO) refers to the practice of structuring digital content and identity signals so that generative AI systems can accurately retrieve, synthesise, and cite a given entity in response to relevant queries.

For student founders and early-stage startups operating under common Indian names, with limited domain authority and zero advertising budgets, this challenge is both practically urgent and largely undocumented in the scholarly literature.

This paper presents a documented single-case exploratory study of a student founder at Sarala Birla University (SBU), Ranchi, India, who implemented a structured, zero-budget sequence of SEO-compatible and GEO-oriented interventions over approximately seven months. The intervention sequence comprised:
(a) keyword-aligned LinkedIn profile optimisation;
(b) a structured founder entity page on the startup domain (Dilwado.com);
(c) a static portfolio site with an identity-phrase domain slug; and
(d) two officially published institutional posts from SBU documenting verifiable achievements.

Evidence documented across fourteen original screenshots indicates that post-intervention queries produced a coherent first-page entity cluster in Google Search, entity-specific filter chips, and at least three independent entity nodes in Google Images. Furthermore, entity-aware descriptions were generated across all four major AI assistant platforms tested.

A quantitative analysis of 28 query-platform trial combinations yielded a correct-entity retrieval rate of 100% within the tested sample, compared with 0% observed in informal pre-intervention checks.

Based on these observations, a three-stage SEO–GEO Integration Model is proposed:

  1. Foundational Presence
  2. Entity Consolidation
  3. Earned Authority Signals

To the authors' knowledge, this represents one of the first screenshot-evidenced case studies of GEO implementation by a student entrepreneur at an Indian regional university. The findings suggest that institutional earned media  specifically, official university announcements of verified achievements may serve as an accessible GEO authority signal not previously identified in existing literature.

detail.abstract: The global hospitality industry is confronted by a confluence of structural pressures: persistent labor shortages, fragmented technology ecosystems, escalating operational costs, and a widening gap between guest expectations and the personalized experiences hotels can feasibly deliver at scale. Existing artificial intelligence deployments in hotel environments have largely addressed these challenges in isolation, yielding incremental improvements rather than systemic transformation. This paper introduces AURA (Adaptive Unified Resort AI), a conceptual framework for a unified, multi-module AI architecture designed to function as an integrated intelligence layer across the full spectrum of hotel operations. AURA is organized around eight interdependent hemispheres, namely the Command Bridge, Unified Guest Intelligence (UGI), Spatial Engine, Empathy Engine, PAR Intelligence, Revenue Intel, Cultural Intel, and Privacy Sovereignty, each addressing a distinct operational domain while sharing a common data substrate. The paper presents the theoretical foundations of this architecture, contextualizes it within the existing literature on hospitality technology, affective computing, revenue management, and privacy-by-design, and proposes a conceptual evaluation framework suitable for future empirical validation. Key contributions include a taxonomy of hospitality AI integration gaps, a modular architecture description with mapped data flows, a scholarly treatment of ethical and governance considerations specific to AI-augmented hospitality environments, and a forward-looking research agenda. All performance projections cited herein are illustrative, drawn from adjacent industry evidence, and await validation through controlled pilot studies.

title: When Conformity Becomes Structural: A Coupled Feedback Loop Model of Agentic AI and Principal Overconfidence

detail.title: When Conformity Becomes Structural: A Coupled Feedback Loop Model of Agentic AI and Principal Overconfidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the research reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Agentic AI systems that execute multi-step tasks with limited supervision are proliferating across professional domains, yet formal models of how these architectures reshape human-AI interaction dynamics remain underdeveloped. This paper extends the coupled feedback loop model of AI sycophancy (Gallacher, 2026a) from conversational to agentic settings, introducing two parameters absent from chatbot architectures: verification capacity (V), the fraction of agent behaviour the principal can observe, and specification clarity (σ), the precision with which task requirements can be communicated. Building on Chandra et al. (2026) and empirical findings from Gao and Xiao (2026) on conformity dynamics in AI-assisted financial analysis, we demonstrate through simulation that agentic architectures are structurally more vulnerable to coupled feedback loops than conversational systems. Under identical metrics, a chatbot baseline produces catastrophic spiralling in 4.4 per cent of simulations at π₀ = 0.3, while the agentic model produces 38.9 per cent under moderate agentic conditions (V = σ = 0.5) and 41.6 per cent under opaque conditions (V = σ = 0.3), an amplification of 8.7 times to 9.4 times over the chatbot baseline. At low initial conformity (π₀ = 0), the amplification exceeds twenty-fold. Conformity emerges endogenously from zero initial rates under all tested update rules. Informed users who perform joint inference over task adequacy and agent conformity achieve 62 to 93 per cent reduction in spiral rates across a range of tested prior shapes, with protection largest under the agentic conditions where naive users are most vulnerable. These findings reframe agentic AI governance as a principal-agent problem where process opacity and specification ambiguity create structural conditions for the coupling dynamics that conversational sycophancy models first identified.

title: Buying the Right to Monitor: Editorial Design in AI-Assisted Peer Review
affiliations: Universite du Luxembourg - Luxembourg School of Finance

detail.title: Buying the Right to Monitor: Editorial Design in AI-Assisted Peer Review
detail.abstract: Generative AI acts as a disruptive technological shock to evaluative organizations. In academic peer review, it enters both sides of the market: authors use AI to polish submissions, and reviewers use it to generate plausible reports without exerting evaluative effort. We develop a three-sided equilibrium model to analyze this dual adoption and derive a counterintuitive managerial implication for journal policy. We show that when AI capability crosses a critical threshold, reviewer effort collapses discontinuously. This transition creates a welfare misalignment: authors benefit from a weakened "rat race," while editors suffer from degraded signal informativeness. Characterizing the editor's optimal constrained response, we identify a strict policy reversal. Before the AI transition, editors should tighten acceptance standards to curb rent-dissipating author polishing. After the transition, conventional intuition fails: editors must loosen acceptance standards while investing in AI detection, because further tightening only amplifies dissipative polishing without improving sorting. We prove analytically that this sign reversal is a structural consequence of the reviewer effort collapse under log-concave quality distributions. Ultimately, addressing AI in evaluative systems requires treating monitoring and loosened selectivity as complementary design instruments.

detail.abstract: This paper compares specialized object detection systems and general-purpose multimodal vision-language models (VLMs) on the task of Euro coin identification from images. YOLObased detectors are trained in a supervised manner using images from the same dataset, whereas VLMs are evaluated in a zero-shot, prompt-based setting without task-specific fine-tuning. Performance is assessed using coin-level metrics, with predictions aggregated over multiple inference seeds to account for stochastic variability. The results show that YOLO models achieve the highest and most consistent performance, reflecting their task-specific design and training. Most VLMs exhibit lower accuracy and greater image-dependent variability. Notably, GPT-4.1 stands out among VLMs, achieving per-image F1 performance that is competitive with several YOLO variants despite its general-purpose nature. Statistical analysis confirms significant differences between model families and indicates that performance differences within each family are often not statistically distinguishable. Overall, the findings highlight the continued advantage of specialized detectors for coin identification, while demonstrating that high-capability generalpurpose VLMs can approach detector-level performance on structured visual recognition tasks without task-specific training.

title: The Translation Trap: A Governance System for Strategic Drift and Institutional Alignment

detail.title: The Translation Trap: A Governance System for Strategic Drift and Institutional Alignment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
A green dashboard does not mean an institution is funding the right things.

Organizations can appear aligned and high-performing while drifting from their stated purpose. This paper argues that this is not primarily a failure of execution, but a consequence of how intent is translated into decision-making. To guide action, intent must be converted into criteria, metrics, and allocation rules—representations that can come to define what counts as success.

The paper introduces Translation Drift: a condition in which decision systems optimize for these representations rather than for the intent they were meant to serve. It further identifies the Double Translation Trap, in which a proxy both guides allocation and serves as the standard by which success is evaluated, making drift difficult to detect.

The paper contributes a practical diagnostic framework that makes this drift observable at the point of allocation by revealing what the system is actually selecting for—enabling institutions to test and correct misalignment before resources are committed.

title: The Governance Gauntlet: A Dual-Rubric Extension of Karpathy's Auto-Research Loop Detecting Silent Metric-Gaming in Recursive Self-Improvement Systems Working Paper

detail.title: The Governance Gauntlet: A Dual-Rubric Extension of Karpathy's Auto-Research Loop Detecting Silent Metric-Gaming in Recursive Self-Improvement Systems Working Paper

detail.abstract: The Karpathy Loop, released in early March 2026 (Karpathy, 2026), has given the machine-learning community a minimal and reproducible recipe for auto-research: a meta-agent edits a single surface of code, a scalar metric is computed, and the edit is kept or reverted. The pattern is already being generalized beyond training-code optimization into harness engineering (Gu, 2026), into production code (Lütke, 2026), and into infrastructure-scale execution platforms (SkyPilot Team, 2026). This working paper accepts Karpathy's design as sound and asks a narrower question: what additional structure is required before the pattern is safe to deploy inside enterprise production systems, regulated domains, or any setting where the meta-agent has access to the metric it is optimizing? We identify one class of failure mode that the canonical loop does not address: silent metric-gaming, in which the meta-agent improves the scalar without improving the underlying capability. Drawing on Manheim and Garrabrant's (2018) four Goodhart variants, Krakovna et al.'s specification-gaming catalog, and Hubinger et al.'s (2019) mesaoptimization framing, we formalize the vulnerability and propose the Governance Gauntlet, a minimal dual-rubric extension in which an adversarial auditor meta-agent issues a binary CLEAN / QUESTIONABLE / GAMING verdict on every proposed edit and its trace. The keep-or-revert rule becomes: accept the edit if and only if the primary scalar improves and the auditor verdict is not GAMING. The construction preserves Karpathy's minimalism, bounds compute at two times the vanilla loop, and is orthogonal to multi-objective optimization. We pre-register a six-subject empirical evaluation (Subject α, Subject β, four gaming archetypes, three arms) on the Open Science Framework and release this version as the priority-date pre-registration; empirical fills follow in v2 within the publication window. The broader implication is that the Karpathy pattern is a public good, and safe deployment requires a standing adversarial check built in the same minimal spirit.
